cards.statement: Returns having lighter tails than the lognormal distribution (platykurtosis) explain a downward-sloping implied volatility term structure.
cards.explanation: Tail thickness affects the shape of the smile across strikes, not the slope of the term structure across maturities.
cards.originalText: Returns have lighter tails than the lognormal distribution (platykurtosis)

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: If volatility follows a GARCH(1,1) process, the implied volatility term structure slopes up when current volatility is below its long-run level and down when it is above.
cards.explanation: GARCH volatility mean reverts to a long-run level, so expected average volatility over longer horizons moves from the current level toward the long-run level.
cards.originalText: It slopes up if current volatility is below the long‑run level and down if it is above

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: If volatility follows a GARCH(1,1) process, the implied volatility term structure is always upward sloping.
cards.explanation: Because GARCH volatility mean reverts, high current volatility reverts downward and produces a downward-sloping term structure.
cards.originalText: It is always upward sloping
cards.correction: If volatility follows a GARCH(1,1) process, the implied volatility term structure slopes upward only when current volatility is below its long-run level.

changes.to: slopes upward only when current volatility is below its long-run level

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: If volatility follows a GARCH(1,1) process, the implied volatility term structure is flat because GARCH volatility is constant.
cards.explanation: GARCH volatility is time-varying and mean reverting, so the term structure is generally not flat.
cards.originalText: It is flat, because GARCH volatility is constant

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: When marking a book of options to market in the presence of a volatility smile, each option should be valued using the implied volatility of the most similar option tradable in the market.
cards.explanation: Each strike and maturity has its own implied volatility, so marking with the market-implied volatility for that strike and maturity is market-consistent, whereas a single volatility ignores the smile.
cards.originalText: For each option, use the implied volatility of the most similar option tradable on the market.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: With a pronounced volatility smile, all options in a book should be marked using the at-the-money implied volatility.
cards.explanation: A single at-the-money volatility ignores the smile, misstates the value of out-of-the-money options and is not market-consistent.
cards.originalText: Use the implied volatility of at‑the‑money options, since volatility estimation is more reliable there.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: With a flat implied volatility curve, the delta of a call option falls as the stock price falls and the option moves out of the money.
cards.explanation: With no smile the delta is the standard BSM $N(d_1)$, which increases with $S/K$, so it falls as the stock falls and the call becomes less in the money.
cards.originalText: Delta falls below 0.5

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: When implied volatility is a decreasing function of $K/S$, as with equity crashophobia, a rise in the stock price moves an option along the skew to a higher implied volatility, so the sensitivity of its price to the stock price, ignoring any shift of the whole curve, exceeds the BSM delta.
cards.explanation: A higher stock price lowers $K/S$ and moves the option to a higher-volatility point on the skew. Positive vega converts this into extra option value on top of the BSM delta.
cards.originalText: It is higher, because the rise in S lowers K/S and moves the option to a point with higher implied volatility

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: When implied volatility is an increasing function of $K/S$, a rise in the stock price moves an option along the smile to a lower implied volatility, so the sensitivity of its price to the stock price, ignoring any shift of the whole curve, is lower than the BSM delta.
cards.explanation: A higher stock price lowers $K/S$, which here means lower implied volatility, so the vega term subtracts from the BSM delta.
cards.originalText: It is lower, because the stock rise lowers K/S and moves the option to a point with lower implied volatility

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: When equity prices and implied volatilities are negatively correlated, the shift of the whole implied volatility curve tends to dominate the movement along it, so the minimum variance delta is lower than the BSM delta.
cards.explanation: The negative correlation moves the whole curve down when the stock rises, outweighing the move along the skew to higher volatility. The volatility used therefore falls as the stock rises, lowering the delta.
cards.originalText: The shift of the whole implied volatility curve tends to dominate the movement along it, so the minimum variance delta is lower than the BSM delta

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: For equity options, the minimum variance delta is higher than the BSM delta.
cards.explanation: Because the whole-curve shift dominates, the minimum variance delta is lower than the BSM delta for equity options.
cards.originalText: The minimum variance delta is higher than the BSM delta
cards.correction: For equity options, the minimum variance delta is lower than the BSM delta.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: The BSM delta already incorporates changes in implied volatility, so it equals the minimum variance delta.
cards.explanation: The BSM delta assumes volatility stays constant and so ignores changes in implied volatility; the minimum variance delta accounts for them.
cards.originalText: The BSM delta already incorporates changes in implied volatility, so it equals the minimum variance delta

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: Under the Black-Scholes-Merton model, vega is always positive and highest for an at-the-money option, but these properties do not predict any particular shape of the implied volatility smile.
cards.explanation: Vega is a model-based sensitivity of price to volatility, whereas the smile is market-implied volatility plotted against strike. A skew, smirk, frown or other shape is therefore allowed.
cards.originalText: Under the Black‑Scholes‑Merton model, vega is always positive and highest for an at‑the‑money option, but these properties do not predict any particular shape of the implied volatility smile; a skew, smirk, frown or other shape is allowed

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: If the implied volatility smile is a perfectly flat, horizontal line, an increase in strike price has no effect on an option's price.
cards.explanation: A flat smile only means the same volatility applies to every strike; a higher strike still lowers a call's price and raises a put's price because moneyness changes.
cards.originalText: If the implied volatility smile is a perfectly flat, horizontal line, then an increase in strike price has no effect on the option’s price

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: If the implied volatility smile is a perfectly flat, horizontal line, vega is zero.
cards.explanation: Vega is the sensitivity of the option price to volatility and stays positive even when volatility is the same across strikes.
cards.originalText: If the implied volatility smile is a perfectly flat, horizontal line, then Greek vega is zero

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: Vega is the first derivative of the implied volatility smile, i.e. it plots the slopes of lines tangent to the implied volatility plot.
cards.explanation: Vega is the derivative of the option price with respect to volatility; the slope of the smile is the derivative of implied volatility with respect to strike.
cards.originalText: Vega is the first derivative of the implied volatility smile; i.e., it plots the slopes of lines tangent to the implied volatility plot

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: For equity options with a pronounced skew, a rise in the stock price shifts the whole implied volatility curve down and this dominates the move along the curve, so the minimum variance delta is below the Black-Scholes-Merton delta for both calls and puts.
cards.explanation: Equity prices and volatility are negatively correlated, so a rising price lowers the whole implied volatility curve. This shift outweighs the move along the curve and makes the true (minimum variance) delta smaller than the BSM delta.
cards.originalText: True call delta is lower than 0.60 and true put delta is lower than −0.40

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: When an equity price changes, the effect of the implied volatility curve moving up or down tends to dominate the effect of moving along the existing curve.
cards.explanation: Because equity prices and volatility are negatively correlated, a price rise shifts the whole curve down. In practice this shift outweighs the movement along the curve, which is why the minimum variance delta is lower than the BSM delta.
cards.originalText: When equity prices change, the effect from movements in the implied volatility curve up or down tends to dominate movements along the existing curve.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: For equity options, the minimum variance delta is higher than the Black-Scholes-Merton delta.
cards.explanation: For equity options the minimum variance delta is lower than the BSM delta, because the downward shift of the implied volatility curve as the price rises dominates the move along the curve.
cards.originalText: The minimum variance delta will be higher than the Black‑Scholes‑Merton model delta.
cards.correction: For equity options, the minimum variance delta is lower than the Black-Scholes-Merton delta.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: If equity prices and volatilities are positively correlated, an equity price increase will move the entire implied volatility curve down.
cards.explanation: The curve falls when the price rises because equity prices and volatilities are negatively correlated, not positively correlated.
cards.originalText: If equity prices and volatilities are positively correlated, equity price increases will move the entire option curve down.
cards.correction: If equity prices and volatilities are negatively correlated, an equity price increase will move the entire implied volatility curve down.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: When a stock faces a single anticipated price jump, the terminal distribution is bimodal and implied volatility is hump-shaped (a frown), highest for strikes near the money and lower away from the money.
cards.explanation: A one-off jump produces a bimodal distribution, so at-the-money options are the expensive ones. Implied volatility therefore peaks around the middle strikes and falls toward the extremes, the opposite of the currency smile.
cards.originalText: p = 0.40; implied volatility is hump‑shaped (a frown), about 47.8% at K = \$40, falling to about 40.4% at K = \$80

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: A single anticipated price jump produces a U-shaped implied volatility smile with its minimum near the at-the-money strike.
cards.explanation: A U-shaped smile is the pattern for fat tails on both sides, as in currencies. A single anticipated jump gives a bimodal distribution and a hump-shaped implied volatility pattern (a frown) with the highest volatility near the money.
cards.originalText: p = 0.40; implied volatility is U‑shaped (a smile) with its minimum near the \$60 strike

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Evaluate estimators of risk measures by estimating their standard errors.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Confidence intervals based on the quantile standard error are symmetric, which makes them the most reliable approach for extreme quantiles such as the 99.9% VaR.
cards.explanation: Symmetry is a weakness of the quantile standard-error approach for extreme quantiles, whose true confidence intervals are asymmetric, so it is not the most reliable approach there.
cards.originalText: The interval narrows, and because the quantile standard error gives symmetric intervals it is the most reliable approach for extreme quantiles such as the 99.9% VaR.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Evaluate estimators of risk measures by estimating their standard errors.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Widening the bin around the quantile widens the confidence interval for a VaR estimate, because a wider bin admits more observations and therefore more sampling noise.
cards.explanation: A wider bin raises the estimated density $f(q)$ and so lowers the standard error, which narrows the interval rather than widening it.
cards.originalText: The interval should have widened, because a wider bin admits more observations and therefore more sampling noise around the quantile.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Evaluate estimators of risk measures by estimating their standard errors.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: The 99% VaR estimate is less precise than the 95% VaR estimate, because the probability mass around the quantile falls faster than $p(1 - p)$ as the quantile moves into the tail.
cards.explanation: Moving into the tail lowers $p(1-p)$ but lowers the density $f(q)$ much more, so the standard error rises. The more extreme the quantile, the less precise its estimator.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Evaluate estimators of risk measures by estimating their standard errors.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: The 99% VaR estimate is more precise than the 95% VaR estimate, because $p(1-p)$ is smaller at $p = 0.01$ than at $p = 0.05$.
cards.explanation: The smaller $p(1-p)$ is outweighed by the much smaller density $f(q)$ in the tail, so the 99% VaR estimator is less precise than the 95% one.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Evaluate estimators of risk measures by estimating their standard errors.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Expected shortfall estimators always have smaller standard errors than VaR estimators, because averaging tail quantiles removes the effect of large but infrequent losses.
cards.explanation: Heavy tails make expected shortfall estimators prone to large but infrequent losses, and for heavy-tailed distributions their standard errors can be much larger than those of VaR. Neither result says expected shortfall is always more precise.
cards.originalText: ES estimators always have smaller standard errors than VaR estimators, because averaging tail quantiles removes the effect of large but infrequent losses.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Evaluate estimators of risk measures by estimating their standard errors.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Once a sample exceeds 1,000 observations, the standard error of a risk-measure estimate no longer needs to be reported alongside the risk measure.
cards.explanation: No sample size makes the standard error irrelevant. It should be reported alongside the risk estimate whatever the sample size.
cards.originalText: Once the sample exceeds 1,000 observations, the standard error no longer needs to be reported alongside the risk measure.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Interpret quantile-quantile (QQ) plots to identify the characteristics of a distribution.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: If the points of a QQ plot against standard normal quantiles lie close to a straight line, the data are consistent with a normal distribution whose mean is given by the intercept and whose standard deviation is given by the slope.
cards.explanation: A linear QQ plot means the empirical distribution has the same shape as the reference up to a linear transformation. The intercept estimates the location and the slope estimates the scale.
cards.originalText: The P/L is consistent with a normal distribution with a mean of about USD 5,000 and a standard deviation of about USD 40,000.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Interpret quantile-quantile (QQ) plots to identify the characteristics of a distribution.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: If a QQ plot of data against standard normal quantiles is a straight line that does not follow the 45-degree line, the data cannot be normally distributed.
cards.explanation: A different intercept or slope only means a different mean or standard deviation. Departure from normality shows up as bending of the plot, not as a line that is off the 45-degree line.
cards.originalText: The P/L is not normal, because the plot does not follow the 45-degree line.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Interpret quantile-quantile (QQ) plots to identify the characteristics of a distribution.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: A positive intercept in a straight-line QQ plot of data against standard normal quantiles indicates that the data are positively skewed.
cards.explanation: The intercept measures location (the mean). Skewness appears as an asymmetric bend in the plot, not as a straight line with a non-zero intercept.
cards.originalText: The P/L is positively skewed, because the intercept of the line is above zero.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Describe the Gaussian copula and explain how to use it to derive the joint probability of default of two assets.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: In a one-factor Gaussian copula model, once the common factor is realised the obligors' defaults are independent, so all default dependence enters through the obligors' loadings on that factor.
cards.explanation: Fixing the common factor leaves only the independent idiosyncratic shocks random, so defaults are conditionally independent. The pairwise correlation comes entirely from the factor loadings.
cards.originalText: Once the common factor is realised, the obligors’ defaults are independent, so all default dependence in the model enters through the obligors’ loadings on that factor.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Describe the Gaussian copula and explain how to use it to derive the joint probability of default of two assets.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: A one-factor Gaussian copula model assumes that the obligors' times to default are jointly normally distributed, so each obligor's marginal default-time distribution must itself be normal.
cards.explanation: The copula maps each time to default percentile-to-percentile into a standard normal variable and assumes only those transformed variables are multivariate normal. The marginal default-time distributions can take any shape.
cards.originalText: The model assumes that the obligors’ times to default are jointly normally distributed, so each obligor’s marginal default-time distribution must itself be normal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Describe the Gaussian copula and explain how to use it to derive the joint probability of default of two assets.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: In a one-factor Gaussian copula model, conditional on a negative realisation of the common factor, an obligor with a higher factor loading has a lower conditional default probability than an otherwise identical obligor.
cards.explanation: When the common factor is negative, a higher loading pushes the obligor's conditional mean further down and its conditional default probability up, so cyclical firms suffer more in a downturn.
cards.originalText: Conditional on a negative realisation of the common factor, an obligor with a higher factor loading has a lower conditional default probability than an otherwise identical obligor.
cards.correction: In a one-factor Gaussian copula model, conditional on a negative realisation of the common factor, an obligor with a higher factor loading has a higher conditional default probability than an otherwise identical obligor.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Describe the Gaussian copula and explain how to use it to derive the joint probability of default of two assets.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: In a Gaussian copula model calibrated to standard index tranche prices, the calibrated correlation is a real-world parameter estimated from the historical default experience of the obligors in the index.
cards.explanation: The implied correlation is inferred from market prices using risk-neutral default probabilities from single-name CDS spreads. It is a risk-neutral market parameter, not a historical estimate.
cards.originalText: The correlation calibrated to the tranche prices is a real-world parameter, estimated from the historical default experience of the obligors in the index.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) and lognormal models.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: The CIR and lognormal short-rate distributions are non-negative and right-skewed, so out-of-the-money option prices can differ significantly from the normal model's even when the means and standard deviations are matched.
cards.explanation: Matching the mean and standard deviation fixes the centre and spread but not the shape. Out-of-the-money options depend on tail probabilities, which differ across the normal, CIR and lognormal shapes.
cards.originalText: The CIR and lognormal distributions are non-negative and right-skewed, so out-of-the-money option prices can differ significantly from the normal model’s.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) and lognormal models.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: Short-rate models whose terminal distributions have the same mean and standard deviation will give the same prices for out-of-the-money interest rate options.
cards.explanation: Two matched moments do not make the tails equal, and out-of-the-money option prices depend on the tails, so the prices can differ significantly.
cards.originalText: Because the three distributions share the same mean and standard deviation, the models will give the same prices for out-of-the-money interest rate options.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) and lognormal models.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: The CIR distribution of the short rate is left-skewed with a floor at the long-run level $\theta$, while the lognormal distribution is symmetric.
cards.explanation: The CIR distribution is right-skewed with a floor at zero, not at $\theta$, and the lognormal distribution is also right-skewed rather than symmetric.
cards.originalText: The CIR distribution is left-skewed with a floor at the long-run level $\theta$, while the lognormal distribution is symmetric around 5%.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) and lognormal models.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: A trader who believes volatility is constant, that negative rates barely affect the prices of her securities, and that computational simplicity is valuable can defend a constant basis-point volatility model even though it allows some probability of negative rates.
cards.explanation: A model that allows some probability of negative rates may be reasonable when that probability has little effect on prices and simplicity has great value. Non-negativity is not a requirement that overrides every other consideration.
cards.originalText: A constant basis-point volatility model, accepting that it allows some probability of negative rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) and lognormal models.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: Any short-rate model that allows a positive probability of negative rates must be rejected regardless of its purpose.
cards.explanation: Models with some probability of negative rates are acceptable when that probability barely affects the prices of the securities being valued and simplicity is valuable.
cards.originalText: The CIR model, because any model that allows negative rates must be rejected regardless of purpose.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) and lognormal models.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: The lognormal short-rate model has a constant basis-point volatility.
cards.explanation: In the lognormal model the basis-point volatility is $\sigma r$ and rises with the rate; it is the yield volatility that is constant. Only the normal model has constant basis-point volatility.
cards.originalText: A lognormal model, because its basis-point volatility is constant and it cannot produce negative rates.
cards.correction: The lognormal short-rate model has a constant yield volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) and lognormal models.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: The terminal distribution of the CIR short rate is normal.
cards.explanation: The CIR terminal distribution is non-negative and right-skewed, not normal. The normal terminal distribution belongs to the constant basis-point volatility model.
cards.originalText: The CIR model, because its terminal distribution is normal and therefore simpler to compute with.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: The lognormal model with deterministic drift, $dr = a(t) r dt + \sigma r dw$, is a Ho-Lee-type process with time-dependent drift applied to the natural logarithm of the short rate, so the short rate is lognormal and every node of its tree is positive.
cards.explanation: By Ito's lemma $\ln r$ follows a Ho-Lee process with a deterministic, time-dependent drift, so $\ln r$ is normal and $r$ is lognormal. Every node is $r_0 e^{(\cdot)} > 0$.
cards.originalText: The natural logarithm of the short rate follows a Ho-Lee-type process with a time-dependent drift, so the short rate is lognormal and every node of its tree is positive.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: In the lognormal short-rate model with deterministic drift, the natural logarithm of the short rate reverts toward a time-dependent central tendency $\ln \theta(t)$.
cards.explanation: Reversion toward $\ln \theta(t)$ describes the Black-Karasinski model, the lognormal model with mean reversion. The deterministic-drift lognormal model has no mean reversion.
cards.originalText: The natural logarithm of the short rate reverts toward a time-dependent central tendency ln $\theta(t)$, so the short rate is lognormal and every node of its tree is positive.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: In the lognormal short-rate model with deterministic drift, the short rate follows a Ho-Lee-type process with time-dependent drift, so the short rate is normal and low nodes of its tree may become negative.
cards.explanation: The Ho-Lee process is applied to the logarithm of the short rate, not to the rate itself. The short rate is therefore lognormal and every node of its tree is positive.
cards.originalText: The short rate follows a Ho-Lee-type process with a time-dependent drift, so the short rate is normal and low nodes of its tree may become negative.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: In the lognormal short-rate model $dr = a(t) r dt + \sigma r dw$, the basis-point volatility of the short rate is proportional to the square root of the rate.
cards.explanation: Basis-point volatility proportional to the square root of the rate describes the CIR model. In the lognormal model the basis-point volatility is $\sigma r$, proportional to the rate itself.
cards.originalText: The basis-point volatility of the short rate is proportional to the square root of the rate, so the short rate is non-negative but not lognormal.
cards.correction: In the lognormal short-rate model $dr = a(t) r dt + \sigma r dw$, the basis-point volatility of the short rate is proportional to the rate.

changes.from: the square root of the rate

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: In the Black-Karasinski model, mean reversion controls the term structure of volatility while time-dependent volatility controls the future volatility of the short rate, so the two should be chosen independently.
cards.explanation: Tying mean reversion to the time-dependent volatility function would let one determine the other. Because they serve distinct purposes, the time step is allowed to vary so that both remain free.
cards.originalText: Mean reversion controls the term structure of volatility while time-dependent volatility controls the future volatility of the short rate, so the two must be chosen independently.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: In the Black-Karasinski model, mean reversion controls the future volatility of the short rate while time-dependent volatility controls the term structure of volatility.
cards.explanation: The roles are the other way round: mean reversion controls the term structure of volatility, and time-dependent volatility controls the future volatility of the short rate.
cards.originalText: Mean reversion controls the future volatility of the short rate while time-dependent volatility controls the term structure of volatility, so the two must be chosen independently.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Explain how the parameters of the Gauss+ model can be estimated from empirical data.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: When estimating the Gauss+ model, the short-term rate is proxied by the fed funds target rate, because general collateral repo rates show occasional idiosyncratic jumps that complicate the estimation without significant offsetting advantages.
cards.explanation: A general collateral repo rate is theoretically more consistent with a Treasury term structure, but its idiosyncratic jumps complicate estimation. The fed funds target is chosen for practical reasons.
cards.originalText: The fed funds target rate, because general collateral repo rates show occasional idiosyncratic jumps that complicate the estimation without significant offsetting advantages.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Explain how the parameters of the Gauss+ model can be estimated from empirical data.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: When estimating the Gauss+ model, a general collateral repo rate is preferred as the short-term rate proxy because its jumps make the estimated volatility more realistic.
cards.explanation: The idiosyncratic jumps of repo rates are the reason they are not used: they complicate the estimation without significant offsetting advantages, so the fed funds target rate is used instead.
cards.originalText: A general collateral repo rate, because it is theoretically more consistent with a Treasury term structure and its jumps make the estimated volatility more realistic.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Explain how the parameters of the Gauss+ model can be estimated from empirical data.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Gauss+ model, the short-term rate $r$ has its own random shock.
cards.explanation: In the Gauss+ model the short rate has no separate random shock of its own; the randomness comes from the medium- and long-term factors, which have the volatility parameters $\sigma_{m}$ and $\sigma_{l}$.
cards.originalText: The fed funds target rate, because the short-term rate in the Gauss+ model carries its own random shock that must match fed funds volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Explain how the parameters of the Gauss+ model can be estimated from empirical data.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In estimating the Gauss+ model, regression coefficients of changes in zero yields on changes in the 2-year and 10-year yields are used to choose the mean reversion parameters $\alpha_{r}$, $\alpha_{m}$ and $\alpha_{l}$ so that the model's implied coefficients match them as closely as possible.
cards.explanation: These regression coefficients implicitly describe the mean reversion parameters of the model. This stage chooses the three reversion speeds so the model's implied coefficients match the empirical ones.
cards.originalText: These coeﬀicients are used to choose $\alpha_{r}$, $\alpha_{m}$ and $\alpha_{l}$ so that the model’s implied coeﬀicients match them as closely as possible.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Explain how the parameters of the Gauss+ model can be estimated from empirical data.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In estimating the Gauss+ model, regression coefficients of changes in zero yields on changes in the 2-year and 10-year yields are used to choose the volatility parameters $\sigma_{m}$ and $\sigma_{l}$ and the correlation $\rho$.
cards.explanation: The regression coefficients identify the mean reversion speeds. The volatility parameters and $\rho$ are matched to the volatility term structure instead.
cards.originalText: These coeﬀicients are used to choose $\sigma_{m}$, $\sigma_{l}$ and $\rho$ so that the model’s implied coeﬀicients match them as closely as possible.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Explain how the parameters of the Gauss+ model can be estimated from empirical data.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In estimating the Gauss+ model, regression coefficients of changes in zero yields on changes in the 2-year and 10-year yields are used to choose $\mu$.
cards.explanation: The regression coefficients identify the mean reversion speeds. The long-run level $\mu$ is estimated last, from yield levels.
cards.originalText: These coeﬀicients are used to choose $\mu$, because the coeﬀicients shift with the level of long-term yields.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Explain how the parameters of the Gauss+ model can be estimated from empirical data.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Gauss+ model, the medium- and long-term factors $m$ and $l$ are by construction equal to the one-year rates two and ten years forward.
cards.explanation: The factors are chosen each day so that the model matches those forward rates, but they are in no way those forward rates themselves. How each forward rate relates to $m$ and $l$ depends on the estimated parameters.
cards.originalText: The medium- and long-term factors $m$ and $l$ are, by construction, equal to the one-year rates two and ten years forward.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Explain how the parameters of the Gauss+ model can be estimated from empirical data.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Gauss+ model, the fitted forward rates are fair by construction, and the relation of every forward rate to the factors $m$ and $l$ depends on the estimated parameters, especially the mean reversion speeds.
cards.explanation: Matching the fed funds target and the two- and ten-year forwards makes those points fair by construction. The factors themselves are not those forwards, and how other rates load on them depends on the mean reversion speeds.
cards.originalText: The fitted forwards are fair by construction, and the relation of every forward rate to $m$ and $l$ depends on the estimated parameters, especially the mean reversion speeds.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Explain how the parameters of the Gauss+ model can be estimated from empirical data.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Gauss+ model, because the fitted forwards are fair by construction, every other point on the curve is also fair, so the model cannot identify rich or cheap securities.
cards.explanation: Only the fitted points are fair by construction. The model is used for relative value precisely because other points on the curve can differ from model values.
cards.originalText: Because the fitted forwards are fair by construction, every other point on the curve is also fair, so the model cannot identify rich or cheap securities.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: When implied volatility is plotted against the strike price, the curve moves to the right as the asset price rises because the at-the-money strike rises with the asset price, which is why implied volatility is usually plotted against $K/S_{0}$ instead.
cards.explanation: The relationship between implied volatility and $K$ depends on the asset price, so the central at-the-money strike drifts with it. Plotting against $K/S_{0}$ removes that drift.
cards.originalText: The curve moved right because the at-the-money strike rises with the asset price; this is why implied volatility is usually plotted against $K/S_{0}$ instead.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: Plotting implied volatility against the strike price is preferred to plotting it against $K/S_{0}$, because the strike is fixed by contract while $K/S_{0}$ changes every day.
cards.explanation: The drift of the strike axis with the asset price is exactly why $K/S_{0}$ is preferred. Plotted against $K/S_{0}$, the curve does not move as the asset price changes.
cards.originalText: Plotting against the strike is preferred, because the strike is fixed by contract while $K/S_{0}$ changes every day.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: Smiles are plotted against $K/F_{0}$ and an at-the-money option is defined as $K = F_{0}$, because $F_{0}$, not $S_{0}$, is the expected value of the underlying on the option's maturity date in a risk-neutral world.
cards.explanation: The forward price for the option's maturity is the risk-neutral expectation of the asset price on that date, which makes it the natural reference point for at-the-money.
cards.originalText: $F_{0}$, not $S_{0}$, is the expected value of the underlying on the option’s maturity date in a risk-neutral world.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: The forward price $F_{0}$ equals the spot price $S_{0}$ whenever interest rates are positive, so the two at-the-money definitions always coincide.
cards.explanation: $F_{0} = S_{0}e^{(r-q)T}$ differs from $S_{0}$ whenever the net carry is not zero, so defining at-the-money by $K = F_{0}$ generally differs from defining it by $K = S_{0}$.
cards.originalText: $F_{0}$ equals $S_{0}$ whenever interest rates are positive, so the two at-the-money definitions always coincide.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: A strike equal to the forward price is the only strike at which a call has a delta of exactly 0.5 and a put has a delta of exactly +0.5.
cards.explanation: A put's delta is negative, so a 50-delta put has a delta of $-0.5$. Defining at-the-money by delta is a different convention from defining it as $K = F_{0}$.
cards.originalText: $K = F_{0}$ is the only strike at which a call has a delta of exactly 0.5 and a put a delta of exactly +0.5.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: Plotting the smile against $K/F_{0}$ makes it independent of the option's maturity without any further adjustment.
cards.explanation: Removing most of the maturity dependence needs the scaled measure $\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}} \ln(K/F_{0})$, not $K/F_{0}$ alone.
cards.originalText: Using $K/F_{0}$ makes the smile independent of the option’s maturity without any further adjustment.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: When the volatility smile is defined as the relationship between implied volatility and delta, an at-the-money option is a call with a delta of 0.5 or a put with a delta of $-0.5$.
cards.explanation: These are the 50-delta options. Because a put's delta equals the call's delta minus one when there are no dividends, a 0.5-delta call and a $-0.5$-delta put at the same strike are consistent.
cards.originalText: As a call with a delta of 0.5 or a put with a delta of −0.5.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: When the volatility smile is defined as the relationship between implied volatility and delta, an at-the-money option is any option whose strike equals the current asset price, whatever its delta.
cards.explanation: That is the strike-based definition. Under the delta approach, at-the-money means a 50-delta option, which is generally not the $K = S_{0}$ option.
cards.originalText: As any option whose strike equals the current asset price, whatever its delta.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: Plotting implied volatility against $\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}} \ln(K/F_{0})$ makes smiles for different maturities lie closer together than plotting against $K$ or $K/S_{0}$.
cards.explanation: Smiles become less pronounced as maturity increases, so curves for different maturities differ when plotted against $K$ or $K/S_{0}$. Scaling the log moneyness by $1/\sqrt{T}$ makes the smile much less dependent on maturity.
cards.originalText: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}} \text{ln}(\frac{K}{F_{0}})$

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: In a volatility surface, entries for options with reliable market data are implied volatilities calculated directly from their market prices, and the remaining entries are typically filled by interpolation.
cards.explanation: The surface is anchored to traded prices where they exist. Entries without reliable market data are typically interpolated.
cards.originalText: Entries for options with reliable market data are implied volatilities calculated directly from their market prices; the rest of the table is typically filled by interpolation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: All entries of a volatility surface are historical volatilities measured over a window equal to each option's maturity and then adjusted for the strike.
cards.explanation: A volatility surface holds implied volatilities backed out from option prices, not historical volatilities.
cards.originalText: All entries are historical volatilities measured over a window equal to each option’s maturity, then adjusted for the strike.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: The entries of a volatility surface are option prices rather than volatilities, so a trader reads the price of a new option straight from the surface.
cards.explanation: The surface holds implied volatilities. The price of a new option comes from putting the looked-up volatility into the Black-Scholes-Merton formula or a binomial tree.
cards.originalText: Entries are BSM option prices rather than volatilities, and a trader reads the price of a new option straight from the table.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: When a stock faces a binary announcement that will move its price to one of two levels, the distribution of the price afterwards is bimodal, with probability concentrated around the two post-announcement prices rather than around the current price.
cards.explanation: The price is a mixture of two lognormals, one around each post-announcement level. The mixture can share its mean and standard deviation with a lognormal; only the shape differs.
cards.originalText: The true distribution is bimodal, with probability concentrated around the two post-decision prices rather than around \$50.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: When implied volatility forms a frown, peaking near the money, using the at-the-money implied volatility to price the in-the-money and out-of-the-money options overprices them.
cards.explanation: The options away from the money have lower implied volatilities than the at-the-money option, so pricing them with the at-the-money volatility is too high and overprices them.
cards.originalText: The pattern is a frown, so using the implied volatility of the \$50-strike option would overprice the \$44 and \$56 options.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: When implied volatility forms a frown, peaking near the money, using the at-the-money implied volatility to price the in-the-money and out-of-the-money options underprices them.
cards.explanation: Away from the money the implied volatilities are lower than at the money, so using the at-the-money volatility is too high and overprices these options.
cards.originalText: The pattern is a frown, so using the implied volatility of the \$50-strike option would under-price the \$44 and \$56 options.
cards.correction: When implied volatility forms a frown, peaking near the money, using the at-the-money implied volatility to price the in-the-money and out-of-the-money options overprices them.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: A single anticipated price jump produces a frown, with at-the-money implied volatility the highest, while heavy tails on both sides produce a smile, with at-the-money implied volatility the lowest.
cards.explanation: A bimodal distribution makes at-the-money options the expensive ones, giving a frown. Heavy tails on both sides make deep in- and out-of-the-money options expensive, giving a smile.
cards.originalText: A single anticipated price jump produces a frown, with at-the-money implied volatility the highest; heavy tails on both sides produce a smile, with at-the-money implied volatility the lowest.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: A single anticipated price jump produces a smile, with at-the-money implied volatility the lowest, while heavy tails on both sides produce a frown, with at-the-money implied volatility the highest.
cards.explanation: The two causes are swapped: a single jump produces a frown and heavy tails on both sides produce a smile.
cards.originalText: A single anticipated price jump produces a smile, with at-the-money implied volatility the lowest; heavy tails on both sides produce a frown, with at-the-money implied volatility the highest.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.loText: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a volatility smile.
cards.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
cards.statement: A single anticipated price jump produces a frown, with at-the-money implied volatility the lowest, while heavy tails on both sides produce a smile, with at-the-money implied volatility the highest.
cards.explanation: In a frown the at-the-money implied volatility is the highest, and in a smile it is the lowest.
cards.originalText: A single anticipated price jump produces a frown, with at-the-money implied volatility the lowest; heavy tails on both sides produce a smile, with at-the-money implied volatility the highest.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: To increase the power of a VaR exception backtest, one can lower the VaR confidence level and apply a higher capital multiplier $k$.
cards.explanation: At a very high confidence level exceptions are rare, so the test has little power. Testing at a lower confidence level produces more exceptions, and scaling the result by a larger $k$ keeps capital comparable.
cards.originalText: To increase the power of her backtest, she can decrease the VaR confidence level and apply a higher (k) capital multiplier.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: At a high VaR confidence level and a relatively short backtest window, the normal approximation fits the number of exceptions better than the binomial distribution.
cards.explanation: With few expected exceptions (the normal approximation needs roughly $np \ge 10$) the count is skewed, so the binomial distribution is the better fit.
cards.originalText: At this high VaR confidence level and relatively short backtest window, the normal approximation is a better fit to test the model’s bias than the binomial distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: A more powerful backtest of the same VaR hypothesis can be obtained, without any additional information, by using several available extensions.
cards.explanation: More powerful extensions, such as independence or duration tests, need extra information such as the timing of exceptions.
cards.originalText: She can achieve more powerful tests of the same hypothesis, without any additional information, by using several available extensions.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Although VaR is always a one-tailed quantile, a VaR exception backtest is always two-tailed, with a lower and an upper cutoff.
cards.explanation: A backtest can be one-tailed or two-tailed. The Basel zone approach, for example, is effectively one-sided.
cards.originalText: Although VaR is always a one‑tailed quantile, the backtest is always a two‑tailed backtest with a lower and an upper cutoff.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: The unconditional coverage (Kupiec) test checks whether the observed frequency of VaR exceptions matches the frequency implied by the confidence level, without regard to when the exceptions occur.
cards.explanation: Unconditional coverage tests the proportion of failures against $1 - c$ using a log-likelihood ratio. Clustering in time is the job of the independence test.
cards.originalText: Unconditional coverage test (Kupiec)

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: The significance test of a VaR exception backtest requires the assumption of a normal distribution in order to avoid a numerical or simulation approach.
cards.explanation: The exact binomial distribution can be used directly. The normal distribution is only a large-sample approximation to the binomial and is not required.
cards.originalText: The significance test of the backtest requires the assumption of a normal distribution in order to avoid a numerical/simulation approach.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Jorion's VaR backtest based on exceptions (failure rates) is nonparametric.
cards.explanation: Counting exceptions requires no assumption about the distribution of returns.
cards.originalText: It is nonparametric.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: If a bank's VaR model is accurate, the sample failure rate is an unbiased estimator of one minus the VaR confidence level.
cards.explanation: For an accurate model each day is an exception with probability $p = 1 - c$, so the expected failure rate equals $1 - c$.
cards.originalText: If the bank’s VaR model is accurate, the sample failure rate is an unbiased estimator of (1 ‑ confidence).

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: The hypothesis test of a VaR model's accuracy can assume a binomial distribution for the number of exceptions, which is easy to use.
cards.explanation: Each day is a Bernoulli trial with exception probability $p$, so the number of exceptions over the sample is binomial.
cards.originalText: The hypothesis test of the model’s accuracy can assume a binomial distribution, which is easy to use.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: A backtest of a 99% VaR model at a 95% test confidence level is invalid because the test confidence level differs from the VaR confidence level.
cards.explanation: The confidence level of the statistical test is separate from the VaR confidence level, so a 95% test of a 99% VaR model is perfectly valid.
cards.originalText: The test is invalid because the 95.0% test confidence level differs from the 99.0% VaR confidence level

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: In a one-sided backtest concerned only with too many exceptions, the whole significance level is placed in the upper tail, so the critical number of exceptions is lower than in a two-sided test at the same confidence level.
cards.explanation: Shifting the full rejection probability into the upper tail lowers the critical exception count, so a count that is accepted in a two-sided test can be rejected in the one-sided test.
cards.originalText: Reject the model, because 16 exceptions fall in the one‑sided rejection region

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Backtesting VaR models with a higher probability of exceptions is difficult because the number of exceptions is not high enough to provide meaningful information.
cards.explanation: It is models with a lower probability of exceptions, that is a higher VaR confidence level, whose backtests are difficult because exceptions are too rare to be informative.
cards.correction: Backtesting VaR models with a lower probability of exceptions is difficult because the number of exceptions is not high enough to provide meaningful information.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: The expected frequency of exceptions in a VaR backtest is determined by the confidence level used for the model.
cards.explanation: The expected failure rate equals one minus the VaR confidence level.
cards.originalText: The frequency of exceptions can be determined with the confidence level used for the model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: According to Kupiec (1995), the hypothesis that a VaR model is correct should be rejected if the log-likelihood ratio exceeds 3.84.
cards.explanation: The statistic 3.84 is the 95% critical value of the chi-square distribution with one degree of freedom used in Kupiec's test.
cards.originalText: According to Kupiec (1995), we should reject the hypothesis that the model is correct if the log‑likelihood ratio (LR) > 3.84.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: The range for the number of exceptions in a VaR backtest must balance the chance of rejecting an accurate model (Type I error) against the chance of failing to reject an inaccurate model (Type II error).
cards.explanation: Widening the acceptance range reduces Type I errors but raises Type II errors, and narrowing it does the reverse.
cards.originalText: The range for the number of exceptions must strike a balance between the chances of rejecting an accurate model (a Type I error) and the chances of failing to reject an inaccurate model (a Type II error).

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: The decision to accept or reject a VaR model from a two-tailed backtest at a given test confidence level is less reliable for a 99% VaR model than for a 95% VaR model.
cards.explanation: A 99% VaR produces few expected exceptions, so the count is very noisy relative to its mean and the test has less power.
cards.originalText: The decision to accept or reject a VaR model from a two‑tailed backtest at the 95% test confidence level is less reliable for a 99% VaR model than for a 95% VaR model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Moving from a 95% to a 99% VaR confidence level lowers the probability of committing both a Type I error and a Type II error in a backtest.
cards.explanation: At a fixed sample size lowering one error probability raises the other, and a higher VaR confidence level actually reduces the power of the test. Only more data can help.
cards.originalText: Using a 99% VaR model will lower the probability of committing both Type I error and Type II error.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Switching from a 99% to a 95% VaR confidence level makes decisions on whether to accept or reject a VaR model based on backtesting more reliable.
cards.explanation: More exceptions are expected at 95%, so the backtest has more information and more power to detect a bad model, while the Type I error rate is set by the test level.
cards.originalText: Decisions on whether to accept or reject VaR models based on backtesting will be more reliable.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Switching from a 99% to a 95% VaR confidence level decreases the power of the statistical tests used to backtest the model.
cards.explanation: More expected exceptions increase the power of the test, so power rises when the VaR confidence level is lowered.
cards.originalText: The power of statistical tests will decrease.
cards.correction: Switching from a 99% to a 95% VaR confidence level increases the power of the statistical tests used to backtest the model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Switching from a 99% to a 95% VaR confidence level increases the probabilities of making both a Type I error and a Type II error in a backtest.
cards.explanation: Neither error probability rises: the Type II error falls because power increases, and the Type I error is fixed by the significance level of the test.
cards.originalText: The probability of making both Type I and Type II errors will increase.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: When a VaR backtest has the null hypothesis that the model is accurate, a Type I error means an accurate model is rejected, causing unnecessary penalties or recalibration, while a Type II error means an inaccurate model is accepted, leaving risk and capital understated.
cards.explanation: Type I is rejecting a true null and Type II is failing to reject a false null. Accepting a bad model is the costly mistake for risk measurement because risk is understated.
cards.originalText: A Type I error means an accurate model is rejected, causing unnecessary penalties or recalibration; a Type II error means an inaccurate model is accepted, leaving risk and capital understated.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: When a VaR backtest has the null hypothesis that the model is accurate, a Type I error means an inaccurate model is accepted, leaving risk and capital understated, while a Type II error means an accurate model is rejected, causing unnecessary penalties.
cards.explanation: The definitions are swapped: a Type I error rejects an accurate model, and a Type II error accepts an inaccurate model.
cards.originalText: A Type I error means an inaccurate model is accepted, leaving risk and capital understated; a Type II error means an accurate model is rejected, causing unnecessary penalties.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: In a VaR backtest, Type I and Type II errors always have the same probability, so their consequences cancel out.
cards.explanation: The two error probabilities are generally not equal. Reducing one tends to raise the other, and their consequences do not cancel.
cards.originalText: Type I and Type II errors always have the same probability, so their consequences cancel out in the backtest.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: By shrinking the Basel green zone (for example to 0 to 2 exceptions), a regulator increases the probability of catching banks that willfully understate their risk.
cards.explanation: A smaller green zone means fewer outcomes lead to acceptance, which lowers the Type II error, at the cost of a higher Type I error.
cards.originalText: By shrinking the green zone (e.g., 0 to 2 exceptions), Basel can maximize the probability of catching banks that willfully understate their risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: By shrinking the Basel red zone (for example to 13 or more exceptions), a regulator can better avoid unduly penalising banks whose VaR is exceeded simply through bad luck.
cards.explanation: A smaller red zone lowers the Type I error, sparing banks with accurate models that were merely unlucky, but it also raises the Type II error.
cards.originalText: By shrinking the red zone (e.g., 13 or more), Basel can better avoid unduly penalizing banks whose VaR is exceeded simply due to bad luck.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: By expanding the Basel red zone (for example to 7 or more exceptions), a regulator can better avoid unduly penalising banks whose VaR is exceeded simply through bad luck.
cards.explanation: A larger red zone raises the Type I error, so more banks with accurate models are penalised. It is shrinking the red zone that spares unlucky banks.
cards.originalText: By expanding the red zone (e.g., 7 or more), Basel can better avoid unduly penalizing banks whose VaR is exceeded simply due to bad luck.
cards.correction: By shrinking the Basel red zone (for example to 13 or more exceptions), a regulator can better avoid unduly penalising banks whose VaR is exceeded simply through bad luck.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: By expanding the Basel red zone (for example to 7 or more exceptions), a regulator increases the probability of catching banks that willfully understate their risk.
cards.explanation: A larger red zone lowers the Type II error, so more banks with understated risk are caught, although more banks with accurate models are penalised too.
cards.originalText: By expanding the red zone (e.g., 7 or more), Basel can maximize the probability of catching banks that willfully understate their risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: A bank can reduce the probability of accepting a bad VaR model in a backtest by decreasing the VaR confidence level, for example from 99% to 95%.
cards.explanation: A lower VaR confidence level produces more exceptions, which gives the test more power to detect an inaccurate model.
cards.originalText: Decrease the VaR model’s confidence level, e.g., 99% to 95%.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Increasing the VaR confidence level, for example from 95% to 99%, reduces the probability of accepting a bad VaR model in a backtest.
cards.explanation: Fewer exceptions are expected at 99%, so the test has less power and the Type II error rises.
cards.originalText: Increase the VaR model’s confidence level, e.g., 95% to 99%.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Decreasing the sample size reduces the probability of accepting a bad VaR model in a backtest.
cards.explanation: A smaller sample lowers the power of the test and so raises the probability of accepting a bad model. A larger sample improves reliability.
cards.originalText: Decrease the sample size in order to observe more recent data.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Increasing the two-tailed non-rejection confidence level of a VaR backtest reduces the probability of accepting a bad VaR model.
cards.explanation: A higher non-rejection confidence level widens the acceptance region, which reduces the Type I error but increases the Type II error, the probability of accepting a bad model.
cards.originalText: Increase the two‑tailed non‑rejection confidence level (i.e., the significance test of the observed number of exceptions versus the null hypothesis).

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: In a VaR backtest, the probability of a Type II error is difficult to quantify because it depends on the unknown true failure rate of the model.
