cards.explanation: Every pseudo-history is generated assuming the fitted GARCH is correct. The interval captures sampling error but not model risk, and can be too narrow if the model is misspecified.
cards.originalText: Resampling treats the estimated GARCH model as the true data‑generating process, so model misspecification is not reflected in the interval.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A GARCH model cannot capture time-varying volatility.
cards.explanation: GARCH is specifically designed to model time-varying volatility.
cards.originalText: The GARCH structure cannot capture time‑varying volatility within the bootstrap samples.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A residual bootstrap for GARCH VaR requires the standardized residuals to be normal in order to preserve the model's distribution.
cards.explanation: The bootstrap uses the empirical distribution of the standardized residuals and needs no normality assumption.
cards.originalText: The bootstrap requires the standardized residuals to be normal in order to preserve the model’s distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Resampling with replacement makes the VaR estimates from different bootstrap samples perfectly correlated.
cards.explanation: Resamples are drawn independently, which is what produces a distribution of VaR estimates from which a confidence interval is built.
cards.originalText: Resampling with replacement makes the VaR estimates from different samples perfectly correlated.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: GARCH VaR tends to produce tighter confidence intervals than historical simulation VaR.
cards.explanation: GARCH reflects current volatility, so it gives more precise VaR estimates and narrower intervals than plain historical simulation.
cards.originalText: GARCH VaR tends to produce tighter confidence intervals than historical simulation VaR.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Confidence intervals for VaR are symmetric around the point estimate.
cards.explanation: VaR confidence intervals are not symmetric around the point estimate.
cards.originalText: Confidence intervals for VaR are symmetric around the point estimate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Using more data generally leads to wider confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.explanation: More data gives more precise estimates, so VaR confidence intervals are tighter, not wider.
cards.originalText: Using more data generally leads to wider confidence intervals.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Order statistics consistently produces tighter VaR confidence intervals than bootstrapping.
cards.explanation: Neither of these two nonparametric methods consistently produces tighter intervals than the other.
cards.originalText: Order statistics consistently produces tighter confidence intervals than bootstrapping.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: The confidence interval for historical simulation VaR is wider when estimated over a stress period than over a calm period of the same length, and a longer history gives a tighter interval than a one-year sample.
cards.explanation: Stress raises estimation uncertainty, while a larger sample reduces it.
cards.originalText: The interval for the stress period is wider than for the calm one‑year period, while the longer history gives a tighter interval than a one‑year sample.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A longer history widens the confidence interval of a historical simulation VaR because it contains more regimes.
cards.explanation: More data tightens the confidence interval, so a longer history gives a tighter interval, not a wider one.
cards.originalText: The interval is widest for the longer history, because it contains more regimes.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: The confidence interval of a historical simulation VaR is narrowest in a stress period because large losses make the quantile easy to locate.
cards.explanation: Stress periods give wider confidence intervals, because VaR is less precisely estimated when markets are turbulent.
cards.originalText: The interval is narrowest for the stress period, because large losses make the quantile easy to locate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Because historical simulation makes no distributional assumption, its VaR confidence interval has the same width whatever the sample period or sample size.
cards.explanation: Being nonparametric does not make the interval insensitive. The dispersion of tail observations and the sample size still drive the interval width.
cards.originalText: The interval is the same for all three periods, because historical simulation makes no distributional assumption.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Neither order statistics nor bootstrapping consistently produces tighter confidence intervals than the other for historical simulation VaR.
cards.explanation: Empirical evidence shows no consistent winner between these two nonparametric methods.
cards.originalText: Neither method consistently produces tighter confidence intervals than the other.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Order statistics consistently produces significantly tighter confidence intervals than bootstrapping for historical simulation VaR.
cards.explanation: Empirical evidence shows no consistent winner between order statistics and bootstrapping.
cards.originalText: Order statistics consistently produces significantly tighter confidence intervals than bootstrapping.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Bootstrapping consistently produces significantly tighter confidence intervals than order statistics for historical simulation VaR.
cards.explanation: Empirical evidence shows no consistent winner between order statistics and bootstrapping.
cards.originalText: Bootstrapping consistently produces significantly tighter confidence intervals than order statistics.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Bootstrapping is applicable only to parametric VaR methods and not to historical simulation.
cards.explanation: Bootstrapping is nonparametric and is applied directly to the historical (pseudo) return history by resampling it with replacement.
cards.originalText: Bootstrapping is applicable only to parametric VaR methods, not to historical simulation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Order statistics produces tighter confidence intervals for VaR than bootstrap techniques.
cards.explanation: Empirical analysis finds that neither order statistics nor bootstrapping produces a tighter interval than the other.
cards.originalText: Order statistics produces tighter confidence intervals for VaR compared to bootstrap techniques.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Confidence intervals for VaR are not symmetric.
cards.explanation: The intervals are asymmetric because the loss tail is sparse, unlike a normal-based interval.
cards.originalText: Confidence intervals are not symmetric.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Larger datasets lead to tighter confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.explanation: A larger sample reduces the sampling error in the quantile estimate.
cards.originalText: Larger datasets lead to tighter confidence intervals.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: GARCH VaR tends to produce much tighter confidence intervals compared to historical simulation VaR.
cards.explanation: GARCH responds to current volatility, so its VaR estimates are more precise than those of unconditional historical simulation.
cards.originalText: GARCH VaR tends to produce much tighter confidence intervals compared to historical simulation VaR.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Plotting the daily VaR of two models over the same period mainly reveals which model is more conservative, so a formal comparison of the models requires statistical tests.
cards.explanation: A visual comparison shows only which VaR is higher, not which is more accurate.
cards.originalText: The plot mainly reveals which model is more conservative; a formal evaluation requires statistical tests.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A plot of the daily VaR of two models shows which model is more accurate, so no further testing is needed.
cards.explanation: A higher or lower line does not indicate accuracy. The plot says nothing about how often or by how much VaR is breached, so formal statistical tests are needed.
cards.originalText: The plot shows which model is more accurate; no further testing is needed.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A plot of the daily VaR of two models proves that the errors of the models are independent and identically distributed.
cards.explanation: Because trading portfolios change frequently, errors are generally not independent and identically distributed, and a plot proves nothing about this.
cards.originalText: The plot proves that the models’ errors are independent and identically distributed.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A loss function-based comparison is a rigorous way to compare the accuracy of two VaR models.
cards.explanation: A loss function evaluates each model's VaR against realized outcomes, which gives a statistical basis for comparing accuracy.
cards.originalText: Using a loss function‑based comparison.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: The VaR model that produces the higher VaR estimate is the more accurate model.
cards.explanation: A higher VaR only means the model is more conservative, not more accurate. It may overstate risk and tie up capital.
cards.originalText: Evaluating which model produces a higher VaR estimate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: The regulatory loss function penalizes underestimation of risk (VaR exceptions) more heavily than overestimation.
cards.explanation: Exceptions raise capital requirements, so the regulatory loss function is asymmetric: it charges a loss when realized loss exceeds VaR and little or nothing when VaR is merely conservative.
cards.originalText: Penalizing underestimation of risk (exceptions) more heavily than overestimation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: The regulatory loss function balances false positives (overestimations) and false negatives (underestimations) of risk symmetrically.
cards.explanation: A symmetric trade-off describes a different loss function. The regulatory loss function is asymmetric and penalizes underestimation more heavily.
cards.originalText: Balancing the trade‑off between false positives (overestimations) and false negatives (underestimations) in risk predictions.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: The sign test comparing two VaR models examines whether the number of positive loss differentials is consistent with a 50% probability, that is, whether neither model has systematically lower loss.
cards.explanation: Under the null of equal performance a positive and a negative differential are equally likely. The test counts positive differentials against a binomial distribution and uses signs only, not magnitudes.
cards.originalText: Whether the number of positive loss differentials is consistent with a 50% probability, i.e., neither model has systematically lower loss.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: The sign test comparing two VaR models examines whether each model's exception rate equals one minus its VaR confidence level.
cards.explanation: That describes a Kupiec-type unconditional coverage backtest of a single model. The sign test compares two models using the signs of their loss differentials.
cards.originalText: Whether each model’s exception rate equals one minus its VaR confidence level.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: The sign test comparing two VaR models examines whether the exceptions of the two models are clustered in time.
cards.explanation: Clustering of exceptions is tested by independence tests. The sign test counts the signs of the daily loss differentials.
cards.originalText: Whether the two models’ exceptions are clustered in time.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: The sign test comparing two VaR models examines whether the average size of the loss differential differs from zero, assuming normally distributed differentials.
cards.explanation: That describes a t-test on the mean differential. The sign test uses only signs and makes no normality assumption.
cards.originalText: Whether the average size of the loss differential is different from zero, assuming normally distributed differentials.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A key challenge in benchmarking VaR models is the assumption of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) errors, which is violated because trading portfolios change frequently.
cards.explanation: Statistical tests that compare VaR models typically assume i.i.d. errors, but frequent portfolio changes mean the errors are not independent and identically distributed.
cards.originalText: The assumption of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) errors.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A GARCH(1,1) VaR fitted to daily trading P&L requires no distributional or model assumptions at all.
cards.explanation: GARCH still assumes a variance process and a distribution for the innovations.
cards.originalText: It requires no distributional or model assumptions at all.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A GARCH(1,1) VaR fitted to daily trading P&L uses detailed position-level risk factors.
cards.explanation: A P&L-based model ignores positions, so it is not a positional model. It is built from the historical P&L series alone.
cards.originalText: It uses detailed position‑level risk factors and so measures positional risk more precisely than the internal model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Benchmarking of VaR models is usually conducted for only a short time period during a bank's transition to a new model.
cards.explanation: Building a competing model is resource intensive, so benchmarking is typically a short-term exercise during a model transition.
cards.originalText: Benchmarking is usually conducted for only a short time period during a bank’s transition to a new model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Benchmarking VaR models is not used for validating their performance.
cards.explanation: Benchmarking, which compares a bank's VaR model with another model, is important for validating performance.
cards.originalText: Benchmarking VaR models is not used for validating their performance.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Banks routinely benchmark their VaR model against several competing models.
cards.explanation: Banks seldom have a formal benchmarking mechanism outside model transitions, because building even one competing model is costly.
cards.originalText: Banks routinely benchmark their VaR model against several competing models.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: In the statistical backtesting of VaR models, the errors are independently, but not identically, distributed.
cards.explanation: Because portfolios change frequently, the errors are neither independent nor identically distributed.
cards.originalText: In the statistical backtesting of VaR models, the errors are independently, but not identically, distributed.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A PIT-based backtest addresses the low power of exceedance-based backtests because it draws on the entire forecast distribution rather than only the exceedance indicator.
cards.explanation: An exceedance backtest reduces each day to a 0/1 indicator, so few exceedances give little power. A PIT-based backtest lets every observation carry information, which raises power.
cards.originalText: Use a PIT‑based backtest, which draws on the entire forecast distribution rather than only the exceedance indicator.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Using overlapping windows to create more backtest observations from the same data adds independent information and so raises the power of an exceedance-based backtest.
cards.explanation: Overlapping windows create serially dependent observations and add no new independent information, violating the independence assumption.
cards.originalText: Use overlapping windows to create more backtest observations from the same data.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Tightening the significance level of a backtest from 5% to 1% raises its power.
cards.explanation: A stricter significance level lowers the Type I error rate but raises the Type II error rate, so it reduces power.
cards.originalText: Tighten the significance level of the test from 5% to 1%.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Relying on the unconditional coverage test alone solves the low power problem of exceedance-based backtests.
cards.explanation: Unconditional coverage uses only the exceedance count, which is exactly the source of the low power.
cards.originalText: Rely on the unconditional coverage test alone, since it uses the total number of exceedances.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: For a PIT-based backtest to reflect the properties of an exceedance-based backtest, the probability integral transforms must be uniformly distributed and independent.
cards.explanation: Uniformity corresponds to unconditional coverage and independence corresponds to the absence of clustering of exceedances, which together mirror conditional coverage.
cards.originalText: Uniform distribution and independence.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Concentration and clustering of the probability integral transforms are properties of an accurate VaR model.
cards.explanation: Concentration (non-uniformity) and clustering (dependence) are symptoms of a deficient model, the opposite of what is required.
cards.originalText: Concentration and clustering.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: An average exceedance rate of 0.4% for one-day 99% VaR models suggests that, on average, the models overestimate risk and are conservative.
cards.explanation: A 99% VaR should be exceeded about 1% of the time. An exceedance rate below this means the VaR thresholds are set too far out.
cards.originalText: On average they overestimate risk (are conservative).

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: An average exceedance rate of 0.4% for one-day 99% VaR models suggests that, on average, the models underestimate risk.
cards.explanation: Underestimation produces more than 1% exceedances for a 99% VaR. An exceedance rate of 0.4% points to overestimation.
cards.originalText: On average they underestimate risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: An average exceedance rate of 0.4% for one-day 99% VaR models suggests that, on average, the models accurately capture risk.
cards.explanation: Accurate calibration would give an exceedance rate of about 1% for a 99% VaR, so 0.4% is well below.
cards.originalText: On average they accurately capture risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A very low exceedance rate for a 99% VaR model, such as 0.4%, may indicate excessive conservatism, potentially leading to inefficient capital allocation.
cards.explanation: Exceedances well below the nominal 1% rate indicate that VaR is set higher than needed, which ties up excess capital.
cards.originalText: The low rate may indicate excessive conservatism, potentially leading to inefficient capital allocation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Exceedance-based backtests use only whether the loss exceeded the VaR threshold, so a model can pass them while misrepresenting the rest of the forecast distribution.
cards.explanation: An exceedance indicator carries information only about one point in the tail, so passing these tests does not validate the full forecast distribution. PIT-based tests use the whole distribution.
cards.originalText: They use only whether the loss exceeded the VaR threshold, so a model can pass while misrepresenting the rest of the forecast distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Exceedance-based backtests can detect only VaR models that are too conservative, not models that are too aggressive.
cards.explanation: Too many exceedances, which indicate an aggressive model, are detected by the unconditional coverage test as readily as too few.
cards.originalText: They can only detect models that are too conservative, not models that are too aggressive.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Exceedance-based backtests require the P&L to be normally distributed.
cards.explanation: Exceedance-based tests make no normality assumption. They rely on binomial and Markov-chain likelihoods.
cards.originalText: They require the P&L to be normally distributed.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Exceedance-based backtests test the independence of exceedances but not their total number.
cards.explanation: They test both: the unconditional coverage test examines the total number of exceedances and the independence test examines clustering.
cards.originalText: They test independence of exceedances but not their total number.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A well-specified VaR model produces probability integral transforms that are uniformly distributed and show no temporal patterns.
cards.explanation: Uniformity reflects correct coverage across the whole forecast distribution, and the absence of temporal patterns reflects independence.
cards.originalText: It indicates uniformity and absence of temporal patterns.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The probability integral transforms of an accurate VaR model show cyclic trends.
cards.explanation: Cyclical patterns mean the PITs are serially dependent, the analogue of clustered exceedances, and indicate a deficient model.
cards.originalText: It highlights cyclic trends and overfitting potential.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The probability integral transforms of an accurate VaR model show deviations at the extremes of the distribution.
cards.explanation: Excess mass at the extremes (a U-shaped or humped PIT histogram) indicates that the forecast tails are too thin or too fat, i.e. a poor model.
cards.originalText: It shows deviations at the distribution extremes.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: To pass the unconditional coverage test, the total number of exceedances of a VaR model must be consistent, within a confidence level, with the expected frequency.
cards.explanation: Unconditional coverage (Kupiec) looks only at the number of exceedances out of the observations, regardless of their timing.
cards.originalText: The total number of exceedances must match the expected frequency within a confidence level.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A VaR model passes the unconditional coverage test only if its exceedances occur in clusters.
cards.explanation: Clustering violates independence and would lead to rejection of the independence and conditional coverage tests. It is not required for coverage.
cards.originalText: Exceedances must occur in clusters.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Passing the unconditional coverage test requires the exceedances to be independent of prior exceedances.
cards.explanation: Independence is a separate property, tested by the independence test and needed for conditional coverage. Unconditional coverage tests only the frequency of exceedances.
cards.originalText: Exceedances must be independent of prior exceedances.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A VaR model has conditional coverage when it cannot be rejected on the basis of its observed number of exceedances, nor for a potential lack of independence.
cards.explanation: Conditional coverage holds when the model passes both the frequency (coverage) test and the independence test.
cards.originalText: The model cannot be rejected on the basis of observed exceedances, nor can it be rejected for potential lack of independence.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A VaR model has conditional coverage when the suggested exceedance rate cannot be rejected even though the exceedances are serially correlated.
cards.explanation: Serial correlation of exceedances means independence is rejected, so conditional coverage fails. Only unconditional coverage could hold.
cards.originalText: The suggested rate of exceedance incidents cannot be rejected; however, there is serial correlation among the exceedance observations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: In deriving a probability integral transform for a single day, the first step is to obtain the forecast distribution of P&L for the period.
cards.explanation: A PIT is a position within a forecast distribution, so the forecast must exist before the realized P&L can be located within it.
cards.originalText: Obtain the forecast distribution of P&L for the period (e.g. normal with mean 0 and standard deviation 500).

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The PIT method passes each day's realized P&L through that day's own forecast CDF to put observations from different forecast distributions on one common [0,1] scale so that they can be tested together.
cards.explanation: Applying the forecast CDF gives the cumulative probability of the realized outcome under that day's forecast. If every forecast is correct, all PITs are Uniform[0,1].
cards.originalText: To put observations drawn from different forecast distributions on one common \[0,1\] scale so they can be tested together.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The PIT method passes each day's realized P&L through its forecast CDF in order to remove outlier days before computing VaR.
cards.explanation: PIT does not remove observations. Extreme outcomes are retained because they reveal tail misforecasts.
cards.originalText: To remove outlier days before computing the VaR.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The PIT method is used to re-estimate the parameters of a VaR model from historical data.
cards.explanation: PIT is a validation tool applied to forecasts, not a way to refine or recalibrate the model.
cards.originalText: To re‑estimate the model parameters from historical data.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The PIT method is used to count how many days exceeded the VaR threshold.
cards.explanation: Counting exceedances is the exceedance-based approach, which uses a single tail cutoff, whereas PIT uses the entire forecast distribution.
cards.originalText: To count how many days exceeded the VaR threshold.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Probability integral transform values convert observed data points into a uniform distribution across the entire forecast distribution, so that the whole forecast distribution can be backtested.
cards.explanation: PITs map each observation through its forecast CDF to a variable that is uniform on [0,1] if the model is correct.
cards.originalText: convert observed data points into a uniform distribution for the entire forecasted distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Probability integral transform values are used to determine the total number of exceedances of a VaR model.
cards.explanation: Counting exceedances is the exceedance-based method. PIT values use the full forecast distribution.
cards.originalText: are used to determine the total number of exceedances for a VaR model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Probability integral transform values are used to analyze the independence of exceedances by forming a Markov chain of observations.
cards.explanation: A Markov-chain independence test is an exceedance-based (Christoffersen-type) technique, not the purpose of PIT values.
cards.originalText: analyze exceedance independence by forming a Markov chain of observations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: If the forecast distributions of a VaR model are correct, the PIT values are uniformly distributed over [0,1] and independent over time.
cards.explanation: Passing an outcome through its own true CDF always yields a Uniform[0,1] variable, and correct forecasts also imply independence across days.
cards.originalText: They are uniformly distributed over \[0,1\] and independent over time.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: If the forecast distributions of a VaR model are correct, the PIT values are skewed toward 0 and 1, reflecting the fat tails of P&L.
cards.explanation: Mass piled near 0 and 1 signals forecasts that are too thin-tailed, a flawed model. Correct forecasts give uniform PITs.
cards.originalText: They are skewed toward 0 and 1, reflecting the fat tails of P&L.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: If the forecast distributions of a VaR model are correct, the PIT values cluster around 0.5, reflecting the central tendency of P&L.
cards.explanation: Clustering in the middle means the forecast tails are too fat, which indicates misspecification. Correct forecasts give uniform PITs.
cards.originalText: They cluster around 0.5, reflecting the central tendency of P&L.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: If the forecast distributions of a VaR model are correct, the PIT values are normally distributed with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
cards.explanation: A PIT is a probability on [0,1] and is uniform for a correct model. A standard normal variable would be the standardized outcome (z-score).
cards.originalText: They are normally distributed with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A VaR model whose PIT values are uniformly distributed but strongly serially correlated fails the independence requirement and its dynamics should be revised.
cards.explanation: A well-calibrated model needs PITs that are both uniform and independent. Serial correlation is the analogue of clustered exceedances and typically arises when the model is slow to update for changing volatility.
cards.originalText: The model fails the independence requirement; forecasts are not adapting to changing conditions such as volatility clustering, so the dynamics of the model should be revised.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Uniformity of the PIT values is the only requirement for a well-calibrated VaR model.
cards.explanation: Uniformity is necessary but not sufficient. The PIT values must also be independent over time.
cards.originalText: The model is well calibrated, because uniformity of the PITs is the only requirement.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A U-shaped histogram of PIT values, with too many observations near 0 and 1, indicates that the forecast distributions are too narrow, so risk is understated in both tails.
cards.explanation: Extreme outcomes occur more often than the model predicts. The remedy is to widen the forecast distribution, for example with higher volatility or fatter tails.
cards.originalText: The forecast distributions are too narrow and risk is understated in both tails; widen the forecast distribution (e.g., higher volatility or fatter tails).

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A PIT histogram with too many observations in the extreme deciles indicates that the forecast distributions are too wide and that risk is overstated.
cards.explanation: Too-wide forecasts produce a hump in the middle deciles with thin tails. Excess mass in the extreme deciles means the forecasts are too narrow and risk is understated.
cards.originalText: The forecast distributions are too wide and risk is overstated; reduce the volatility estimate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: PIT values clustered around the middle of [0,1], with few near 0 or 1, suggest that the forecast distributions are too wide and the model is conservative, overstating risk.
cards.explanation: Outcomes are less variable than the forecast implies, so tail outcomes occur less often than predicted and VaR is overstated.
cards.originalText: The model is conservative: forecast distributions are too wide, overstating risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: PIT values clustered around the middle of [0,1], with few near 0 or 1, suggest that the forecast distributions are too narrow and the model underestimates risk.
cards.explanation: Narrow forecasts give a U-shaped histogram with mass near 0 and 1. A central hump indicates forecasts that are too wide.
cards.originalText: The model is aggressive: forecast distributions are too narrow, underestimating risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: PIT values clustered around the middle of [0,1] indicate a perfectly balanced risk model.
cards.explanation: Only a uniform (flat) PIT histogram indicates good calibration. A central hump is a systematic departure from uniformity.
cards.originalText: Middle clustering indicates a perfectly balanced risk model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A PIT histogram that slopes steadily in one direction, with realized outcomes systematically falling on one side of the forecast distribution, indicates a location bias in the forecast distribution rather than a problem with its width.
cards.explanation: A monotone sloped PIT histogram means outcomes consistently land in the upper (or lower) part of the forecast distribution, so the forecast mean is off. Too-narrow forecasts give a U-shape and too-wide forecasts give a central hump instead.
cards.originalText: The forecast distributions are biased in location: realized P&L is systematically higher than forecast, so the forecast is too pessimistic and the location (mean) should be adjusted.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A concentration of PITs near 0 indicates that realized losses repeatedly fall in the extreme left tail of the forecast distribution, so large losses are underestimated.
cards.explanation: A PIT is the forecast CDF evaluated at the realized P&L, so losses map to low values. A pile-up near 0 means losses land far in the forecast tail much more often than the model predicts.
cards.originalText: The PIT distribution has a concentration of values near 0 (31% of PITs in the lowest decile versus 10% expected), indicating frequent underestimation of large losses.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A PIT distribution that is uniform on the interval from 0 to 1, with no clustering in the tails or the centre, indicates that a VaR model is poorly calibrated.
cards.explanation: Uniform PITs are the hallmark of a well-calibrated forecast distribution. Clustering in the tails or centre, not its absence, signals miscalibration.
cards.originalText: The PIT distribution is uniform on \[0,1\], with no clustering in the tails or center.
cards.correction: A PIT distribution that is uniform on the interval from 0 to 1, with no clustering in the tails or the centre, indicates that a VaR model is well calibrated.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Well-calibrated PITs should have skewness near 0 and kurtosis near 3.
cards.explanation: Skewness 0 and kurtosis 3 are the moments of a normal distribution. Well-calibrated PITs are uniform on the interval 0 to 1, which has skewness 0 and kurtosis of 1.8.
cards.originalText: The PIT distribution has skewness near 0 and kurtosis near 3, indicating balanced calibration.
cards.correction: Well-calibrated PITs should have skewness near 0 and kurtosis near 1.8.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: When backtesting VaR models, a QQ plot of PITs should ideally be close to a straight line from (0,0) to (1,1).
cards.explanation: If PITs are uniform, the fraction of PITs at or below each value u equals u, which plots as the 45-degree line from (0,0) to (1,1). Deviations from that line show the forecast distribution is mis-specified.
cards.originalText: straight line from \[0,0\] to \[1,1\].

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: When backtesting VaR models, a QQ plot of PITs should ideally be close to a horizontal line.
cards.explanation: A horizontal line would mean all PITs sit in one region, an extreme departure from uniformity. Uniform PITs give the 45-degree line from (0,0) to (1,1).
cards.originalText: horizontal line.
cards.correction: When backtesting VaR models, a QQ plot of PITs should ideally be close to a straight line from (0,0) to (1,1).

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: For a perfect distribution forecast, each of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling and Cramér-von Mises statistics is expected to converge toward zero as the number of observations grows.
cards.explanation: All three statistics measure the distance between the empirical PIT distribution and the uniform distribution. With a perfect forecast the PITs are truly uniform, so the distance shrinks toward zero and lower values are better.
cards.originalText: For a perfect distribution forecast, each of the KS, Anderson‑Darling and Cramér‑von Mises statistics is expected to converge toward zero as the number of observations grows.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is the mean squared deviation between the actual and theoretical distributions.
cards.explanation: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is the maximum vertical distance between the actual and theoretical distributions. The Cramér-von Mises statistic is the one based on the mean squared deviation.
cards.originalText: The KS statistic is the mean squared deviation between the actual and theoretical distributions, while the Cramér‑von Mises statistic is the maximum vertical distance.
cards.correction: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is the maximum vertical distance between the actual and theoretical distributions.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The Anderson-Darling test treats all discrepancies between the actual and theoretical distributions equally.
cards.explanation: It is the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test that treats all discrepancies equally. The Anderson-Darling test places higher emphasis on the tails, which is why it is preferred for risk management.
cards.originalText: The Anderson‑Darling test treats all discrepancies between the distributions equally, which is why it is preferred over KS for risk management.
cards.correction: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test treats all discrepancies between the actual and theoretical distributions equally.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A goodness-of-fit statistic that is larger than zero but below its critical value shows that the PITs are exactly uniform.
cards.explanation: Being below the critical value only means uniformity is not rejected at that confidence level. It does not prove the PITs are exactly uniform.
cards.originalText: A statistic that is larger than zero but below its critical value means the PITs are exactly uniform.
cards.correction: A goodness-of-fit statistic that is larger than zero but below its critical value shows that uniformity of the PITs is not rejected.

changes.from: shows that the PITs are exactly uniform
changes.to: shows that uniformity of the PITs is not rejected

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test measures the maximum vertical distance between the actual and theoretical distributions but treats all discrepancies equally, so it gives no extra weight to the tails.
cards.explanation: KS takes the largest gap between the empirical and uniform CDFs wherever it occurs, so tail discrepancies get no special weight. This is the criticism that motivates the Anderson-Darling test.
cards.originalText: It measures the maximum vertical distance between the actual and theoretical distributions but treats all discrepancies equally, so it gives no extra weight to the tails.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is the most sensitive of the three tests to deviations in the tails of the distribution.
cards.explanation: The Anderson-Darling test, not KS, places the heaviest emphasis on the tails. KS treats all discrepancies equally.
cards.originalText: It is the most sensitive of the three tests to deviations in the tails of the distribution.
cards.correction: The Anderson-Darling test is the most sensitive of the three tests to deviations in the tails of the distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test averages squared deviations over the whole distribution.
cards.explanation: Averaging squared deviations over the whole distribution describes the Cramér-von Mises statistic. KS uses the single maximum vertical distance between the distributions.
cards.originalText: It averages squared deviations over the whole distribution and therefore cannot detect a single large deviation.
cards.correction: The Cramér-von Mises test averages squared deviations over the whole distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The Cramér-von Mises test is very similar to the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test but, instead of the maximum difference, it considers the mean squared deviation between the distributions.
cards.explanation: Both tests compare the empirical PIT distribution with the uniform distribution. Cramér-von Mises replaces the maximum gap with the mean squared deviation, so it assesses fit across the whole distribution.
cards.originalText: CvM is very similar to KS but, instead of the maximum difference, it considers the mean squared deviation between the distributions.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Among the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Cramér-von Mises and Anderson-Darling tests, the Cramér-von Mises test places the greatest emphasis on tail observations.
cards.explanation: The Anderson-Darling test, not Cramér-von Mises, emphasises tail observations. Cramér-von Mises averages squared deviations across the whole distribution.
cards.originalText: CvM is the test with the greatest emphasis on tail observations among the three.
cards.correction: Among the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Cramér-von Mises and Anderson-Darling tests, the Anderson-Darling test places the greatest emphasis on tail observations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The Cramér-von Mises test tests the independence of successive PIT values rather than their distribution.
cards.explanation: Cramér-von Mises is a goodness-of-fit test of whether PITs follow the uniform distribution. Independence is tested separately, for example with the Berkowitz approach on normal-transformed PITs.
cards.originalText: CvM tests the independence of successive PIT values rather than their distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The Kupiec test evaluates the full distribution of PITs.
cards.explanation: The Kupiec test looks only at the frequency of VaR exceedances. It does not examine the shape of the PIT distribution.
cards.originalText: Kupiec test, because it evaluates the full distribution of PITs.
cards.correction: The Kupiec test evaluates only the frequency of VaR exceedances.

changes.to: only the frequency of VaR exceedances

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A Cramér-von Mises test that does not reject uniformity proves that a VaR model is well calibrated in the tails.
cards.explanation: Cramér-von Mises averages deviations across the whole distribution, so passing it says nothing reliable about the tails. A tail-sensitive test such as Anderson-Darling can still reject.
cards.originalText: The Cramér‑von Mises test proves the model is well calibrated in the tails.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Large Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramér-von Mises statistics with very small p-values indicate that the PITs closely fit the uniform distribution.
cards.explanation: Large statistics and tiny p-values mean a large deviation from uniformity and a rejection of the null that PITs are uniform. A good fit shows small statistics and high p-values.
cards.originalText: Model Y passes both tests, because its large test statistics indicate a close fit to the uniform distribution.
cards.correction: Large Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramér-von Mises statistics with very small p-values indicate that the PITs deviate substantially from the uniform distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Among the goodness-of-fit tests used to evaluate the distribution of PITs, the Anderson-Darling test best captures tail events.
cards.explanation: The Anderson-Darling statistic places higher emphasis on tail observations. KS looks only at the single largest gap and Cramér-von Mises averages squared deviations equally across the distribution.
cards.originalText: Anderson‑Darling test.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Calculate a mean reversion rate using standard regression and calculate the corresponding autocorrelation.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: A low one-period autocorrelation of the average correlation series indicates a high mean reversion rate (gravity).
cards.explanation: In the mean-reversion regression the autocorrelation equals one minus the mean reversion rate, so a low autocorrelation means a high mean reversion rate.
cards.originalText: The mean reversion rate (aka, gravity) is high

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Calculate a mean reversion rate using standard regression and calculate the corresponding autocorrelation.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: With mean reversion, the slope coefficient in the regression of the change in correlation on the lagged correlation level is positive.
cards.explanation: The slope equals minus the mean reversion rate, so it is negative when correlation reverts to its mean.
cards.originalText: The regression coefficient is positive
cards.correction: With mean reversion, the slope coefficient in the regression of the change in correlation on the lagged correlation level is negative.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: The Johnson SB distribution is the best fit to the empirical distribution of equity correlations.
cards.explanation: Johnson SB is a flexible bounded distribution that matches equity correlations well across economic states, whereas normal, lognormal and beta fit poorly.
cards.originalText: Johnson SB

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: The generalized extreme value distribution is the best fit to the empirical distribution of equity correlations.
cards.explanation: The generalized extreme value distribution is the best fit for bond correlations. Equity correlations are best fit by Johnson SB.
cards.originalText: Generalized extreme value
cards.correction: The Johnson SB distribution is the best fit to the empirical distribution of equity correlations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: Default probability correlations are best modeled using the Johnson SB distribution, whereas bond correlations are best modeled using the generalized extreme value distribution.
cards.explanation: Default probability correlations behave like equity correlations and are best fit by Johnson SB. Bond correlations are best fit by the generalized extreme value distribution, with the normal also fitting well.
cards.originalText: The default probability correlation distribution is best modeled using the Johnson SB distribution, whereas the bond correlation distribution is best modeled using the generalized extreme value distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations.
