cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: Default probability correlations and bond correlations are both best modeled using the Johnson SB distribution.
cards.explanation: Only default probability correlations (like equity correlations) are best fit by Johnson SB. Bond correlations are best fit by the generalized extreme value distribution.
cards.originalText: Both the default probability correlation distribution and the bond correlation distribution are best modeled using the Johnson SB distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: The best-fit distributions for equity, bond and default probability correlations are Johnson SB, generalized extreme value and Johnson SB, respectively.
cards.explanation: Equity and default probability correlations share the Johnson SB best fit. Bond correlations are best fit by the generalized extreme value distribution, with the normal as a secondary fit.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A DV01-neutral hedge assumes that yield changes are parallel across maturities, which is rarely the case in practice.
cards.explanation: DV01 neutrality presumes the position and the hedging instrument have the same basis-point yield change. Real yield changes differ across maturities, so the hedge is imprecise.
cards.originalText: It assumes yield changes are parallel across maturities, which is rarely the case.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A DV01-neutral hedge captures non-parallel yield curve shifts across multiple bond maturities.
cards.explanation: A DV01-neutral hedge cannot capture non-parallel shifts. That is one of its main weaknesses.
cards.originalText: It captures non‑parallel yield curve shifts across multiple bond maturities.
cards.correction: A DV01-neutral hedge cannot capture non-parallel yield curve shifts across multiple bond maturities.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A DV01-neutral hedge neutralizes spread-related risks in addition to interest rate (yield) risk.
cards.explanation: A DV01-neutral hedge addresses only yield (rate) risk. Spread and other risks remain in the position.
cards.originalText: The strategy inherently assumes that all spread‑related risks are neutralized.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A DV01-neutral hedge assumes that the yields on the position and on the hedging instrument change by the same number of basis points, whereas actual changes can be proportionally larger or smaller and dispersed.
cards.explanation: The DV01 hedge hard-wires a one-for-one yield change. When actual yield changes differ in size or are dispersed, the hedge is imprecise.
cards.originalText: It assumes the yields on the position and the hedging instrument change by the same number of basis points, whereas the actual changes can be proportionally larger or smaller and dispersed.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A DV01-neutral hedge requires estimating a regression of historical yield changes.
cards.explanation: A DV01-neutral hedge uses no historical data. It is the regression hedge that estimates a regression of yield changes, which can be unstable over time.
cards.originalText: It requires estimating a regression of historical yield changes, which may be unstable over time.
cards.correction: A regression hedge requires estimating a regression of historical yield changes.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A DV01-neutral hedge accounts for convexity.
cards.explanation: DV01 is a first-order measure of price sensitivity and ignores convexity. It includes no convexity adjustment.
cards.originalText: It accounts for convexity and so over‑hedges when yields change by large amounts.
cards.correction: A DV01-neutral hedge does not account for convexity.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: When a trader is concerned about the dispersion of the change in the nominal yield for a given change in the real yield, the DV01 hedge is the least effective hedging methodology, because it hard-wires a one-for-one yield change.
cards.explanation: Regression and principal components hedges are calibrated to the observed relationships between yield changes. The DV01 hedge alone assumes both yields change by the same number of basis points.
cards.originalText: DV01 hedge.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A DV01-neutral hedge of a nominal Treasury bond with TIPS assumes that the nominal yield and the real yield change by the same number of basis points.
cards.explanation: This one-for-one assumption is the main drawback, because nominal and real yields do not move one-for-one in practice, so the hedge is imprecise.
cards.originalText: It assumes the nominal yield and the real yield change by the same number of basis points, whereas empirically the nominal yield tends to move by more than one basis point per basis point of real‑yield change.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A DV01-neutral hedge can only be applied when the bond and the hedging instrument have identical maturities.
cards.explanation: DV01 hedges are routinely used with instruments of different maturities, such as hedging a nominal bond with TIPS. No identical-maturity restriction exists.
cards.originalText: It can only be applied when the bond and the hedging instrument have identical maturities.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe a regression hedge and explain how it can improve a standard DV01-neutral hedge.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A regression hedge improves on a DV01-neutral hedge by setting the hedge amount from the historical relationship between the two yield changes (the regression slope), rather than assuming a one-for-one move.
cards.explanation: The regression hedge adjusts the DV01-neutral hedge by the historical slope beta of the exposure's yield changes on the hedge instrument's yield changes, so it reflects how the yields have actually co-moved.
cards.originalText: It sets the hedge amount using the historical relationship between the two yield changes (the regression slope), rather than assuming a one‑for‑one move.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe a regression hedge and explain how it can improve a standard DV01-neutral hedge.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A regression hedge eliminates basis risk completely, because the regression residual is forced to zero.
cards.explanation: The residual, which is the basis risk, remains. The regression only minimises its variance, and the standard error measures it.
cards.originalText: It eliminates basis risk completely, because the regression residual is forced to zero.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe a regression hedge and explain how it can improve a standard DV01-neutral hedge.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: In a single-variable regression hedge, the risk weight applied to the hedging instrument equals the regression slope coefficient beta from historical yield changes, which can differ from 1.0.
cards.explanation: The DV01-neutral hedge is the special case with a risk weight of 1. The regression hedge scales the hedge by the estimated beta.
cards.originalText: It equals the regression slope coefficient $\beta$ from historical yield changes, which can differ from 1.0.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe a regression hedge and explain how it can improve a standard DV01-neutral hedge.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: In a single-variable regression hedge, the risk weight applied to the hedging instrument equals the regression R-squared.
cards.explanation: The risk weight is the regression slope coefficient beta. R-squared measures the share of variance explained and is not used to scale the hedge.
cards.originalText: It equals the regression R‑squared, the proportion of variance explained.
cards.correction: In a single-variable regression hedge, the risk weight applied to the hedging instrument equals the regression slope coefficient.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe a regression hedge and explain how it can improve a standard DV01-neutral hedge.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: Compared with a yield-based DV01 hedge, a regression hedge minimizes the variance of the hedged position's profit and loss over the historical sample used to estimate it.
cards.explanation: Least squares chooses beta to minimise the sum of squared residuals, and the residual is the hedged position's P&L. The DV01 hedge makes no such minimisation.
cards.originalText: The regression hedge minimizes the profit and loss (P&L) variance of the hedged position.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe a regression hedge and explain how it can improve a standard DV01-neutral hedge.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A regression hedge is based on economic theory and future developments rather than on empirical analysis.
cards.explanation: A regression hedge is empirical: it uses the historical relationship between yield changes. It is not theory- or forecast-based.
cards.originalText: The regression hedge is based on economic theory and future developments rather than empirical analysis.
cards.correction: A regression hedge is based on empirical analysis of historical yield changes rather than on economic theory and future developments.

changes.from: economic theory and future developments rather than on empirical analysis
changes.to: empirical analysis of historical yield changes rather than on economic theory and future developments

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe a regression hedge and explain how it can improve a standard DV01-neutral hedge.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A key advantage of a regression hedge is that it gives an estimate of the hedged portfolio's volatility over time.
cards.explanation: The regression automatically yields a standard error. Multiplied by the position's DV01 it estimates the volatility of the hedged P&L.
cards.originalText: It gives an estimate of the hedged portfolio’s volatility over time.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe a regression hedge and explain how it can improve a standard DV01-neutral hedge.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A single-variable regression hedge assumes that the beta estimated from historical yield changes stays constant over the hedging horizon.
cards.explanation: Using the historical beta going forward presumes a stable relationship between the two yield changes. In practice beta varies, so it should be estimated over several periods.
cards.originalText: Beta is constant over time, so the historical estimate is assumed to hold over the hedging horizon.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: Principal component analysis decomposes yield curve changes into uncorrelated components ordered by the variance they explain, so a few components capture most of the term structure's volatility.
cards.explanation: PCA turns correlated rate changes into uncorrelated principal components. A few of them describe most term structure risk, which greatly simplifies hedging.
cards.originalText: It decomposes yield curve changes into uncorrelated components, ordered by the variance they explain, so a few components capture most of the term structure’s volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: Principal component analysis assumes that all rates are perfectly correlated, so a single factor describes every rate change.
cards.explanation: PCA estimates correlations from the data and does not assume perfect correlation. If rates were perfectly correlated only one component would exist.
cards.originalText: It assumes that all rates are perfectly correlated, so a single factor describes every rate change.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: Principal component analysis guarantees that the slope of the yield curve stays constant, so hedge ratios never need updating.
cards.explanation: PCA only describes how the curve has moved. Slope is itself one of the components, and it varies over time.
cards.originalText: It guarantees that the slope of the yield curve stays constant, so hedge ratios never need updating.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A principal components hedge computes the portfolio's exposure to the first few dominant principal components, such as level and slope, and chooses hedge positions that make the net exposure to each of them zero.
cards.explanation: Neutralising the few dominant, uncorrelated components hedges the bulk of term structure risk without hedging every rate separately.
cards.originalText: Compute the portfolio’s exposure to the first few (dominant) principal components, such as level and slope, and choose hedge positions that make the net exposure to each of them zero.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A principal components hedge sets the hedge ratio equal to the beta from regressing the portfolio's yield changes on the hedging instrument's yield changes.
cards.explanation: That describes a regression hedge, which uses one hedging instrument and a beta from historical yield changes. A PCA hedge zeroes exposure to the dominant principal components.
cards.originalText: Regress the portfolio’s yield changes on the hedging instrument’s yield changes and set the hedge ratio equal to the regression beta.
cards.correction: A regression hedge sets the hedge ratio equal to the beta from regressing the portfolio's yield changes on the hedging instrument's yield changes.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A principal components hedge computes only the portfolio DV01 and offsets it with a single instrument, assuming that all rates move in parallel.
cards.explanation: That describes a DV01 hedge, which covers only the level (parallel shift) factor. A PCA hedge also neutralises exposure to slope and other dominant components.
cards.originalText: Compute only the portfolio DV01 and offset it with a single instrument, assuming all rates move in parallel.
cards.correction: A DV01 hedge computes only the portfolio DV01 and offsets it with a single instrument, assuming that all rates move in parallel.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A covariance matrix of 13 rates has 78 distinct covariances plus 13 variances, whereas the covariance matrix of the corresponding principal components is diagonal.
cards.explanation: With 13 rates there are 13 x 12 / 2 = 78 distinct covariances. Principal components are uncorrelated, so their covariance matrix has only the variances on the diagonal.
cards.originalText: The rate covariance matrix has 78 distinct covariances (plus 13 variances), whereas the PC covariance matrix is diagonal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: Principal components are fundamental economic factors that the analyst specifies in advance, which is why names such as level, slope and short rate are assigned before the analysis is run.
cards.explanation: Principal components are derived from the covariance structure of the rates. Labels such as level, slope and short rate are descriptive interpretations given after estimation.
cards.originalText: The PCs are fundamental economic factors that the analyst specifies in advance, which is why the names level, slope and short rate are assigned before the analysis is run.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: Principal component analysis produces as many principal components as there are rates, but only a few are needed to characterize term structure fluctuations.
cards.explanation: For 13 rates PCA gives 13 components, yet the first three explain almost all of the variance, so they suffice for hedging.
cards.originalText: PCA produces 13 principal components, but only a few (here three) are needed to characterize term structure fluctuations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: Principal component analysis provides a single empirical, multi-factor description of term structure behavior that can be applied across all bonds.
cards.explanation: The same small set of factors describes all rates, unlike a regression hedge, which is tied to a few specific bonds.
cards.originalText: PCA provides a single empirical, multi‑factor description of term structure behavior that can be applied across all bonds.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: The first three principal components of the term structure, for example level, slope and short rate, tend to explain 90% or more of interest rate volatility.
cards.explanation: A few components capture the vast majority of term structure volatility, which is what makes PCA hedging practical.
cards.originalText: The first three components (for example, level, slope and short rate) tend to explain 90% or more of interest rate volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: In principal component analysis, the number of components needed grows roughly in proportion to the size of the portfolio, so for large portfolios a regression hedge becomes more practical.
cards.explanation: A small, fixed number of components describes the term structure for any number of bonds. The required number of factors does not scale with portfolio size, which is an advantage of PCA.
cards.originalText: The number of components needed grows roughly in proportion to the size of the portfolio, so for large portfolios a regression hedge becomes more practical.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: Because principal components are uncorrelated with each other, the variance of a rate equals the sum of the squared loadings on the principal components.
cards.explanation: Principal components are orthogonal by construction, so variances add with no covariance terms. The volatility of a rate is the square root of the sum of its squared loadings.
cards.originalText: Principal components are uncorrelated with each other, so the variance of a rate equals the sum of the squared loadings on the PCs.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Explain the difference between true and risk-neutral probabilities and apply this difference to interest rate drift.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In a calibrated interest rate tree, a bond's current market price equals its expected discounted value computed with real-world probabilities.
cards.explanation: The tree's probabilities are risk-neutral: they are the ones chosen so that the model price equals the observed market price. Real-world probabilities are not used for pricing in the tree.
cards.originalText: The bond’s current market price of \$952.79 assumes real‑world probabilities applied to its expected discounted value (EDV)
cards.correction: In a calibrated interest rate tree, a bond's current market price equals its expected discounted value computed with risk-neutral probabilities.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Explain the difference between true and risk-neutral probabilities and apply this difference to interest rate drift.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Extending an interest rate tree to further dates requires assumptions about future short-rate values and risk-neutral probabilities that recover a given set of bond prices.
cards.explanation: Each added date must be calibrated to the observed prices of additional bonds, so the new rates and probabilities have to reproduce them.
cards.originalText: Extending the tree to further dates (e.g., 2 years, 2.5 years) requires assumptions about future short‑rate values and risk‑neutral probabilities that recover a given set of bond prices

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Compared with noncallable bonds, callable bonds have their capital gains capped as yields rise.
cards.explanation: The issuer's call option caps price gains when yields fall, because the bond is likely to be called. When yields rise the call is far out of the money and the bond behaves like a noncallable bond.
cards.originalText: Capital gains are capped as yields rise.
cards.correction: Compared with noncallable bonds, callable bonds have their capital gains capped as yields fall.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Callable bonds have less price volatility than otherwise identical noncallable bonds.
cards.explanation: A callable bond is a noncallable bond minus an issuer call option. The short call dampens price moves, especially when yields are low.
cards.originalText: They have less price volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Compared with noncallable bonds, callable bonds have negative convexity.
cards.explanation: When yields are low the price is compressed toward the call price, so the price-yield curve flattens. That is negative convexity, whereas noncallable bonds are positively convex.
cards.originalText: They have negative convexity.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: For callable bonds, reinvestment rate risk rises at low yields.
cards.explanation: At low yields the issuer is likely to call, returning the call price plus coupon that must be reinvested at lower rates.
cards.originalText: At low yields, reinvestment rate risk rises.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: If a security's market price is below its model value, its option-adjusted spread is positive and the security is trading cheap relative to the model.
cards.explanation: A market price below model value requires a higher discount rate, so a positive constant spread must be added to the tree's short rates. A positive OAS corresponds to a cheap security.
cards.originalText: The OAS is positive; the security is trading cheap relative to the model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: If a security is not priced in accordance with the model (its OAS is not zero), its cash flows in the tree are discounted at the short-term rate plus the OAS.
cards.explanation: The OAS is the constant spread added to every one-period discount rate in the tree so that model value equals market price.
cards.originalText: The short‑term rate plus the OAS

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: If a security's OAS is not zero, its cash flows in the tree are discounted at the short-term rate minus the OAS.
cards.explanation: The OAS is added to the short rates. If the market price exceeds model value the OAS is simply negative.
cards.originalText: The short‑term rate minus the OAS
cards.correction: If a security's OAS is not zero, its cash flows in the tree are discounted at the short-term rate plus the OAS.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: When a bond's embedded options are removed, its option-adjusted spread reduces to the Z-spread, the constant spread over the spot curve that matches the bond's price.
cards.explanation: Without optionality, interest rate paths no longer affect cash flows, so volatility is irrelevant and the OAS collapses to the zero-volatility spread.
cards.originalText: Z‑spread

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: An option-adjusted spread requires the security to have an embedded option.
cards.explanation: OAS applies to any security valued on a tree, with or without an embedded option. It is the spread that equates the model value with the market price.
cards.originalText: The OAS cannot be interpreted because this is a CMT swap, and an OAS requires an embedded option.
cards.correction: An option-adjusted spread does not require the security to have an embedded option.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: If all investors agree with certainty that the current one-year spot rate of 1.0% will rise to 2.0% next year and to 3.0% the year after, the three-year spot rate should be almost 2.0% with annual compounding.
cards.explanation: The three-year spot rate is the geometric average of the expected one-year rates: (1.01 x 1.02 x 1.03) to the power 1/3 minus 1 is about 1.9967%.
cards.originalText: If all investors agree with certainty that the current one‑year spot rate of 1.0% will increase to 2.0% next year and again to 3.0% in two years, the three‑year spot rate should be almost 2.0% (with annual compounding)

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Pure (strict) expectations theory cannot be expected to fully characterize the term structure in practice.
cards.explanation: The actual curve also reflects risk premiums and convexity, which pure expectations theory ignores.
cards.originalText: It is unreasonable and impractical to expect pure (and strict or narrow) expectations theory to fully characterize the term structure in practice

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Under pure expectations, a downward-sloping term structure implies that investors are forecasting a drop in future short-term interest rates.
cards.explanation: With pure expectations, forward rates equal expected future spot rates, so a declining curve signals that lower short rates are expected.
cards.originalText: Under an assumption of pure expectations, it is valid to hypothesize (infer) from a downward‑sloping term structure that investors are forecasting a drop in future short‑term (e.g., one year) interest rates

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Apply a risk-neutral interest rate tree to assess the effect of volatility on the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: If investors are risk neutral and agree on a binomial interest rate tree, higher volatility decreases yields and increases bond prices because of the convexity effect.
cards.explanation: Bond prices are convex in rates, so by Jensen's inequality the expected discount factor exceeds the discount factor at the expected rate. A higher expected price means a lower yield, and the effect grows with volatility.
cards.originalText: Higher volatility will decrease the yield and increase bond prices due to the convexity effect

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Apply a risk-neutral interest rate tree to assess the effect of volatility on the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: If investors are risk neutral and agree on a binomial interest rate tree, higher volatility increases yields and decreases bond prices because of the convexity effect.
cards.explanation: The convexity effect raises expected bond prices and lowers yields. Higher yields would require a positive risk premium, which is absent here.
cards.originalText: Higher volatility will increase the yield and decrease bond prices due to the convexity effect
cards.correction: If investors are risk neutral and agree on a binomial interest rate tree, higher volatility decreases yields and increases bond prices because of the convexity effect.

changes.from: increases yields and decreases bond prices
changes.to: decreases yields and increases bond prices

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Apply a risk-neutral interest rate tree to assess the effect of volatility on the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: If investors are risk neutral and agree on a binomial interest rate tree, then with expected future short-term rates unchanged, greater interest rate volatility has no impact on the term structure.
cards.explanation: Holding expected rates fixed does not neutralise volatility. Through Jensen's inequality the expected bond price rises, so spot rates fall.
cards.originalText: If expected future short‑term interest rates are unchanged, greater interest rate volatility has no impact
cards.correction: If investors are risk neutral and agree on a binomial interest rate tree, then with expected future short-term rates unchanged, greater interest rate volatility lowers spot rates through the convexity effect.

changes.from: has no impact on the term structure
changes.to: lowers spot rates through the convexity effect

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Apply a risk-neutral interest rate tree to assess the effect of volatility on the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: When expected short-term rates are flat and the tree reflects a risk premium and significant volatility, yields rise at the short end of the term structure but fall at the long end.
cards.explanation: The risk premium grows roughly linearly with maturity, so it dominates at short maturities. The convexity effect grows roughly with the square of maturity and eventually overwhelms it, giving a humped curve.
cards.originalText: In the shorter end, the yield increases, but in the longer end, the yield decreases

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Apply a risk-neutral interest rate tree to assess the effect of volatility on the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: With flat expected short-term rates and a volatile risk-neutral binomial tree, the term structure of spot rates is slightly downward sloping because of convexity.
cards.explanation: With no risk premium, convexity is the only influence and averaging discount factors gives a higher price, hence a lower yield, at longer maturities.
cards.originalText: Slightly downward sloping, since discounting the terminal cash flow over longer time periods when interest rates exhibit volatility results in slightly lower spot rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Apply a risk-neutral interest rate tree to assess the effect of volatility on the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: When expected short-term rates and risk premiums are the same, long-dated spot rates in a higher-volatility market sit further below the expected short rate than in a lower-volatility market, and the gap widens with maturity.
cards.explanation: Only the convexity effect differs. It always lowers yields and is larger with higher volatility and longer maturity.
cards.originalText: Market A’s long‑dated spot rates will sit further below the expected short rate than Market B’s, and the gap will widen with maturity in both markets.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Estimate the convexity effect using Jensen’s inequality.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: As the maturity of a zero-coupon bond increases, all else equal, its price-yield curve becomes more convex.
cards.explanation: The value of convexity rises with maturity (for example about 1.84 bp for a 2-year zero and about 5 bp for a 3-year zero).
cards.originalText: more convex.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Identify the components into which the return on a bond can be decomposed, and calculate the expected return on a bond for a risk-averse investor.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: If investors are risk neutral (zero risk premium), the expected one-year return on a zero-coupon bond equals the short-term rate regardless of its maturity or duration.
cards.explanation: Expected return equals r0 plus lambda times duration, and lambda is zero. Convexity does not create an expected excess return.
cards.originalText: It is the same: both have an expected return equal to the short‑term rate $r_{0}$.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Identify the components into which the return on a bond can be decomposed, and calculate the expected return on a bond for a risk-averse investor.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: If investors are risk neutral, the greater convexity of a longer-maturity zero-coupon bond earns it a higher expected return than a shorter-maturity zero-coupon bond.
cards.explanation: Convexity raises the return component but lowers the forward rate by the same amount, so the net expected return is unchanged and equals the short-term rate.
cards.originalText: It is higher, because the 10‑year bond has greater convexity that earns extra return from rate volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Identify the components into which the return on a bond can be decomposed, and calculate the expected return on a bond for a risk-averse investor.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: The forward rate increases with the expected change in the short-term rate, scaled by the bond's duration.
cards.explanation: The expectations term in the forward rate decomposition is the expected change in the short rate multiplied by duration.
cards.originalText: The forward rate increases with the expected change in the short‑term rate, scaled by the bond’s duration.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Identify the components into which the return on a bond can be decomposed, and calculate the expected return on a bond for a risk-averse investor.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: The forward rate increases with the risk premium in proportion to the bond's duration.
cards.explanation: The risk premium term in the decomposition is lambda times duration.
cards.originalText: The forward rate increases with the risk premium in proportion to duration.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Identify the components into which the return on a bond can be decomposed, and calculate the expected return on a bond for a risk-averse investor.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Greater interest rate volatility lowers the forward rate through the convexity effect.
cards.explanation: The convexity effect is subtracted in the forward rate decomposition and grows with volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Identify the components into which the return on a bond can be decomposed, and calculate the expected return on a bond for a risk-averse investor.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Because convexity raises a bond's return, it also raises the forward rate, so greater volatility steepens the forward curve.
cards.explanation: Convexity enters the forward rate with a negative sign, so greater volatility lowers forward rates rather than raising them.
cards.originalText: Because convexity raises a bond’s return, it also raises the forward rate, so greater volatility steepens the forward curve.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Identify the components into which the return on a bond can be decomposed, and calculate the expected return on a bond for a risk-averse investor.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: The risk premium component in the decomposition of forward rates is the compensation investors demand for bearing interest rate risk.
cards.explanation: Risk-averse investors require extra return proportional to duration for bearing interest rate risk, and that extra return is the risk premium.
cards.originalText: The compensation investors demand for bearing interest rate risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Identify the components into which the return on a bond can be decomposed, and calculate the expected return on a bond for a risk-averse investor.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: The risk premium component in the decomposition of forward rates is the compensation investors demand for convexity effects.
cards.explanation: Convexity is a separate component, a Jensen's inequality effect of rate volatility. The risk premium is the compensation for bearing interest rate risk.
cards.originalText: The compensation investors demand for convexity effects.
cards.correction: The risk premium component in the decomposition of forward rates is the compensation investors demand for bearing interest rate risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Forcing negative rates in a short-rate tree to zero changes the original distribution only where rates are very low, leaving rates away from zero unchanged.
cards.explanation: Only nodes that would otherwise be negative are reset to zero, so the distribution is altered only in a very low rate environment. This is why the method may be preferred to switching to a non-negative distribution.
cards.originalText: It changes the original distribution only where rates are very low, leaving rates away from zero unchanged.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Forcing negative rates in a short-rate tree to zero introduces skewness and inappropriate volatilities across the entire distribution of rates.
cards.explanation: Skewness and inappropriate volatilities are drawbacks attached to non-negative distributions such as the lognormal, which reshape the whole distribution. Flooring at zero alters only the nodes that would be negative.
cards.originalText: It introduces skewness and inappropriate volatilities across the entire distribution of rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Using a lognormal distribution for the short rate avoids negative short-term rates in a term structure model.
cards.explanation: Lognormal rates cannot be negative, although this comes at the cost of skewness and inappropriate volatilities.
cards.originalText: Using a lognormal distribution for the short rate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Adjusting an interest rate tree so that any negative rate is set to zero avoids negative short-term rates in the model.
cards.explanation: Flooring negative tree rates at zero is a valid remedy and changes the distribution only at very low rates.
cards.originalText: Adjusting the interest rate tree so that any negative rate is set to zero.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Increasing the number of time steps so that the terminal distribution approaches a continuous normal distribution avoids negative short-term rates in a normally distributed short-rate model.
cards.explanation: A finer tree converges to a normal distribution, which still assigns positive probability to negative rates. It is not a remedy.
cards.originalText: Increasing the number of time steps so the terminal distribution approaches a continuous normal distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Negative short-term rates are a drawback of normally distributed rate models because investors can hold cash and earn a zero rate, so lending at a materially negative rate makes little economic sense.
cards.explanation: Cash offers a zero return, so no one would lend at a materially negative rate. A model that generates such rates is economically unrealistic.
cards.originalText: Investors can instead hold cash and earn a zero rate, so lending at a materially negative rate makes little economic sense.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The problem of negative rates in a normally distributed short-rate model becomes smaller as the investment horizon lengthens.
cards.explanation: Negative rates become more likely as the horizon lengthens, because the terminal distribution widens, and when the current rate is low.
cards.originalText: Negative rates occur only for short horizons, so the problem is smaller as the investment horizon lengthens.
cards.correction: The problem of negative rates in a normally distributed short-rate model becomes larger as the investment horizon lengthens.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Explain the need to consider conditional coverage in the backtesting framework.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: The conditional coverage statistic adds Kupiec's unconditional coverage statistic to Christoffersen's independence statistic and can reject a model even though its exception count is acceptable.
cards.explanation: The joint test checks both the level of exceptions and whether they cluster. It catches a model whose exceptions are right in number but wrong in timing.
cards.originalText: The conditional coverage statistic adds Kupiec’s $LR_{uc}$ to Christoffersen’s $LR_{ind}$ and can reject this model even though its exception count is acceptable.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Explain the need to consider conditional coverage in the backtesting framework.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Kupiec's proportion of failures test rejects a model because its exceptions are bunched together in time.
cards.explanation: Kupiec's test counts exceptions only and ignores their timing. Three clustered exceptions give the same failure rate as three spread-out ones, so clustering is detected by the independence test.
cards.originalText: Kupiec’s proportion of failures test should reject the model, because exceptions bunched within two weeks raise the failure rate measured by the test.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Explain the need to consider conditional coverage in the backtesting framework.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: If a correct VaR model is rejected because of bad luck, the error committed is a Type 2 error.
cards.explanation: Rejecting a correct model is a Type 1 error. A Type 2 error is failing to reject an incorrect model.
cards.originalText: If the model is in fact correct and is rejected because of bad luck, the error committed is a Type 2 error, the risk that the Basel zones are designed to keep low.
cards.correction: If a correct VaR model is rejected because of bad luck, the error committed is a Type 1 error.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Explain the need to consider conditional coverage in the backtesting framework.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Christoffersen's independence test detects dependence between exceptions at any lag.
cards.explanation: Christoffersen's test is a first-order Markov chain test, so it examines only whether an exception depends on the previous day's state. It does not detect dependence at longer distances.
cards.originalText: Christoffersen’s independence test would also reject a model whose exceptions occur exactly one week apart, because it detects dependence between exceptions at any lag.
cards.correction: Christoffersen's independence test detects dependence only between exceptions on consecutive days.

changes.from: detects dependence between exceptions at any lag
changes.to: detects dependence only between exceptions on consecutive days

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Differentiate among the three methods for mapping portfolios of fixed-income securities.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Principal mapping understates the true risk of a bond portfolio because it ignores the intervening coupon payments.
cards.explanation: Principal mapping overstates the true risk because it maps the whole market value to the maturity of the principal and ignores intervening coupons. It gives the highest VaR of the three mapping methods.
cards.originalText: Principal mapping understates the true risk of the portfolio, because it maps the market value to the average maturity of principal and ignores the intervening coupon payments.
cards.correction: Principal mapping overstates the true risk of a bond portfolio because it ignores the intervening coupon payments.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Differentiate among the three methods for mapping portfolios of fixed-income securities.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Principal mapping and duration mapping, unlike cash-flow mapping, fail to preserve the market value of the portfolio.
cards.explanation: All three mapping methods preserve market value. What separates cash-flow mapping is that it also preserves market risk more closely.
cards.originalText: Cash-flow mapping is preferred because it preserves the market value of the portfolio, a property that principal mapping and duration mapping do not have.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe some important considerations for a bank in assessing the conceptual soundness of a VaR model during the validation process.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A VaR model fitted to a desk's historical actual P&L does not reflect the risk of the positions now held, so it would neither reveal the tail risk of short out-of-the-money option positions nor fall when positions are cut.
cards.explanation: A short deep out-of-the-money put book earns small gains until the market moves, so its P&L history hides the tail risk. Only a VaR on the current positions shows the risk and responds to position changes.
cards.originalText: The P&L history does not reflect the risk of the positions now held, so VaR would neither reveal the tail risk in the puts nor fall when positions are cut.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe some important considerations for a bank in assessing the conceptual soundness of a VaR model during the validation process.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A GARCH(1,1) model fitted to a desk's daily P&L cannot capture volatility clustering.
cards.explanation: GARCH is designed to capture volatility clustering. The weakness of a VaR fitted to actual P&L is that the history does not reflect the positions currently held.
cards.originalText: A GARCH model fitted to actual P&L cannot respond to volatility clustering, so the reported VaR is too stable over time.
cards.correction: A GARCH(1,1) model fitted to a desk's daily P&L is designed to capture volatility clustering.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe some important considerations for a bank in assessing the conceptual soundness of a VaR model during the validation process.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Berkowitz and O'Brien found that a GARCH model fitted to banks' actual P&L was less accurate than banks' own VaR models.
cards.explanation: Berkowitz and O'Brien found the GARCH model on actual P&L was more accurate than the banks' VaR models. The concern is conceptual soundness for the positions held, not accuracy.
cards.originalText: A P&L-based GARCH VaR is known to be less accurate than banks’ positional VaR models, so it would fail a backtest.
cards.correction: Berkowitz and O'Brien found that a GARCH model fitted to banks' actual P&L was more accurate than banks' own VaR models.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe some important considerations for a bank in assessing the conceptual soundness of a VaR model during the validation process.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A VaR model fitted by applying a GARCH model to a desk's actual P&L history fails the conceptual soundness test, because its VaR would not fall when the trader cuts positions.
cards.explanation: The key purpose of a VaR model is to show how risk changes when positions change. A VaR built on actual P&L history is unaffected when positions are cut, whereas a VaR built on the pseudo history of the current portfolio does fall, so the P&L-based model is not fit for purpose.
cards.originalText: A VaR model fitted by applying a GARCH model to the desk’s actual P&L history would fail the conceptual soundness test, because its VaR would not fall when the trader cuts positions.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe some important considerations for a bank in assessing the conceptual soundness of a VaR model during the validation process.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Confidence intervals for historical-simulation VaR are typically narrower than those for filtered historical simulation, and they become narrower still when estimated over stress periods.
cards.explanation: Historical-simulation intervals are wider than those for filtered historical simulation, which gives more efficient VaR estimates, and they become particularly wide in stress periods.
cards.correction: Confidence intervals for historical-simulation VaR are typically wider than those for filtered historical simulation, and they become wider still when estimated over stress periods.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe some important considerations for a bank in assessing the conceptual soundness of a VaR model during the validation process.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Under the regulatory loss function, which penalizes only exceedances, a P&L-based GARCH VaR outperformed the banks' positional VaR models at most of the banks studied.
cards.explanation: Under the regulatory loss function the positional VaR significantly outperformed the P&L-based VaR in every case, reflecting the conservatism of banks' positional models. The P&L-based VaR won on accuracy only under the check loss function.
cards.originalText: Under the regulatory loss function, which penalizes only exceedances, a P&L-based GARCH VaR outperformed the banks’ positional VaR models at most of the banks studied.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe some important considerations for a bank in assessing the conceptual soundness of a VaR model during the validation process.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: The component VaR of a position with scarce valuation data is best estimated by regressing changes in portfolio value on the full time series of that position's value changes.
cards.explanation: The regression approach requires a full time series of the position's value changes, which is exactly what is missing. For such a position, component VaR is instead estimated from its loss on the VaR-determining day, or from an average of ordered observations near it.
cards.originalText: The component VaR of a position with scarce valuation data is best estimated by regressing changes in portfolio value on the full time series of that position’s value changes.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Because VaR is linear homogeneous in positions, component VaRs sum to total VaR, and a position's sensitivity depends on its portfolio share and on how its value moves with the portfolio.
cards.explanation: Linear homogeneity and Euler's equation make the component VaRs add up exactly to total VaR. Each component equals VaR times the position's share $w_i$ times its sensitivity $\beta_i$ to the portfolio.
cards.originalText: Because VaR is linear homogeneous in positions, component VaRs sum to total VaR, and a position’s sensitivity depends on its portfolio share and on how its value moves with the portfolio.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Because VaR is subadditive, component VaRs sum to more than total VaR, and the excess measures each position's contribution to diversification.
cards.explanation: Euler's equation, which follows from linear homogeneity, makes the component VaRs sum exactly to total VaR, not to more. Subadditivity is a separate property of risk measures.
cards.originalText: Because VaR is subadditive, component VaRs sum to more than total VaR, and the excess measures each position’s contribution to diversification.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Marginal VaR measures the change in portfolio value caused by a small change in a position's price, so it does not depend on the position's share of the portfolio.
cards.explanation: Marginal VaR is the change in VaR for a small change in the size of a position, not the change in portfolio value. It depends on the position's weight and on its sensitivity to the portfolio.
cards.originalText: Marginal VaR measures the change in portfolio value caused by a small change in a position’s price, so it does not depend on the position’s share of the portfolio.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: For a position valued on only a few days, component VaR in a historical-simulation model can be estimated from the change in the position's value on the day that determines the VaR, or from an average of ordered observations near that day.
cards.explanation: When the full time series needed for the regression is missing, component VaR can be approximated by the position's change in value on the scenario that sets the historical-simulation VaR. Because one day is noisy, an average of the ordered observations near it may be used instead.
cards.originalText: Use the change in the note’s value on the day that determines the historical-simulation VaR, or an average of ordered observations near that day.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A liquid proxy used in place of a thinly traded position is at least as volatile and as correlated with the portfolio as that position.
cards.explanation: A proxy may be less volatile or less correlated with the portfolio than the position it replaces, so using its beta can understate the position's contribution to VaR.
cards.originalText: Replace the note with a liquid proxy and use the proxy’s beta, since a proxy is at least as volatile and as correlated with the portfolio as the note.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A thinly traded position can be excluded from a VaR model because a material omission would already have produced an unexpected cluster of exceptions in the backtest.
cards.explanation: A backtest does not show whether the omission of a specific position is material. Sensitivity analysis is the tool used to assess that.
cards.originalText: Exclude the note, since a material omission would already have produced an unexpected cluster of exceptions in the desk’s backtest.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Sensitivity analysis tests whether the assumption that omitted terms and positions are immaterial holds, and gives a consistent way to prioritise which risk factors or higher-order terms to add.
cards.explanation: Sensitivity analysis checks whether the model is sensitive to its assumptions, such as omitted basis risk or a truncated Taylor expansion. It provides a consistent framework for quantifying omitted risks and for prioritising model changes.
cards.originalText: It tests whether the assumption that the omitted terms and positions are immaterial holds, and gives a consistent way to prioritise which risk factors or higher-order terms to add.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Sensitivity analysis proves that omitted positions and risk factors are immaterial whenever the VaR model passes its backtest with fewer than five exceptions over 250 days.
cards.explanation: A good backtest result does not prove that a particular omission is immaterial. Sensitivity analysis is used to test the immateriality assumption directly.
cards.originalText: It proves that the omissions are immaterial whenever the VaR model passes its backtest with fewer than five exceptions over the past 250 days.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Sensitivity analysis removes the need to track data proxies, because supervisors accept sensitivity results in place of an inventory of the risks not in VaR.
cards.explanation: Supervisors increasingly require banks to track their data proxies and their risks not in VaR. Sensitivity analysis supports that tracking but does not replace it.
cards.originalText: It removes the need to track data proxies, because supervisors accept sensitivity results in place of an inventory of the risks not in VaR.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Sensitivity analysis estimates omitted risks precisely, because the scarcer the data on a position, the easier its effect on VaR is to isolate.
cards.explanation: The scarcer the data on a position, the harder it is to estimate precisely the effect of omitting it from the VaR model.
cards.originalText: It estimates the omitted risks precisely, because the scarcer the data on a position, the easier its effect on VaR is to isolate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: When Jorion's asymptotic standard error of a quantile is used to place a confidence interval around VaR, the density at the VaR, $f(\text{VaR})$, must be specified, and assuming a normal density is probably a mistake because returns are non-normal.
cards.explanation: In the standard error formula the VaR, the sample size $T$ and the coverage level $c$ are known, so the hard input is the density at the VaR. Imposing a normal density is convenient but probably wrong for non-normal returns; non-parametric methods such as order statistics or the bootstrap avoid the problem.
cards.originalText: The density at the VaR, $f(\text{VaR})$, must be specified, and assuming a normal density is probably a mistake because returns are non-normal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: In Jorion's asymptotic standard error of a quantile for VaR, the coverage level $c$ and the sample size $T$ are unknown and must first be estimated from the pseudo history.
cards.explanation: The coverage level $c$ and the sample size $T$ are chosen and known, as is the VaR itself. The difficult input is the density at the VaR.
cards.originalText: The coverage level $c$ and the sample size $T$ are unknown and must first be estimated from the pseudo history.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Jorion's standard error formula for VaR gives intervals that are too narrow whenever more data are used, so $T$ must be kept to one year or less.
cards.explanation: More data correctly narrows the interval, since $T$ sits in the denominator of the standard error. Nothing in the formula makes the interval too narrow or limits $T$ to one year.
cards.originalText: The formula gives intervals that are too narrow whenever more data are used, so $T$ must be kept to one year or less.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: A quantile standard error formula cannot be applied to VaR, because VaR is not a quantile of the distribution of portfolio value changes.
cards.explanation: VaR is a quantile of the distribution of portfolio value changes, which is why a quantile standard error such as Jorion's can be applied to it.
cards.originalText: The formula cannot be applied to VaR at all, because VaR is not a quantile of the distribution of portfolio value changes.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: For a historical-simulation VaR, bootstrapping by resampling the pseudo history with replacement assumes daily value changes are independent, so dependence over time is not reflected.
cards.explanation: Drawing observations with replacement treats the changes as independent over time. The method is non-parametric, like historical simulation itself, but it does not capture dependence.
cards.originalText: For the historical-simulation VaR, resampling the pseudo history with replacement assumes daily value changes are independent, so dependence over time is not reflected.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: For a GARCH VaR, the bootstrap should resample the raw daily value changes directly, because the GARCH model already accounts for their dependence.
cards.explanation: Raw value changes are not independent and identically distributed under GARCH. The standardised residuals are, so they are resampled and the series is rebuilt from them.
cards.originalText: For the GARCH VaR, the analyst should resample the raw daily value changes directly, because the GARCH model already accounts for their dependence.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: In bootstrapping a confidence interval for a GARCH VaR, the parameters estimated on the original sample should be held fixed in every bootstrap sample, so that estimation risk is kept out.
cards.explanation: The GARCH equation is re-estimated on each bootstrap sample precisely so that estimation risk is included in the interval.
cards.originalText: For the GARCH VaR, the parameters estimated on the original sample should be held fixed in every bootstrap sample, so that estimation risk is kept out.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
