cards.loText: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Filtered historical simulation typically yields the widest VaR confidence intervals, because it combines GARCH volatility with an empirical distribution.
cards.explanation: Filtered historical simulation gives the narrowest intervals among the common approaches, because it provides more efficient VaR estimates. Plain historical simulation gives the wider ones.
cards.originalText: Filtered historical simulation typically yields the widest intervals of the three, because it combines GARCH volatility with an empirical distribution.
cards.correction: Filtered historical simulation typically yields the narrowest VaR confidence intervals, because it combines GARCH volatility with an empirical distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: In the Berkowitz and O'Brien comparison of US bank holding companies, positional VaR outperformed a GARCH P&L VaR in every case under the regulatory loss function, while the P&L VaR was more accurate at 16 of 19 banks under the check loss function.
cards.explanation: The regulatory loss function penalises only exceedances, so conservative positional VaR wins every time. The check loss function rewards accuracy, and there the P&L-based GARCH VaR won at sixteen of nineteen banks.
cards.originalText: Under the regulatory loss function the positional VaR outperformed in every case, while under the check loss function the P&L VaR was more accurate at 16 of 19 banks.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Under the regulatory loss function a GARCH P&L VaR outperformed banks' positional VaR at most banks, showing that positional VaR models are too aggressive.
cards.explanation: Under the regulatory loss function the positional VaR won in every case, which shows that banks' positional models are conservative, not aggressive.
cards.originalText: Under the regulatory loss function the P&L VaR outperformed the positional VaR at most banks, showing that positional VaR models are too aggressive.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Under the check loss function banks' positional VaR outperformed a GARCH P&L VaR at 16 of 19 banks, because conservatism is rewarded when accuracy is measured.
cards.explanation: The 16 of 19 result belongs to the P&L VaR, which was more accurate under the check loss function. Conservatism is rewarded under the regulatory loss function, not when accuracy is measured.
cards.originalText: Under the check loss function the positional VaR outperformed at 16 of 19 banks, because conservatism is rewarded when accuracy is measured.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them.
cards.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
cards.statement: Under both the regulatory and check loss functions positional and GARCH P&L VaR were statistically indistinguishable, so a plot of the two VaR series is sufficient benchmarking.
cards.explanation: The differences were significant in most cases. A plot of the two VaR series shows only their relative conservatism, not which is more accurate.
cards.originalText: Under both loss functions the two models were statistically indistinguishable, so a plot of the two VaR series is suﬀicient benchmarking.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The Christoffersen-Pelletier duration test models the time between exceedances, which is memoryless under a correct model, so it can flag clustering beyond a one-day lag.
cards.explanation: Under a correct model the durations between exceedances follow a memoryless exponential distribution, tested against a Weibull alternative. Unlike Christoffersen's first-order Markov test, it can detect dependence at distances greater than one lag.
cards.originalText: The Christoffersen–Pelletier duration test models the time between exceedances, which is memoryless under a correct model, so it can flag clustering beyond a one-day lag.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Kupiec's test would reject a model whose exceedances bunch together, so clustering can be ruled out when a model passes it.
cards.explanation: Kupiec's test only counts exceedances. Bunched exceedances give the same unconditional coverage statistic as spread-out ones, so passing it says nothing about clustering.
cards.originalText: Kupiec’s test would have rejected the model if exceedances had bunched together, so clustering can be ruled out.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The Ljung-Box test examines a single lag of the hit series, so it adds nothing beyond Christoffersen's independence test.
cards.explanation: The Ljung-Box test examines $m$ lags jointly, with $Q = T(T+2)\sum_{k=1}^{m} r_k^2/(T-k) \sim \chi^2(m)$. That is exactly what it adds beyond a single-lag test.
cards.originalText: The Ljung-Box test examines a single lag of the hit series, so it adds nothing beyond Christoffersen’s independence test.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The joint conditional coverage test is more powerful than either individual test when only one of the two properties is violated.
cards.explanation: Joint tests have significant limitations in detecting misspecification when only one of the two properties is violated. In that case the individual test can be more powerful.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Uniformity of the PITs on the interval from 0 to 1 is the counterpart of unconditional coverage, so a PIT test uses information from every percentile of the forecast distribution.
cards.explanation: Unconditional coverage at every VaR level is analogous to uniformity of the PITs. An exceedance count tests the model at a single percentile, whereas well-estimated PITs show how accurate the model is at any percentile of the forecast distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A hump-shaped PIT histogram, with realised P&L clustering in the middle of the forecast distribution, signals aggressive misspecification because the model distribution is too narrow.
cards.explanation: Realised P&L clustering in the middle of the forecast distribution signals conservative misspecification, because the model distribution is too wide. Aggressive misspecification, with a distribution too narrow, shows realised P&L in the tails.
cards.correction: A hump-shaped PIT histogram, with realised P&L clustering in the middle of the forecast distribution, signals conservative misspecification because the model distribution is too wide.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is the preferred uniformity test for a 99% VaR model, because it places more weight on the tails of the PIT distribution than the Anderson-Darling test.
cards.explanation: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test lacks sensitivity at the extremes. The Anderson-Darling test is the modification that places more weight on the tails and so better detects tail misspecification relevant to a 99% VaR model.
cards.correction: The Anderson-Darling test is the preferred uniformity test for a 99% VaR model, because it places more weight on the tails of the PIT distribution than the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Because PITs use the whole forecast distribution, a subportfolio that passes Kupiec's unconditional coverage test will also pass a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of PIT uniformity.
cards.explanation: Passing an exceedance test does not guarantee passing a distributional test. In the Iercosan et al. study 67% of subportfolios passed Kupiec but only 21% passed the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, so banks perform better on exceedance tests than on tests of the whole distribution.
cards.originalText: Because PITs use the whole forecast distribution, a subportfolio that passes Kupiec’s unconditional coverage test will also pass a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of PIT uniformity.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The probability integral transform for day $t+1$ is the previous day's forecast CDF evaluated at the realised P&L of day $t+1$, that is, the model's probability of a P&L at or below the one realised.
cards.explanation: The PIT is $p_{t+1} = F_t(\text{P\&L}_{t+1})$: the forecast distribution made on day $t$ evaluated at the realised P&L. It is a cumulative probability, so it always lies between 0 and 1.
cards.originalText: The PIT for day $t + 1$ is the previous day’s forecast CDF evaluated at the realised P&L of day $t + 1$, i.e. the model’s probability of a P&L at or below the one realised.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The probability integral transform for day $t+1$ is the realised P&L for day $t+1$ divided by the standard deviation forecast for that day.
cards.explanation: That ratio is the $z$-score for a zero-mean forecast. It must still be passed through the forecast CDF to become a PIT.
cards.originalText: The PIT for day $t + 1$ is the realised P&L for day $t + 1$ divided by the standard deviation forecast for that day.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The probability integral transform is a point-in-time version of the exceedance indicator, equal to 1 when the loss exceeds VaR and 0 otherwise.
cards.explanation: The 0/1 series is the exceedance (hit) indicator used in exceedance-based backtests. A PIT is a cumulative probability between 0 and 1 obtained from the forecast CDF, and the name has nothing to do with point in time.
cards.originalText: The PIT is a point-in-time version of the exceedance indicator, equal to 1 when the loss exceeds VaR and 0 otherwise.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The probability integral transform for day $t+1$ is the forecast CDF re-estimated after observing day $t+1$'s P&L, evaluated at the VaR threshold.
cards.explanation: The PIT uses the forecast made before the outcome, evaluated at the realised P&L rather than at the VaR threshold. A forecast re-estimated after the outcome is no longer a forecast.
cards.originalText: The PIT for day $t + 1$ is the forecast CDF re-estimated after observing day $t + 1$’s P&L, evaluated at the VaR threshold.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The probability integral transform puts days with different forecast distributions on one comparable scale from 0 to 1.
cards.explanation: Raw returns cannot be compared across days when the forecast standard deviation differs. The PIT evaluates each outcome under its own forecast distribution, so outcomes become comparable.
cards.originalText: Day 15 is the more extreme outcome relative to its own forecast; the PIT puts days with different forecast distributions on one comparable \[0,1\] scale.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Probability integral transforms from different days can be compared only if the forecast standard deviation is the same every day.
cards.explanation: The PIT exists precisely because forecasts change from day to day. Evaluating each outcome under its own forecast CDF makes values comparable across days.
cards.originalText: Neither PIT is informative, because PITs can only be compared when the forecast standard deviation is the same every day.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A PIT close to zero indicates a large gain relative to the forecast distribution.
cards.explanation: A PIT near zero means a loss deep in the left tail of the forecast distribution. A large gain would give a PIT near 1.
cards.originalText: A PIT close to zero indicates a large gain relative to the forecast, so Day 15 was an unusually good day for the desk.
cards.correction: A PIT close to one indicates a large gain relative to the forecast distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A pooled PIT histogram that is humped across the middle deciles but spikes in the lowest and highest bins indicates models that are conservative in the body of the distribution but whose tails are thinner than realised P&L requires, so extreme outcomes are understated.
cards.explanation: The hump means outcomes cluster near the centre of the forecasts, so the body is too wide. Spikes at both ends mean extreme outcomes land beyond the forecast tails more often than predicted, so the tails are too thin.
cards.originalText: The models are conservative in the body of the distribution, but their tails are thinner than realised P&L requires, so extreme outcomes are understated.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A PIT histogram that is humped across the middle deciles but also spikes in the lowest and highest bins indicates forecast distributions that are too wide everywhere, including the tails.
cards.explanation: A distribution too wide everywhere would have thin ends in the PIT histogram, not spikes. Spikes at the ends show the tails are too thin.
cards.originalText: The models are uniformly conservative: the forecast distributions are too wide everywhere, including the tails.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A PIT histogram that is humped across the middle deciles but also spikes in the lowest and highest bins indicates models that are aggressive in the body but conservative in the tails, so the 99% VaR overstates extreme losses.
cards.explanation: The hump shows conservatism in the body, and the end spikes show that the tails are too thin, so extreme losses are understated. Both halves of the statement are reversed.
cards.originalText: The models are aggressive in the body but conservative in the tails, so the 99% VaR overstates extreme losses.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The shape of a PIT histogram reflects serial dependence of the PITs rather than any miscalibration of the forecast distribution.
cards.explanation: A histogram shows the distribution of PITs, not their order in time. Serial dependence needs a separate test, and the histogram shape signals miscalibration of the forecast distribution.
cards.originalText: The shape reflects serial dependence of the PITs rather than any miscalibration of the forecast distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: To test PITs for independence following Berkowitz (2001), each PIT is transformed into a standard normal value with the inverse normal CDF, and the transformed series is then tested for dependence, for example by regressing it on its own lag and on lagged P&L.
cards.explanation: PITs live on the bounded interval from 0 to 1, so each is mapped to $\Phi^{-1}(p_t)$ to avoid inference problems due to bounded support. Significant coefficients on lagged values then show that the forecasts ignore information already available.
cards.originalText: Transform each PIT into a standard normal value with the inverse normal CDF, then test the transformed series for dependence, for example by regressing it on its own lag and on lagged P&L.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: The Anderson-Darling test can be used to test whether PITs are independent over time, because it weights the tails where clustered losses show up.
cards.explanation: The Anderson-Darling test is a goodness-of-fit test of the PIT distribution. It says nothing about the order of PITs in time.
cards.originalText: Apply the Anderson-Darling test to the PITs, because it weights the tails where clustered losses show up.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Kupiec's proportion of failures test applied to the count of exceedances tests whether PITs are independent over time.
cards.explanation: Kupiec's test examines the number of exceedances, which is unconditional coverage. It does not test independence.
cards.originalText: Count the exceedances of the 99% VaR and apply Kupiec’s proportion of failures test to the count.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: Because PITs have bounded support between 0 and 1, the normal transformation is unnecessary and raw PITs can be regressed directly on their lags to test independence.
cards.explanation: The bounded support is exactly why the normal transformation is used: it is easier to test for dependence outside a bounded range.
cards.originalText: Regress the raw PITs directly on their lags, because their \[0,1\] support makes the normal transformation unnecessary.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: US bank VaR models perform better on exceedance tests than on tests of the whole PIT distribution, and the Anderson-Darling test, which weights the tails, has the most power to detect the misspecification.
cards.explanation: In the Iercosan et al. study 67% of subportfolios passed Kupiec's test, but only 11% to 21% passed the PIT uniformity tests. Anderson-Darling rejected the most, as the tail-weighted and most powerful test.
cards.originalText: The models perform better on exceedance tests than on tests of the whole distribution, and Anderson-Darling, which weights the tails, has the most power to detect the misspecification.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: A model that passes Kupiec's unconditional coverage test has a correctly specified forecast distribution.
cards.explanation: Kupiec's test checks exceedances at a single percentile only. Passing it does not validate the rest of the forecast distribution.
cards.originalText: The PIT tests must be wrong, because a model that passes Kupiec’s test has a correctly specified forecast distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
cards.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models
cards.statement: When the most tail-sensitive uniformity test rejects the most models, the models' main weakness lies in the centre of the forecast distribution.
cards.explanation: A tail-sensitive test rejecting the most models points to misspecification in the tails, not the centre.
cards.originalText: Because the most tail-sensitive test rejected the most subportfolios, the models’ main weakness lies in the centre of the forecast distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Calculate a mean reversion rate using standard regression and calculate the corresponding autocorrelation.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: A negative slope when the change in a correlation is regressed on its previous level means that correlations tend to move away from their long-run mean, so the series shows no mean reversion.
cards.explanation: A negative slope of the change on the level is exactly what mean reversion means: when the level is above the mean the expected change is negative, and below it the change is positive.
cards.originalText: The negative slope of −0.7903 means correlations tend to move away from their long-run mean, so the series shows no mean reversion.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Calculate a mean reversion rate using standard regression and calculate the corresponding autocorrelation.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: When the change in a variable is regressed on its previous level, the long-run mean implied by the regression equals the value of the intercept.
cards.explanation: The intercept equals the mean reversion rate times the long-run mean, $a\mu$. The long-run mean is the intercept divided by the mean reversion rate $a$.
cards.originalText: The long-run mean correlation implied by the regression is 25.6%, the value of the intercept.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: The Johnson SB distribution has four parameters, two shape parameters, one location and one scale parameter, and is flexible enough to fit the bounded, skewed shape of correlations.
cards.explanation: In Meissner's study the Johnson SB has shape parameters $\gamma$ and $\delta$, a location $\mu$ and a scale $\sigma$. It is bounded and can take skewed shapes, which suits a variable such as correlation.
cards.originalText: A four-parameter distribution with two shape parameters, one location and one scale parameter, flexible enough to fit the bounded, skewed shape of correlations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: The Johnson SB distribution is a one-parameter distribution defined on positive values only, like the chi-squared distribution.
cards.explanation: That describes the chi-squared distribution. The Johnson SB has four parameters, and correlations can be negative.
cards.originalText: A one-parameter distribution defined on positive values only, like the chi-squared distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: The Johnson SB distribution is a three-parameter distribution with location, scale and shape, used to model block maxima in extreme value theory.
cards.explanation: That describes the generalised extreme value (GEV) distribution. The Johnson SB has four parameters.
cards.originalText: A three-parameter distribution (location, scale and shape) used to model block maxima in extreme value theory.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: The Johnson SB distribution is an unbounded, heavy-tailed distribution like the Pareto, chosen because correlations have fat right tails.
cards.explanation: The Johnson SB is a bounded distribution, and correlations are bounded too. A Pareto-type tail describes unbounded heavy tails, not the shape of correlations.
cards.originalText: An unbounded, heavy-tailed distribution like the Pareto, chosen because correlations have fat right tails.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: In Meissner's empirical study, the Johnson SB distribution best fits equity and default probability correlations, while the generalised extreme value distribution best fits bond correlations.
cards.explanation: Default probability correlations resemble equity correlations and are best replicated by the Johnson SB. Bond correlations have a more normal shape and are best fitted by the generalised extreme value distribution.
cards.originalText: Use the Johnson SB distribution for equity and default probability correlations, and the generalised extreme value distribution for bond correlations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: In Meissner's empirical study, the Johnson SB distribution gave the best fit for equity, bond and default probability correlations alike.
cards.explanation: Bond correlations have a more normal shape and are best fitted by the generalised extreme value distribution, not the Johnson SB.
cards.originalText: Use the Johnson SB distribution for all three correlation types, since it gave the best fit for equity, bond and default probability correlations alike.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: In Meissner's empirical study, the Johnson SB distribution best fits equity and bond correlations, while the generalised extreme value distribution best fits default probability correlations.
cards.explanation: The bond and default probability fits are the other way round: default probability correlations resemble equity correlations (Johnson SB), and bond correlations fit the generalised extreme value distribution.
cards.originalText: Use the Johnson SB distribution for equity and bond correlations, and the generalised extreme value distribution for default probability correlations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: Equity correlations are best fitted by the Johnson SB distribution in expansions but by the normal distribution in recessions, when correlations are high.
cards.explanation: Fitting equity correlations by state of the economy gave results that were slightly but not significantly different. The normal distribution fits equity correlations poorly in any state.
cards.originalText: Use the Johnson SB distribution for equity correlations in expansions, but switch to the normal distribution in recessions when correlations are high.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A 95% interval for the regression constant that includes zero shows that the data are consistent with parallel shifts in the two yields.
cards.explanation: Parallel shifts concern the slope: they imply a beta of one. The constant does not enter the hedge ratio and says nothing about whether the shifts are parallel.
cards.originalText: It is appropriate: the 95% interval for the constant includes zero, so the data are consistent with parallel shifts in the two yields.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A DV01-neutral hedge minimizes the variance of the hedged P&L, because by construction the DV01s of the two legs are equal.
cards.explanation: Variance minimisation is the property of the regression hedge. Equal DV01s minimise the variance only if the regression beta equals one, that is, if yields shift in parallel.
cards.originalText: It is appropriate: equal DV01s on the two legs make it the hedge that minimizes the variance of the hedged P&L.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A DV01-neutral hedge of a 40-year corporate bond with a 30-year Treasury can lose money because it assumes the two yields change by the same number of basis points, while the corporate bond trades at a changing spread to Treasuries and 40- and 30-year rates are not perfectly correlated.
cards.explanation: A DV01-neutral hedge is exact only if both yields move by the same number of basis points. Changing spreads and imperfect correlation between the two maturities create basis risk that the hedge cannot address, even on small yield moves.
cards.originalText: The hedge assumes the two yields change by the same number of basis points, but the corporate bond trades at a changing spread to Treasuries and 40- and 30-year rates are not perfectly correlated.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: Because DV01 is a first-order measure, a DV01-neutral hedge fails only when yields move by large amounts and is exact for small daily moves.
cards.explanation: The parallel-shift assumption fails on small moves too. If the two yields do not change by the same number of basis points, the hedge loses money whatever the size of the move.
cards.originalText: DV01 is a first-order measure, so the hedge fails only when yields move by large amounts; for small daily moves it is exact.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A DV01-neutral hedge sets the face amounts of the two bonds equal, so it ignores the difference in their price sensitivities to yield changes.
cards.explanation: A DV01-neutral hedge equates the DV01s of the two positions, not their face amounts, so it does account for the bonds' different price sensitivities.
cards.originalText: The hedge sets the face amounts of the two bonds equal, so it ignores the difference in their price sensitivities to yield changes.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A DV01-neutral hedge relies on a regression estimated over a historical window, so it becomes unreliable when the relationship between the two yields changes.
cards.explanation: Dependence on a historical regression is a weakness of the regression hedge. A DV01-neutral hedge uses no regression; it simply assumes the two yields change by the same number of basis points.
cards.originalText: The hedge relies on a regression estimated over a historical window, so it becomes unreliable when the relationship between the two yields changes.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe a regression hedge and explain how it can improve a standard DV01-neutral hedge.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: When estimating a regression hedge, too short a window may not give statistically reliable estimates and too long a window may include less relevant data, and an earlier episode can be more relevant than the recent past.
cards.explanation: Choosing the estimation window is part of the art of regression hedging. For example, if the central bank is expected to raise rates, an earlier tightening episode may be more relevant than a recent period of unchanged rates.
cards.originalText: Too short a window may not give statistically reliable estimates and too long a window may include less relevant data, and an earlier episode can be more relevant than the recent past.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe a regression hedge and explain how it can improve a standard DV01-neutral hedge.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A longer estimation window is always preferable for a regression hedge, because more observations reduce the standard errors of the regression coefficients.
cards.explanation: More data reduce standard errors but may bring in less relevant regimes, so longer is not always better.
cards.originalText: A longer estimation window is always preferable, because more observations reduce the standard errors of the regression coeﬀicients.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe a regression hedge and explain how it can improve a standard DV01-neutral hedge.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: Because least-squares estimates are unbiased, the in-sample standard error of a regression hedge is a reliable guide to future hedged P&L volatility, so out-of-sample tests add little.
cards.explanation: Unbiasedness is an in-sample property under the model's assumptions. Unstable coefficients show up as poor out-of-sample performance, so out-of-sample tests matter.
cards.originalText: Because least-squares estimates are unbiased, the in-sample standard error of the regression is a reliable guide to future hedged P&L volatility, so out-of-sample tests add little.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe a regression hedge and explain how it can improve a standard DV01-neutral hedge.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: The most recent period is the relevant one for a regression hedge by definition, because the hedge assumes that beta changes each day with the latest data.
cards.explanation: A regression hedge assumes a constant beta over the estimation window, and the recent past is not relevant by definition; an earlier episode can be more relevant.
cards.originalText: The most recent period is the relevant one by definition, because a regression hedge assumes that beta changes each day with the latest data.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: In a principal component analysis of swap rates, the short-rate component is most important at the long end of the curve, where it explains the largest share of each rate's variance.
cards.explanation: The short-rate component matters at the short end of the curve. It explains about half of the variance of the one-year rate but under 1% of the variance of the 30-year rate.
cards.originalText: The short-rate PC is most important at the long end of the curve, where it explains the largest share of each rate’s variance.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: Because three principal components explain nearly all of the variance of swap rates, hedging a position with any three swaps removes all but a small fraction of its risk.
cards.explanation: The share of rate variance explained describes the rates, not the risk left after an arbitrary three-swap hedge. A hedge must be solved so that exposures to each principal component are neutralised.
cards.originalText: Because three PCs explain 99.84% of the total variance, hedging a position with any three swaps removes all but 0.16% of its risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A PCA hedge using two hedging swaps can neutralize exposure to only two principal components, so the residual exposure to the third must be measured and either accepted or hedged.
cards.explanation: Each principal component hedged adds one equation, and two hedging swaps can solve only two equations. The exposure to the remaining component is left over.
cards.originalText: A PCA hedge using two hedging swaps can neutralize exposure to only two PCs, so the residual exposure to the third PC must be measured and either accepted or hedged.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A PCA hedge is efficient because the principal components are constructed to be highly correlated, so neutralizing the level component also neutralizes the others.
cards.explanation: Principal components are constructed to be uncorrelated, which is why each one needs its own neutralising equation.
cards.originalText: A PCA hedge is eﬀicient because the principal components are constructed to be highly correlated, so neutralizing the level PC also neutralizes the others.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A PCA hedge of a butterfly always sets the risk weights of the two hedging swaps so that they sum to 100% of the DV01 of the position being hedged.
cards.explanation: Risk weights sum to 100% only under parallel shifts. A PCA butterfly hedge can need risk weights that sum to more or less than 100%.
cards.originalText: A PCA hedge of the butterfly sets the risk weights of the two hedging swaps so that they always sum to 100% of the DV01 of the position being hedged.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Explain the difference between true and risk-neutral probabilities and apply this difference to interest rate drift.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Risk-neutral probabilities put extra weight on high-rate, low-price states, so the risk-neutral drift exceeds the true drift.
cards.explanation: Investors pay less than expected discounted value for risky bonds, so risk-neutral probabilities must put more weight on states where bond prices are low, that is, where rates are high. This gives a positive risk-neutral drift relative to the true drift.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Explain the difference between true and risk-neutral probabilities and apply this difference to interest rate drift.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Risk-neutral probabilities are the market's best forecasts of future rate moves, which is why they recover market prices.
cards.explanation: Risk-neutral probabilities are not forecasts. They embed investors' aversion to price risk, which is exactly why they differ from true probabilities.
cards.originalText: Risk-neutral probabilities are the market’s best forecasts of future rate moves, which is why they recover market prices.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Explain the difference between true and risk-neutral probabilities and apply this difference to interest rate drift.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Any tree whose up probability differs from 0.50 is a risk-neutral tree, since true probabilities are always 0.50.
cards.explanation: True probabilities need not be 0.50. A probability is risk-neutral because it recovers market prices, not because of its value.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Explain the difference between true and risk-neutral probabilities and apply this difference to interest rate drift.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The arbitrage price of an option on a zero depends directly on the true probabilities of the up and down moves.
cards.explanation: The replicating portfolio, and so the arbitrage price, does not depend directly on true probabilities. They enter only through current bond prices.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: For a security with a positive OAS that is hedged against factor risk and financed at the short-term rate, if the model is correct, the expected return is the OAS plus any gain from the OAS converging toward zero.
cards.explanation: Hedging removes the interest rate term, and financing at the short rate pays away the short-rate part of the carry. What remains is the OAS, plus any gain if the OAS converges toward zero, which is why OAS is used as a relative value measure.
cards.originalText: The OAS plus any gain from the OAS converging toward zero.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: For a security with a positive OAS that is hedged against factor risk and financed at the short-term rate, if the model is correct, the expected return is the short-term rate plus the OAS, whatever the financing cost.
cards.explanation: Financing at the short rate cancels the short-rate component of the return, leaving the OAS rather than the short rate plus the OAS.
cards.originalText: The short-term rate plus the OAS, whatever the financing cost.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: For a security with a positive OAS that is hedged against factor risk and financed at the short-term rate, if the model is correct, the expected return is the risk premium on interest rate risk plus the OAS.
cards.explanation: The risk premium terms cancel once the factor risk is hedged away, so they are not part of the expected return.
cards.originalText: The risk premium on interest rate risk plus the OAS.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: For a security with a positive OAS that is hedged against factor risk and financed at the short-term rate, if the model is correct, the expected return is the short-term rate only, because the factor risk is hedged.
cards.explanation: This ignores the OAS that the cheap security earns. Net of financing, the expected return is the OAS plus any convergence gain.
cards.originalText: The short-term rate only, because the factor risk is hedged.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: When investors know future one-year rates with certainty and are risk neutral, forward rates equal the expected one-year rates, so the forward curve is completely determined by expectations.
cards.explanation: With certainty there is no volatility, so no convexity effect, and risk neutrality removes any risk premium. Forward rates then equal the expected one-year rates exactly.
cards.originalText: The one-year forward rates are 8%, 7% and 6%, so the forward curve slopes downward and is completely determined by expectations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: When investors know future one-year rates with certainty, forward rates lie below the expected one-year rates because bond prices are convex in interest rates.
cards.explanation: The convexity effect needs volatility. With certain rates there is none, so forward rates equal expected rates exactly.
cards.originalText: Forward rates lie below the expected one-year rates, because bond prices are convex in interest rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: When investors are risk neutral, forward rates lie above the expected one-year rates because investors demand compensation for holding longer bonds.
cards.explanation: Risk neutrality excludes any risk premium, so no compensation for holding longer bonds is demanded and forward rates are not pushed above expected rates.
cards.originalText: Forward rates lie above the expected one-year rates, because investors demand compensation for holding longer bonds.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Detailed short-horizon views, such as central bank meetings and funding pressures, can be used to shape the front of the forward curve, while a long-run macroeconomic estimate of the real rate plus inflation can anchor the level of long-horizon expected rates.
cards.explanation: Short-horizon views are specific enough to shape the front of the curve. Far out, expectations are not granular, but macroeconomics can anchor the level, for example 1% long-run real rate plus 3% long-run inflation gives a 4% expected short rate.
cards.originalText: Use the short-horizon views to shape the front of the curve, and the 4% macroeconomic estimate to anchor the level of long-horizon expected rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Money market analysis of near-term events can be used to project how the expected one-year rate in 29 years differs from the expected one-year rate in 30 years.
cards.explanation: Money market analysis is unlikely to reveal any difference between expected one-year rates in 29 and in 30 years. Expectations at long horizons are not granular.
cards.originalText: Use the short-horizon views to project how the expected one-year rate in 29 years differs from the expected one-year rate in 30 years.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Macroeconomic estimates can set both the level and the detailed shape of the long end of the curve, because inflation forecasts are as granular as views on individual central bank meetings.
cards.explanation: Macroeconomic estimates can anchor the level of long-horizon expected rates, but they are not granular enough to give the long end a detailed shape.
cards.originalText: Use the macroeconomic estimate to set both the level and the detailed shape of the long end, because inflation forecasts are as granular as meeting-date views.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: The long end of the curve is determined by convexity alone, so expectations beyond one year can be ignored.
cards.explanation: Expectations still set the level of the long end of the curve, and the risk premium also acts there.
cards.originalText: Ignore expectations beyond one year, because the long end of the curve is determined by convexity alone.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Under the pure expectations hypothesis, $\lambda = 0$, and the natural no-change scenario is that short-term rates evolve as expected so that forward rates are realized.
cards.explanation: With $\lambda = 0$ forward rates are set by expected rate changes, so the no-change scenario is that short rates evolve as expected and forwards are realised.
cards.originalText: Under the pure expectations hypothesis, $\lambda= 0$, and the natural no-change scenario is that short-term rates evolve as expected so that forward rates are realized.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Under the pure expectations hypothesis, $E[dr/dt] = 0$, and the natural no-change scenario is that the term structure stays unchanged.
cards.explanation: Both statements belong to the pure risk premium hypothesis. Under pure expectations $\lambda = 0$ and the no-change scenario is that forward rates are realised.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Under the pure risk premium hypothesis, forward rates are set by expected rate changes, so an upward-sloping curve signals that rates are expected to rise.
cards.explanation: Under the pure risk premium hypothesis there are no expected rate changes, so an upward slope reflects the risk premium, not expected rises.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Under the pure risk premium hypothesis, the natural no-change scenario is that short-term rates evolve so that forward rates are realized.
cards.explanation: Forward rates being realised is the no-change scenario of the pure expectations hypothesis. Under pure risk premium the no-change scenario is that short rates stay the same and the term structure is unchanged.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Forward rates alone cannot split a rise between a higher expected path of short-term rates and a higher risk premium, because a drift of a given number of basis points has the same pricing effect as a risk premium of that number per year of duration.
cards.explanation: Expectations enter forwards as $D\,E[dr]/dt$ and the risk premium as $\lambda D$, so both raise forwards more at longer terms. Increasing either by the same amount is indistinguishable in observed forward rates; only the combined risk-neutral drift is observable.
cards.originalText: Forward rates alone cannot split the move, because a drift of a given number of basis points has the same pricing effect as a risk premium of that number per year of duration.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: A rise in forward rates that is larger at longer terms must be a higher risk premium, because a higher expected path of short-term rates would raise all forward rates by the same amount.
cards.explanation: The expectations term is also scaled by duration, so expected rate rises do not move all forwards equally.
cards.originalText: The move must be a higher risk premium, because a higher expected path of short-term rates would raise all forward rates by the same amount.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: A rise in forward rates that is larger at longer terms must reflect higher expected rates, because a risk premium depends on the characteristics of individual bonds rather than on duration.
cards.explanation: The risk premium does not depend on the characteristics of any individual bond. It enters as $\lambda D$, scaled by duration.
cards.originalText: The move must reflect higher expected rates, because a risk premium depends on the characteristics of individual bonds rather than on duration.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Expectations and risk premium can be separated by comparing forward rates with the risk-neutral probabilities used in a pricing tree.
cards.explanation: Risk-neutral probabilities embed the combined drift. They do not reveal how much of it is expectation and how much is risk premium.
cards.originalText: The two can be separated by comparing forward rates with the risk-neutral probabilities used in a pricing tree.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Higher expected short-term rates and a higher risk premium each raise forward rates in proportion to duration, so long-dated bonds lose more value than short-dated bonds.
cards.explanation: The expectations term $D\,E[dr]/dt$ and the risk premium term $\lambda D$ both scale with duration, so their effect on forwards is largest at the long end. Higher volatility works through the convexity term and offsets part of this at long maturities.
cards.originalText: Higher expected short-term rates and a higher risk premium each raise forward rates in proportion to duration, so long-dated gilts lose more value than short-dated gilts.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: A rise in interest rate volatility raises long-term forward rates through the convexity term, so long-dated bonds cheapen relative to short-dated bonds for that reason.
cards.explanation: The convexity term $-\frac{1}{2}C\sigma^2$ lowers long forward rates when volatility rises. Volatility supports long bond prices rather than cheapening them.
cards.originalText: The rise in rate volatility raises long-term forward rates through the convexity term, so long-dated gilts cheapen relative to short-dated gilts for that reason.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: A higher risk premium raises all forward rates by the same number of basis points, because the premium per unit of duration does not depend on any individual bond.
cards.explanation: The premium per unit of duration $\lambda$ is common to all bonds, but it enters as $\lambda D$, so the effect grows with duration and is not parallel.
cards.originalText: The higher risk premium raises all forward rates by the same number of basis points, because the premium per unit of duration does not depend on any individual bond.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Observed forward rates allow an analyst to fully separate the part of a move due to higher expected inflation from the part due to a higher risk premium.
cards.explanation: The term structure cannot on its own separate expectations of rate changes from risk premium. Only their combined risk-neutral drift is observable.
cards.originalText: Observed forward rates allow the analyst to fully separate the part of the move due to higher expected inflation from the part due to a higher risk premium.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Estimate the convexity effect using Jensen’s inequality.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: When rates are volatile, the expected one-year rate is the same at every date and there is no risk premium, the value of convexity increases with rate volatility and with maturity, so forward rates lie below the expected short rate and fall further at longer terms.
cards.explanation: By Jensen's inequality the expected price of a zero exceeds the price at the expected rate, which pushes implied forwards below the expected rate. The reduction is $\frac{1}{2}C\sigma^2$, which rises with volatility and, through the convexity $C$, with term.
cards.originalText: The value of convexity increases with rate volatility and with maturity, so forward rates lie below the expected short rate and fall further at longer terms.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Estimate the convexity effect using Jensen’s inequality.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Because bond prices are convex in rates, the price of a zero at the expected rate exceeds its expected price, so forward rates lie above the expected short rate.
cards.explanation: Jensen's inequality goes the other way: the expected price exceeds the price at the expected rate, so forward rates lie below the expected short rate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Estimate the convexity effect using Jensen’s inequality.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: Convexity lowers every forward rate by the same number of basis points, because the volatility of each one-year rate transition is the same at every node.
cards.explanation: Equal per-transition volatility does not make the effect equal across terms. The convexity effect grows with the convexity of longer zeros, so longer forwards are lowered by more.
cards.originalText: Convexity lowers every forward rate by the same number of basis points, because the volatility of each one-year rate transition in the tree is the same at every node.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.loText: Estimate the convexity effect using Jensen’s inequality.
cards.reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
cards.statement: A position that is long convexity earns an expected return above the short rate in every scenario, because convexity adds to return whether rates rise or fall.
cards.explanation: The forward rate is reduced by exactly the convexity gain, so the expected return condition leaves no net advantage to convexity.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In a normal short-rate model, the possibility of negative rates matters most for an option to buy a long-term bond at a yield of 0%, which the model overvalues, and much less for a coupon bond.
cards.explanation: A coupon bond depends mostly on the average rate path, so a small probability of negative rates does not rule the model out. An option struck at a 0% yield is asymmetrically sensitive to very low rates, so the model assigns it too high a value.
cards.originalText: At ten years a negative shock of only about 1.73 standard deviations takes the rate below zero; this matters most for the option, which the model overvalues, and much less for the bond.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In a normal short-rate model, the possibility of negative rates matters most for a coupon bond, whose value depends on the average rate path, and little for an option to buy a long-term bond at a yield of 0%.
cards.explanation: It is the option, not the coupon bond, that is asymmetrically sensitive to low rates.
cards.originalText: At ten years a negative shock of only about 1.73 standard deviations takes the rate below zero; this matters most for the bond, whose value depends on the average rate path, and little for the option.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In a normal short-rate model with no drift, the probability of negative rates falls as the horizon lengthens, because the recombining tree pulls the short rate back toward its starting level.
cards.explanation: The standard deviation of the short rate grows with the horizon, so the probability of negative rates rises. A recombining tree is not mean reversion, and the model has no force pulling rates back to the starting level.
cards.originalText: The probability of negative rates falls as the horizon lengthens, because the recombining tree pulls the short rate back toward its starting level of 6.18%.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In Black's shadow-rate approach, when the observed rate reaches zero it can stay there for several periods, until the shadow rate moves back above zero.
cards.explanation: The original (unfloored) tree holds the shadow rates and the floored tree holds the observed rates. The observed rate remains at zero until the shadow rate crosses back to a positive value.
cards.originalText: When the observed rate reaches zero it can stay there for several periods, until the shadow rate moves back above zero.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In the shadow-rate approach to flooring a normal rate tree, the rates in the original tree are the observed rates and the floored rates are the shadow rates, so the shadow rate can never fall below zero.
cards.explanation: The names are the other way round: the floored rates are the observed rates, and the shadow rate, which is the original unfloored rate, can be negative.
cards.originalText: The rates in the original tree are the observed rates and the floored rates are the shadow rates, so the shadow rate can never fall below zero.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The justification for the shadow-rate approach is that aggregate saving and investment decisions can never produce a negative equilibrium rate, so flooring recovers the true rate.
cards.explanation: The shadow (equilibrium) rate may well be negative. The observed rate is floored at zero because investors can hold cash instead.
cards.originalText: The justification is that aggregate saving and investment decisions can never produce a negative equilibrium rate, so the floor recovers the true rate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Flooring negative rates at zero changes the dynamics of the rate across the entire range of rates, which is why it is less attractive than switching to a lognormal model.
cards.explanation: Flooring is localised around zero and negative rates. It is changing the distribution, for example to lognormal, that alters dynamics across the entire range of rates.
cards.originalText: Flooring changes the dynamics of the rate across the entire range of rates, which is why it is less attractive than switching to a lognormal model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Flooring negative rates at zero in a normal model has an effect localised around zero, whereas switching to a distribution that rules out negative rates alters rate dynamics, including volatilities, across all rates.
cards.explanation: Building the model on a distribution that rules out negative rates may produce unacceptable volatilities and changes dynamics at every rate level, which matters when pricing options across many strikes. The floor changes only rates near and below zero.
cards.originalText: Flooring is preferable here, because its effect is localised around zero, whereas changing the distribution alters rate dynamics, including volatilities, across all rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
