cards.statement: Switching from a normal to a lognormal model rules out negative rates without changing the model's volatility at any level of rates.
cards.explanation: A lognormal model changes the volatility behaviour: basis-point volatility becomes proportional to the rate level.
cards.originalText: The lognormal switch is preferable, because it rules out negative rates without changing the model’s volatility at any level of rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Adding time steps to a normal rate tree makes the terminal distribution continuous and so removes the negative rates.
cards.explanation: A finer normal tree still has probability mass below zero.
cards.originalText: Neither is needed, because adding time steps to the normal tree makes the terminal distribution continuous and so removes the negative rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Any distribution that rules out negative rates has the same volatility structure as a floored normal model.
cards.explanation: The two methods have different volatility structures, and that difference is the whole trade-off between them.
cards.originalText: The two are equivalent, because any distribution that rules out negative rates has the same volatility structure as a floored normal model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate VaR using a historical simulation approach.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Extending historical simulation to longer holding periods poses no theoretical difficulty, but the number of non-overlapping P/L observations falls sharply as the holding period lengthens, so longer-horizon estimates rest on very few data points.
cards.explanation: With 1,000 daily observations, 5-day sums give only 200 observations and 20-day sums only 50. With so few observations, especially in the tail, longer-horizon VaR and expected shortfall become imprecise.
cards.originalText: As the holding period lengthens, the number of non‑overlapping P/L observations falls sharply, so longer‑horizon HS estimates rest on very few data points.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate VaR using a historical simulation approach.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: As the holding period shortens, the number of available P/L observations falls, so daily historical-simulation estimates are the least reliable.
cards.explanation: Shorter holding periods give more observations, not fewer.
cards.originalText: As the holding period shortens, the number of available P/L observations falls, so daily HS estimates are the least reliable.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate VaR using a historical simulation approach.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Historical simulation requires a parametric distribution to be fitted to P/L, and its parameters must be re-estimated for each new holding period.
cards.explanation: Historical simulation is non-parametric and fits no distribution. That description fits parametric approaches.
cards.originalText: HS requires a parametric distribution to be fitted to P/L, and its parameters must be re‑estimated for each new holding period.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate VaR using a historical simulation approach.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: As the holding period lengthens, historical simulation can no longer produce an expected shortfall estimate, because expected shortfall requires daily data.
cards.explanation: Expected shortfall can be computed from $h$-day P/L just like VaR, as the average of tail losses. The issue is the small number of observations, not the data frequency.
cards.originalText: As the holding period lengthens, HS can no longer produce an expected shortfall estimate because ES requires daily data.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Expected shortfall is a special case of a coherent risk measure: it gives equal weight, $1/(1-c)$, to every quantile in the tail and zero weight to all other quantiles.
cards.explanation: A coherent risk measure is a weighted average of loss quantiles with weights reflecting risk aversion. Expected shortfall sets the weight to $1/(1-c)$ on every tail quantile and zero elsewhere.
cards.originalText: ES is a special case of a coherent risk measure: it gives equal weight, $1/(1 - c)$, to every quantile in the tail and zero weight to all other quantiles.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Expected shortfall is a coherent risk measure that gives progressively greater weight to the higher, more extreme tail quantiles.
cards.explanation: Expected shortfall weights are flat across the tail. Increasing weights on extreme quantiles describe a more general, more risk-averse coherent measure.
cards.originalText: ES is a coherent risk measure that gives progressively greater weight to the higher (more extreme) tail quantiles.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Expected shortfall is a coherent risk measure that gives progressively smaller weight to the higher, more extreme tail quantiles.
cards.explanation: Expected shortfall gives equal weights across the tail. Decreasing weights would downplay the worst losses, the opposite of risk aversion.
cards.originalText: ES is a coherent risk measure that gives progressively smaller weight to the higher (more extreme) tail quantiles.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Expected shortfall places all of its weight on the single quantile at the confidence level $c$ and zero weight on every other quantile.
cards.explanation: Putting all weight on one quantile is VaR, which ignores losses beyond the threshold. Expected shortfall averages over the whole tail.
cards.originalText: ES places all of its weight on the single quantile at the confidence level $c$ and zero weight on every other quantile.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Expected shortfall averages VaR quantiles over the tail only, with zero weight elsewhere, whereas a general coherent risk measure weights quantiles across the entire distribution using a risk-aversion function, so expected shortfall is a special case.
cards.explanation: Expected shortfall uses equal weights in the tail and zero elsewhere. A general coherent measure divides the distribution into equal-probability slices and applies a risk-aversion weighting function to each quantile.
cards.originalText: ES averages VaR quantiles over the tail only (zero weight elsewhere), whereas a general coherent risk measure weights quantiles across the entire distribution using a risk‑aversion function; ES is a special case.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Expected shortfall and a general coherent risk measure both place non-zero weight only on quantiles in the tail region.
cards.explanation: A general coherent measure can use quantiles over the entire distribution. Only expected shortfall is confined to the tail.
cards.originalText: ES and a general coherent risk measure both place non‑zero weight only on quantiles in the tail region.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Expected shortfall weights quantiles across the entire distribution, whereas a coherent risk measure uses only tail quantiles.
cards.explanation: This is reversed: expected shortfall is confined to the tail, and the general coherent measure may span the whole distribution.
cards.originalText: ES weights quantiles across the entire distribution, whereas a coherent risk measure uses only tail quantiles.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: A coherent risk measure always places equal weights on all quantiles, whereas expected shortfall uses a risk-aversion weighting function.
cards.explanation: Equal weights on tail quantiles characterise expected shortfall, while general coherent measures use user-specific risk-aversion weights.
cards.originalText: A coherent risk measure always places equal weights on all quantiles, whereas ES uses a risk‑aversion weighting function.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: The key to estimating a coherent risk measure, which can be expressed as a weighted average of loss quantiles, is the ability to estimate quantiles.
cards.explanation: Every coherent measure, including expected shortfall, is built from quantiles of the loss distribution. The weights are chosen by the user, so the estimation task is obtaining the quantiles.
cards.originalText: ability to estimate quantiles.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Among standard deviation, VaR, expected shortfall and spectral risk measures, spectral risk measures are the least commonly used in risk management practice.
cards.explanation: Spectral risk measures require choosing a user-specific risk-aversion weighting function over all quantiles, which is complex and rarely done in practice.
cards.originalText: Spectral risk measures

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: A risk measure defined as a weighted average of loss quantiles is coherent if the weights applied to the tail-loss quantiles are weakly increasing.
cards.explanation: Coherence requires weights that do not fall as losses get worse, reflecting risk aversion. Expected shortfall satisfies this, whereas VaR, with all weight on one quantile, does not.
cards.originalText: If the weights applied to the tail‑loss quantiles are weakly increasing, this measure is coherent.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: All risk measures defined as a weighted average of loss quantiles are coherent.
cards.explanation: Weighting functions that decrease in the tail, such as the one for VaR, give measures that are not coherent.
cards.originalText: All cases of this general risk measure are coherent.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: A risk measure defined as a weighted average of loss quantiles is not coherent if the weights applied to the tail-loss quantiles are unequal.
cards.explanation: Unequal weights are fine if they are weakly increasing. Equal weights, as in expected shortfall, are only one coherent case.
cards.originalText: If the weights applied to the tail‑loss quantiles are unequal, this measure is not coherent.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: The weakness of a risk measure defined as a weighted average of loss quantiles is that it cannot represent different degrees of risk aversion.
cards.explanation: The weighting function is exactly what represents risk aversion, so this is a strength of the measure, not a weakness.
cards.originalText: The weakness of this measure is that it cannot represent different degrees of risk aversion.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Although VaR is not subadditive, and so not coherent, there is no case where this lack of coherence causes a practical problem for market risk measurement.
cards.explanation: The non-subadditivity of VaR is not merely academic. It can mislead risk measurement and portfolio optimization, for example by encouraging portfolio splitting or concentration.
cards.originalText: Although VaR is not subadditive (and so not coherent), the literature has produced no case where this lack of coherence causes a practical problem for market risk measurement.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: VaR measures only a loss quantile, so by disregarding losses beyond the VaR level a manager relying only on VaR may be tempted to avoid losses within the confidence level while increasing losses beyond it.
cards.explanation: This is the standard tail-blindness criticism of VaR, which expected shortfall addresses.
cards.originalText: VaR measures only a loss quantile; by disregarding losses beyond the VaR level, a manager relying only on VaR may be tempted to avoid losses within the confidence level while increasing losses beyond it.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Subadditivity reflects diversification, and using non-subadditive risk measures in portfolio optimization may lead to very concentrated portfolios that would be judged risky.
cards.explanation: Without subadditivity, splitting or concentrating positions can lower measured risk, so optimization can favour concentration.
cards.originalText: Subadditivity reflects diversification; using non‑subadditive measures in portfolio optimization may lead to very concentrated portfolios that would be judged risky.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: A spectral risk measure places weight only on the quantile at the chosen confidence level and ignores worse losses.
cards.explanation: Placing all weight on a single quantile is VaR. A spectral measure spreads weights across many quantiles, including worse tail losses.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: An advantage of spectral risk measures over VaR and expected shortfall is that they are not tied to a single confidence level.
cards.explanation: A spectral measure averages many quantiles with a weighting function, so it does not depend on one confidence level.
cards.originalText: An advantage of spectral measures over VaR and ES is that they are not tied to a single confidence level.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: For a spectral risk measure to be coherent, the weighting function must be weakly increasing over the unit interval.
cards.explanation: Coherence requires weights that are weakly increasing in the quantile level, so larger losses get at least as much weight.
cards.originalText: For the measure to be coherent, the weighting function must be weakly increasing over \[0,1\].

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: VaR is a coherent risk measure that applies equal weights to all quantiles in the tail.
cards.explanation: Equal tail weights describe expected shortfall. VaR puts all its weight on a single quantile and is not coherent.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Expected shortfall is the best coherent risk measure for every user regardless of risk aversion.
cards.explanation: The best weighting depends on each user's risk aversion. Expected shortfall is just one choice of weighting function.
cards.originalText: ES is the best coherent risk measure for every user regardless of risk aversion.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Expected shortfall gives equal weight to every quantile of the entire loss distribution, which makes it a simple average of all quantiles.
cards.explanation: Equal weight on every quantile of the whole distribution gives the mean of the distribution, not a tail measure. Expected shortfall puts zero weight outside the tail.
cards.originalText: ES gives equal weight to every quantile of the entire loss distribution, which makes it a simple average of all quantiles.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: A coherent risk measure estimated by slicing the loss distribution into equal-probability slices can be computed by starting with a small number of slices and doubling it until the estimate stabilizes, that is, until the halving error is close to zero.
cards.explanation: The estimate is a discretized integral of weighted quantiles. Doubling the number of slices and comparing successive estimates shows when the approximation has converged.
cards.originalText: The analyst can start with a small n and keep doubling it until the estimate stabilizes, i.e., the halving error becomes close to zero.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: A coherent risk measure must assign the same weight to every quantile of the loss distribution.
cards.explanation: Weights are user-specific and need not be equal. Equal weights in the tail give expected shortfall, which is only one special case.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: The halving error is the standard error of a quantile-based risk estimator and falls as more historical observations are collected.
cards.explanation: The halving error measures discretization, that is, the number of slices used. Standard error reflects sampling variability and falls with sample size.
cards.originalText: The halving error is the standard error of the estimator and falls as more historical observations are collected.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
cards.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: QQ plots are the standard tool for judging how precisely a quantile-based estimator approximates the true risk measure.
cards.explanation: QQ plots assess whether a sample's distribution matches a theoretical one. They do not quantify the precision of an estimator.
cards.originalText: QQ plots are the standard tool for judging how precisely the quantile‑based estimator approximates the true risk measure.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: By smoothing the data, non-parametric density estimation creates new information, so with 100 observations a 99.9% VaR beyond the largest observed loss can be estimated reliably.
cards.explanation: Non-parametric density estimation only redistributes area between existing observations to fill gaps. It interpolates and cannot supply information about losses worse than the worst observation.
cards.originalText: By smoothing the data, it creates new information, so with 100 observations a 99.9% VaR beyond the largest observed loss can be estimated reliably.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: Historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation is free from restrictive assumptions about the shape of the underlying distribution.
cards.explanation: The method works from the empirical histogram of the data and imposes no distribution.
cards.originalText: It is free from restrictive assumptions about the shape of the underlying distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: Connecting the midpoints of successive histogram bars allows VaR to be estimated at confidence levels between observed data points.
cards.explanation: Connecting the midpoints makes the density continuous, which fills the gaps between ordered observations so that VaR can be read at any confidence level.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: When the midpoints of histogram bars are connected, the area gained by the lower bar equals the area lost by the upper bar, so total probability remains one.
cards.explanation: Area is displaced between bars, not created or lost, so the smoothed surrogate is still a valid density with total area of one.
cards.originalText: When midpoints are connected, the area gained by the lower bar equals the area lost by the upper bar, so total probability remains one.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: With 100 P/L observations, basic historical simulation can estimate VaR only at discrete confidence levels such as 95% and 96%, so a 95.5% VaR cannot be obtained.
cards.explanation: With $n$ observations basic historical simulation provides only $n$ distinct confidence levels. Non-parametric density estimation smooths the histogram to remove this limitation.
cards.originalText: With 100 P/L observations, basic HS can estimate VaR only at discrete confidence levels (e.g., 95%, 96%), so a 95.5% VaR cannot be obtained.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: With 100 P/L observations, basic historical simulation requires the assumption that P/L is normally distributed.
cards.explanation: Basic historical simulation is non-parametric and assumes no distribution. Requiring normality describes the variance-covariance method.
cards.originalText: With 100 P/L observations, basic HS requires the assumption that P/L is normally distributed.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: Non-parametric density estimation solves the problem that the discreteness of the data in historical simulation rules out VaR estimates between data points.
cards.explanation: Smoothing the empirical distribution into a continuous density permits VaR at any confidence level, not just the $n$ discrete ones.
cards.originalText: Non‑parametric density estimation

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: Historical simulation with non-parametric density estimation smooths between data points, so VaR can be estimated at any confidence level, not only at those implied by the ordered observations.
cards.explanation: Smoothing the empirical histogram creates a continuum of attainable confidence levels without distributional assumptions.
cards.originalText: It smooths between data points so VaR can be estimated at any confidence level, including 98%.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: Non-parametric density estimation generates additional independent observations, enlarging the effective sample beyond the number of actual observations.
cards.explanation: Smoothing reshapes the existing observations. It does not create new independent observations.
cards.originalText: It generates additional independent observations, enlarging the effective sample beyond 80.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: Non-parametric density estimation allows reliable VaR estimates at levels beyond the worst observed loss, such as 99.9%.
cards.explanation: The method interpolates between observations. It cannot add information about losses worse than the worst observation.
cards.originalText: It allows reliable VaR estimates at levels beyond the worst observed loss, such as 99.9%.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: Historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation fits a normal distribution with the sample mean and standard deviation and reads VaR from the fitted curve.
cards.explanation: The method smooths the empirical histogram and imposes no distribution. Fitting a distribution with estimated parameters is a parametric approach.
cards.originalText: Fitting a normal distribution with the sample mean and standard deviation, then reading VaR from the fitted curve.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: Historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation connects the midpoints of successive histogram bars to create a smooth surrogate density.
cards.explanation: The surrogate density formed by connecting bar midpoints lets VaR be read at confidence levels between ordered observations.
cards.originalText: Connecting the midpoints of successive histogram bars to create a smooth surrogate density.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: The primary advantage of historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation over basic historical simulation is that VaR can be calculated at a continuum of confidence levels, not just the $n$ levels implied by the ordered observations.
cards.explanation: Smoothing the empirical distribution lets VaR be read at any confidence level while remaining free of restrictive distributional assumptions.
cards.originalText: VaR can be calculated at a continuum of confidence levels, not just the n levels implied by the ordered observations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: Historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation is simpler to implement than basic historical simulation, because no smoothing step is required.
cards.explanation: The extra smoothing step makes the method more involved, not simpler. Simplicity is the advantage of basic historical simulation.
cards.originalText: It is simpler to implement because no smoothing step is required.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: Historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation places more weight on recent observations than on older observations.
cards.explanation: That describes age-weighted historical simulation, a different refinement. Non-parametric density estimation smooths between data points.
cards.originalText: It places more weight on recent observations than on older observations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.loText: Describe historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation.
cards.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
cards.statement: Historical simulation using non-parametric density estimation calibrates a familiar distribution, such as the beta or gamma, to the data and reads VaR from it.
cards.explanation: That describes a parametric approach. Non-parametric density estimation assumes no distribution.
cards.originalText: It calibrates a familiar distribution (e.g., beta or gamma) to the data and reads VaR from it.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of extreme values in risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: The primary reason that modeling extreme events is typically problematic is a lack of credible, reliable input data.
cards.explanation: Extreme events are rare by definition, so there are very few tail observations, and some possible extremes have never occurred. A distribution fitted mainly to central observations will not match the true tail.
cards.originalText: A lack of credible, reliable input data.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of extreme values in risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: The primary reason that modeling extreme events is typically problematic is a lack of models that can estimate the effects of certain extreme but possible events.
cards.explanation: Models for extremes do exist, such as extreme value theory. The problem is the lack of data to calibrate them.
cards.originalText: A lack of models that can estimate the effects of certain extreme but possible events.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of extreme values in risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: The primary reason that modeling extreme events is typically problematic is a lack of qualified personnel to oversee the modeling process.
cards.explanation: Staffing is not the fundamental obstacle. The core challenge is data scarcity in the tail.
cards.originalText: A lack of qualified personnel to oversee the modeling process.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of extreme values in risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: The main challenge posed by extreme values is that there are only a few observations from which a credible, reliable analytical model can be built.
cards.explanation: Extreme values occur rarely, so little tail data is available, and any fitted model is subject to considerable error.
cards.originalText: There are only a few observations from which a credible, reliable analytical model can be built.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of extreme values in risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: The main challenge posed by extreme values is that they do not conform to any of the established loss distributions.
cards.explanation: Extremes can be described by distributions such as the generalized Pareto. The issue is sparse data, not nonconformity.
cards.originalText: They do not conform to any of the established loss distributions.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of extreme values in risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: The main challenge posed by extreme values is that they are so large that the resulting loss estimates are infinitely large.
cards.explanation: Loss estimates from a fitted tail model are finite. Infinite estimates are not the challenge; data scarcity is.
cards.originalText: They are so large that the resulting loss estimates are infinitely large.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of extreme values in risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: The central limit theorem does not apply to extreme losses, because extremes are not described by the normal limit of averages.
cards.explanation: The central limit theorem concerns averages, whereas extremes are governed by different limit laws, so the CLT does not describe them.
cards.originalText: The central limit theorem (CLT) does not apply.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of extreme values in risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: Extreme value theory estimates are subject to considerable model risk.
cards.explanation: Tail estimates are fitted from few observations and are highly sensitive to the chosen model and its parameters.
cards.originalText: EVT estimates are subject to considerable model risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of extreme values in risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: Extreme value theory cannot, by definition, provide loss estimates beyond the worst actual observed loss in the historical sample.
cards.explanation: EVT fits a parametric tail model and extrapolates beyond the sample maximum, so its loss estimates are not capped at the worst observed loss.
cards.originalText: EVT cannot, by definition, provide loss estimates beyond (in excess of) the worst actual observed loss in the historical sample.
cards.correction: Extreme value theory can provide loss estimates beyond the worst actual observed loss in the historical sample.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of extreme values in risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: Extreme value theory is inherently difficult because the sample contains few relevant loss observations.
cards.explanation: Extreme losses are rare by definition, so the scarcity of tail observations is the core difficulty of EVT.
cards.originalText: EVT is inherently difficult because our sample contains few relevant loss observations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of extreme values in risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: Extreme events tend to recur at rather regular time intervals.
cards.explanation: Extreme events are rare and irregular; they are taken seriously because they are very costly, not because they recur on a schedule.
cards.correction: Extreme events do not tend to recur at regular time intervals.

changes.from: tend to recur at rather regular
changes.to: do not tend to recur at regular

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of extreme values in risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: Extreme events rarely have warning signs, so markets cannot prepare for them in any way.
cards.explanation: This overstates the case: markets can prepare for extreme events using tools such as stress testing and extreme value theory.
cards.originalText: Extreme events rarely have warning signs and thus markets cannot prepare for them in any way.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of extreme values in risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: Extreme events, although rare, are taken seriously in finance because they are normally very costly and can create a ripple effect on the global market.
cards.explanation: Extreme events have a low probability but a huge loss when they occur, and the losses can cascade through the system, so they must be identified and managed.
cards.originalText: Extreme events are normally very costly and can create a ripple effect on the global market.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the multivariate EVT for risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: The central focus of multivariate extreme value theory is modelling the tail dependence structure among extreme values using extreme value copulas.
cards.explanation: Univariate EVT already handles each marginal tail; what the multivariate extension adds is the joint behaviour of extremes, captured by tail dependence through EV copulas.
cards.originalText: Modeling the tail dependence structure among the extreme values, using extreme value copulas

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the multivariate EVT for risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: Multivariate extreme value theory fits a separate generalized Pareto distribution to each risk factor and ignores joint behaviour.
cards.explanation: Fitting each factor separately is univariate EVT; the point of the multivariate extension is to model the tail dependence between the factors.
cards.originalText: Fitting a separate generalized Pareto distribution to each risk factor and ignoring joint behavior

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the multivariate EVT for risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: The central focus of multivariate extreme value theory is estimating the pairwise linear correlation matrix under an elliptical distribution.
cards.explanation: Linear correlation and elliptical assumptions capture tail dependence poorly; multivariate EVT instead models tail dependence with extreme value copulas.
cards.originalText: Estimating the pairwise linear correlation matrix under an elliptical distribution

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the multivariate EVT for risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: The central focus of multivariate extreme value theory is calibrating the central limit theorem to the sample means of the risk factors.
cards.explanation: The CLT describes the distribution of averages, whereas EVT concerns the tails, so it is the wrong tool for extremes.
cards.originalText: Calibrating the central limit theorem to the sample means of the risk factors

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the multivariate EVT for risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: As the number of random variables increases, multivariate extreme value theory suffers from a curse of dimensionality.
cards.explanation: Adding variables makes joint extreme observations rarer and the number of parameters larger.
cards.originalText: As the number of random variables increases, multivariate EVT suffers from a ”curse of dimensionality”

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the multivariate EVT for risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: Multivariate extreme value dependence can be modelled by assuming an extreme value copula.
cards.explanation: The limiting distribution of multivariate extremes belongs to the extreme value copula family, so dependence is modelled by assuming one.
cards.originalText: We can model multivariate extreme value dependence by assuming an EV copula

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the multivariate EVT for risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: In multivariate extreme value theory, extreme events can generally be assumed to be independent.
cards.explanation: The rationale for multivariate EVT is that extremes are typically dependent (tail dependence, for example a disaster hitting many markets), so independence cannot generally be assumed.
cards.originalText: We can generally assume that extreme events are independent
cards.correction: In multivariate extreme value theory, extreme events cannot generally be assumed to be independent.

changes.from: can generally be assumed to be independent
changes.to: cannot generally be assumed to be independent

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.loText: Explain the multivariate EVT for risk management.
cards.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
cards.statement: In multivariate extreme value theory, as dimensionality increases there are fewer multivariate extreme observations but more parameters to estimate.
cards.explanation: Joint extremes become very scarce (for example about 1 in 10,000 for two variables each extreme 1 time in 100) while the number of parameters grows.
cards.originalText: As dimensionality increases, there are fewer multivariate extreme observations but more parameters to estimate

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: A VaR model at 99% confidence is consistent with accuracy when its exception rate is close to 1%, for example about 5 exceptions over 500 trading days.
cards.explanation: An accurate model produces exceptions at a rate equal to 1 minus the confidence level, apart from sampling variation.
cards.originalText: About 5 exceptions, so that the exception rate is close to 1%

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: About 25 exceptions over 500 trading days, a 5% exception rate, is consistent with an accurate 99% one-day VaR model.
cards.explanation: A 5% exception rate is what a 95% VaR should produce; at 99% confidence it would show that the model understates risk.
cards.originalText: About 25 exceptions, so that the exception rate is close to 5%

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: A VaR backtest should show zero exceptions, since a loss should never exceed VaR.
cards.explanation: Zero exceptions is not the goal: too few exceptions signals an overly conservative model that overstates risk and ties up capital.
cards.originalText: Zero exceptions, since a loss should never exceed VaR

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: In a VaR backtest the number of exceptions is irrelevant if the average daily loss is below VaR.
cards.explanation: Backtesting looks at the frequency of losses beyond VaR, not at the average loss, so the exception count is the key test statistic.
cards.originalText: The number of exceptions is irrelevant if the average daily loss is below VaR

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: A VaR backtest works the same way for any VaR method: daily VaR is compared with the realized P&L and the exceptions are counted against the expected number, such as 2.5 over 250 days at 99% confidence.
cards.explanation: The backtest depends only on the stated confidence level and the realized outcomes, so it is independent of the method used to compute VaR.
cards.originalText: It works the same for any VaR method: daily VaR is compared with the realized P&L and the exceptions counted against the expected 2.5

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: A VaR backtest is only meaningful if VaR is computed with the parametric (delta-normal) method.
cards.explanation: Parametric VaR gets no special treatment in a backtest; the exceptions are counted and compared with the expected number whatever the method.
cards.originalText: It is only meaningful if VaR is computed with the parametric (delta‑normal) method

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Backtesting is easier with historical simulation VaR because the VaR is based on actual returns.
cards.explanation: Historical simulation VaR is no more testable than other methods; using actual past returns does not change the exception count or the expected frequency.
cards.originalText: It is easier with historical simulation because the VaR is based on actual returns

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: A VaR backtest requires Monte Carlo VaR because only then can the expected number of exceptions be derived.
cards.explanation: The expected number of exceptions comes from the confidence level (for example 250 x 1% = 2.5), not from simulation.
cards.originalText: It requires Monte Carlo VaR because only then can the expected number of exceptions be derived

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Backtesting compares VaR forecasts with subsequently realized profits and losses.
cards.explanation: This is the definition of VaR backtesting.
cards.originalText: Backtesting compares VaR forecasts with subsequently realized profits and losses

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: A significantly higher number of exceptions than expected suggests that a VaR model understates risk.
cards.explanation: Excess exceptions mean losses exceeded VaR too often, so the model underestimates risk.
cards.originalText: A significantly higher number of exceptions than expected suggests the model understates risk

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Under the Basel internal models approach, banks must backtest their VaR models.
cards.explanation: Basel requires backtesting, with a higher capital multiplier applied when there are too many exceptions.
cards.originalText: Under the Basel internal models approach, banks must backtest their VaR models

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: A VaR model with zero exceptions over a long sample is necessarily the most accurate.
cards.explanation: Accuracy means exceptions occur at the expected rate; zero exceptions over a long sample points to an overly conservative model that overstates risk.
cards.originalText: A model with zero exceptions over a long sample is necessarily the most accurate
cards.correction: A VaR model with zero exceptions over a long sample is not necessarily the most accurate.

changes.to: is not necessarily the most accurate

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: When a VaR model produces more exceptions than forecast, it understates risk, so the risk-taking units of the bank are likely to be allocated less capital than they should be.
cards.explanation: Too many exceptions mean VaR is too low, and capital allocated on the basis of that VaR is therefore too low.
cards.originalText: The risk‑taking units of the bank will likely be allocated less capital than they should be.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: A VaR model that produces more exceptions than forecast is most likely overestimating the market risk faced by the bank.
cards.explanation: Overestimation would produce fewer exceptions than forecast; more exceptions than forecast indicate that risk is underestimated.
cards.originalText: The model is most likely overestimating the market risk faced by the bank.
cards.correction: A VaR model that produces more exceptions than forecast is most likely underestimating the market risk faced by the bank.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Explain the significant difficulties in backtesting a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Employing Monte Carlo simulated p-values instead of asymptotic distributions addresses the small-sample problem in VaR backtesting and gives a correctly sized test.
cards.explanation: Simulating the test statistic's null distribution at the actual sample size replaces the unreliable large-sample approximation.
cards.originalText: Employing Monte Carlo simulated p‑values instead of relying on asymptotic distributions.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Explain the significant difficulties in backtesting a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Using asymptotic (chi-squared) distributions for p-value calculation addresses the small-sample problem in VaR backtesting.
cards.explanation: The asymptotic chi-squared approximation is the source of the poor test size when exceptions are few, not the cure for it.
cards.originalText: Using asymptotic (chi‑squared) distributions for p‑value calculation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Explain the significant difficulties in backtesting a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Increasing the VaR confidence level, for example from 99% to 99.9%, addresses the small-sample problem in VaR backtesting.
cards.explanation: A higher confidence level lowers the expected number of exceptions (for example 250 x 0.001 = 0.25), which worsens the small-sample problem.
cards.originalText: Increasing the VaR confidence level (e.g., from 99% to 99.9%).

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Explain the significant difficulties in backtesting a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Including fees, commissions and intraday trading revenue in the P&L used for VaR backtesting can mask actual portfolio losses and make the VaR model appear more accurate than it is.
cards.explanation: Such non-risk revenue is typically positive and offsets trading losses, so fewer exceptions are recorded than the model actually deserves.
cards.originalText: It could have masked actual portfolio losses, making the VaR model appear more accurate than it was.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Explain the significant difficulties in backtesting a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Including fees, commissions and intraday trading revenue in the P&L used for VaR backtesting leads to an underestimation of VaR and insufficient capital reserves.
cards.explanation: The contamination affects the P&L series used in the backtest, not the VaR estimate itself, which is not computed from these items.
cards.originalText: It could have led to an underestimation of VaR, resulting in insufficient capital reserves.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Explain the significant difficulties in backtesting a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: Including fees, commissions and intraday trading revenue in the P&L used for VaR backtesting significantly increases the computational complexity of VaR calculations.
cards.explanation: The VaR calculation is unchanged; only the P&L series it is compared with is affected.
cards.originalText: It increased the computational complexity of VaR calculations significantly.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Explain the significant difficulties in backtesting a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: A VaR model that fails a backtest on hypothetical returns indicates that the VaR modelling methodology itself must be adjusted, because VaR assumes a static portfolio.
cards.explanation: Hypothetical returns isolate the model's own assumption of a constant portfolio from non-modelled P&L effects such as intraday trading and fees.
cards.originalText: Hypothetical returns

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.loText: Explain the significant difficulties in backtesting a VaR model.
cards.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
cards.statement: VaR backtesting should use both actual returns, the total return on the trading portfolio, and hypothetical returns, the returns obtained by freezing the starting positions.
cards.explanation: Backtesting both series separates model error (hypothetical returns fail) from intraday trading and fee effects (only actual returns fail).
cards.originalText: The actual returns, which correspond to the total return on the bank’s trading portfolio, and the hypothetical returns, which represent the returns obtained from freezing the starting positions in the bank’s trading portfolio

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: VaR mapping replaces the current values of many positions with exposures to a smaller set of selected primitive risk factors, because modelling each position separately is impractical.
cards.explanation: Mapping aggregates many positions into exposures on a limited set of primitive risk factors, which simplifies risk measurement.
cards.originalText: The current values of many positions are replaced by exposures to a smaller set of selected primitive risk factors, because modeling each position separately is impractical.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: In VaR mapping, only the most extreme (abnormal) risk factors are retained, because normal factors do not contribute to tail losses.
cards.explanation: Mapping covers the factors that drive the portfolio's risk; it does not filter down to only abnormal factors.
cards.originalText: Only the most extreme (abnormal) risk factors are retained, because normal factors do not contribute to tail losses.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: In VaR mapping, each position is mapped to every risk factor that could affect its price, so that no approximation error is introduced.
cards.explanation: Using every factor would defeat the simplifying purpose of mapping, which deliberately accepts some approximation.
cards.originalText: Each position is mapped to every risk factor that could affect its price, so that no approximation error is introduced.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: In VaR mapping, every portfolio is mapped to exactly five risk factors regardless of its composition.
cards.explanation: The number of risk factors is chosen to fit the portfolio, as a trade-off between accuracy and speed; five is arbitrary.
cards.originalText: Every portfolio is mapped to exactly five risk factors regardless of its composition.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: VaR mapping is especially useful for instruments whose characteristics change over time, such as a fixed-rate bond whose maturity and interest rate sensitivity shrink as it ages, or an option whose sensitivity to the underlying changes with the market.
cards.explanation: Past prices of such instruments misstate their current risk, so they are mapped to risk factors that reflect their current profile.
cards.originalText: A fixed‑rate bond whose maturity and interest rate sensitivity shrink as it ages, or an option whose sensitivity to the underlying changes with the market.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: If a position's exposures to its risk factors sum to less than its market value and no relevant risk factor has been omitted, the remainder is held in cash, which is not a risk factor and contributes no market risk.
cards.explanation: A valid mapping preserves market value, so value not allocated to any risk factor is cash, which carries no market risk factor.
cards.originalText: The remainder is held in cash, which is not a risk factor and so contributes no market risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: The choice of primitive risk factors in a VaR mapping reflects a trade-off between a better approximation of risk (more factors) and faster, simpler modelling (fewer factors).
cards.explanation: More factors approximate portfolio risk better but make modelling more time consuming, while fewer factors are faster but leave more residual risk.
cards.originalText: A trade‑off between a better approximation of risk (more factors) and faster, simpler modeling (fewer factors).

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Using as many risk factors as possible in a VaR mapping eliminates specific risk entirely.
cards.explanation: More risk factors reduce specific risk but never eliminate it, and they raise modelling cost, which defeats the purpose of mapping.
cards.originalText: The use of as many factors as possible, so that specific risk is eliminated entirely.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: In a VaR mapping, the amount of specific risk does not depend on which risk factors are chosen.
cards.explanation: Specific risk is the residual left after the chosen general factors, so adding factors such as credit or currency reduces it.
cards.originalText: The use of a single market factor, because specific risk does not depend on which factors are chosen.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Whichever approach is used to map a position onto risk factors, the mapping should preserve both the market value and the market risk of the position.
cards.explanation: A valid mapping reproduces the position's current market value and also how that value responds to the risk factors.
cards.originalText: The market value and the market risk of the position.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Whichever approach is used to map a position onto risk factors, the mapping should preserve only the market value of the position.
cards.explanation: Matching value alone ignores risk, which is the purpose of mapping; the market risk must be preserved as well.
cards.originalText: Only the market value of the position.
cards.correction: Whichever approach is used to map a position onto risk factors, the mapping should preserve both the market value and the market risk of the position.

changes.to: both the market value and the market risk

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Whichever approach is used to map a position onto risk factors, the mapping should preserve the par value and the market risk of the position.
cards.explanation: Par value is not the economic value of the position; the mapping preserves its market value.
cards.originalText: The par value and the market risk of the position.
cards.correction: Whichever approach is used to map a position onto risk factors, the mapping should preserve the market value and the market risk of the position.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: A large equity portfolio is a good candidate for mapping because a small set of risk factors needs far fewer estimates than a full covariance matrix of all its positions.
cards.explanation: The factor approach cuts the number of parameters to estimate dramatically compared with a covariance matrix of, say, 1,000 positions.
cards.originalText: The large equity portfolio is a good candidate for mapping because a small set of general and specific factors needs far fewer estimates than a full covariance matrix of 1,000 positions.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: A corporate bond portfolio can be mapped to a small set of general risk factors, such as maturity vertices and rating spreads, rather than one factor per bond.
cards.explanation: Fixed income positions are mapped to a limited set of general factors, not to one factor for each bond.
cards.originalText: The corporate bond portfolio can be mapped to a small set of general risk factors, such as maturity vertices and rating spreads, rather than one factor per bond.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Equity mapping contains model risk, including factor-sensitivity (beta) estimation error, subjective choice of risk factors, and omission of specific risk.
cards.explanation: These are genuine sources of model risk in mapping equity positions to risk factors.
cards.originalText: Equity mapping contains model risk, including factor‑sensitivity (beta) estimation error, subjective choice of risk factors, and omission of specific risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Positions with little historical data, such as IPO funds and emergent assets, cannot be mapped to risk factors because their sensitivities cannot be estimated.
cards.explanation: Lack of history is a reason to use mapping, not a barrier to it: such positions are expressed as exposures to similar risk factors that do have histories.
cards.originalText: The IPO and emergent‑asset funds cannot be mapped because they lack historical data, so sensitivities cannot be estimated.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: One valid reason to map portfolio positions to risk factors is that a large portfolio has too many positions to model individually.
cards.explanation: Too many positions make position-by-position computation impractical.
cards.originalText: In a large portfolio there are too many positions to model individually.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: One valid reason to map portfolio positions to risk factors is that risk factors are common to various positions and/or instruments.
cards.explanation: Common factors allow positions to be aggregated into a small set of exposures.
cards.originalText: Risk factors are common to various positions and/or instruments.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Mapping portfolio positions to risk factors allows for more accurate pricing (valuation) of the portfolio.
cards.explanation: Mapping is a risk-measurement simplification, not a valuation tool; if anything it is less accurate than full valuation.
cards.originalText: Risk factors allow for more accurate pricing (valuation) of the portfolio.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: One valid reason to map portfolio positions to risk factors is that it is typically easier to stress test the risk factors.
cards.explanation: Stress scenarios are simpler to apply to a small set of risk factors than to every position.
cards.originalText: It is typically easier to stress test the risk factors.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Mapping aggregates risk exposures when it is impractical to treat each position separately.
cards.explanation: This is a first principle of mapping: modelling each position separately would require too many computations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Mapping helps when there is insufficient price history for an investment, such as a recent IPO.
cards.explanation: With no usable price history, mapping to risk factors replaces position-level history.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Mapping helps with positions whose characteristics change over time, such as bonds that move toward maturity.
cards.explanation: As a bond ages, its exposure is re-mapped to the relevant spot yields.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Aggregating many positions into one risk factor is as acceptable for pricing a portfolio as it is for measuring its risk.
cards.explanation: VaR mapping aggregates positions into common risk factors for risk measurement only; prices themselves cannot be aggregated.
cards.correction: Aggregating many positions into one risk factor is acceptable for measuring a portfolio's risk but not for pricing it.

changes.from: is as acceptable for pricing a portfolio as it is for measuring its risk
changes.to: is acceptable for measuring a portfolio's risk but not for pricing it

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: The market value of a commodity forward position is a primitive risk factor in a VaR mapping.
cards.explanation: A position's market value is what gets allocated to risk factors; primitive risk factors are underlying market variables such as spot prices, FX rates and zero-coupon yields.
cards.originalText: The market value of a commodity forward position

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: The spot price of a commodity is a primitive risk factor in a VaR mapping.
cards.explanation: Spot prices are standard primitive risk factors onto which position values are mapped.
cards.originalText: The spot price of the commodity

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: The spot foreign exchange rate is a primitive risk factor in a VaR mapping.
cards.explanation: Spot FX rates are classic primitive risk factors.
cards.originalText: The spot foreign exchange rate

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: A zero-coupon yield is a primitive risk factor in a VaR mapping.
cards.explanation: Zero-coupon yields are the primitive risk factors used for mapping fixed-income positions.
cards.originalText: A zero‑coupon yield

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Measuring the current market value of each position is a step in the VaR mapping process.
cards.explanation: Valuing the current positions is the first step.
cards.originalText: Measure the current market value of each position.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Allocating the market value of each position to one or more common risk factors is a step in the VaR mapping process.
cards.explanation: Allocating each position to common factors is the core step of mapping.
cards.originalText: Allocate the market value of each position to one or more common risk factors.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Summing the allocated exposures across positions for each risk factor is a step in the VaR mapping process.
cards.explanation: Summing by factor produces the vector of risk-factor exposures to which the factor distributions are applied.
cards.originalText: Sum the allocated exposures across positions for each risk factor.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Building a separate model from the full price history of every individual position is a step in the VaR mapping process.
cards.explanation: Mapping works at the risk-factor level; modelling each position's own history is the position-by-position approach that mapping is designed to replace.
cards.originalText: Build a separate model from the full price history of every individual position.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.statement: Aggregating positions into risk factor exposures is acceptable for risk measurement even though prices themselves cannot be aggregated.
cards.explanation: Risk measurement tolerates aggregation to risk factors, whereas pricing needs position-level precision.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-5: VaR Mapping
cards.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
cards.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
