cards.loText: Estimate the impact of different correlations between assets in the trading book on the VaR capital charge.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: When two assets are perfectly correlated, portfolio VaR is strictly less than the sum of the two stand-alone VaRs.
cards.explanation: A strict inequality holds only when $\rho < 1$. At perfect correlation there is no diversification benefit and portfolio VaR equals the sum.
cards.originalText: When the assets are perfectly correlated, expression I is correct.
cards.correction: When two assets are perfectly correlated, portfolio VaR is equal to the sum of the two stand-alone VaRs.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Estimate the impact of different correlations between assets in the trading book on the VaR capital charge.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Under the variance-covariance method, portfolio VaR equals the simple sum of the individual position VaRs only when the returns of the positions are perfectly positively correlated.
cards.explanation: At $\rho = 1$ the cross term is at its maximum and the VaR formula collapses to the sum. Any $\rho < 1$ gives a portfolio VaR strictly below the sum.
cards.originalText: Perfectly positively correlated

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Estimate the impact of different correlations between assets in the trading book on the VaR capital charge.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Under the variance-covariance method, portfolio VaR equals the simple sum of the individual position VaRs when the returns of the positions are positively correlated with a correlation coefficient below 1.
cards.explanation: Positive correlation below 1 still leaves portfolio VaR strictly below the sum of the individual VaRs. Only perfect positive correlation removes all diversification.
cards.originalText: Positively correlated, with a correlation coefficient below 1
cards.correction: Under the variance-covariance method, portfolio VaR equals the simple sum of the individual position VaRs when the returns of the positions are perfectly positively correlated.

changes.from: positively correlated with a correlation coefficient below 1

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Estimate the impact of different correlations between assets in the trading book on the VaR capital charge.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Under the variance-covariance method, portfolio VaR equals the simple sum of the individual position VaRs when the returns of the positions are perfectly negatively correlated.
cards.explanation: At $\rho = -1$ portfolio VaR is the absolute difference of the VaRs, its minimum possible value. The sum is reached at $\rho = 1$.
cards.originalText: Perfectly negatively correlated
cards.correction: Under the variance-covariance method, portfolio VaR equals the simple sum of the individual position VaRs when the returns of the positions are perfectly positively correlated.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Estimate the impact of different correlations between assets in the trading book on the VaR capital charge.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Portfolio VaR is maximised when the pairwise correlations between the returns of the underlying assets are perfectly positive.
cards.explanation: VaR rises with correlation through the cross term and is capped at the sum of the stand-alone VaRs when $\rho = 1$.
cards.originalText: Perfectly positive

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Estimate the impact of different correlations between assets in the trading book on the VaR capital charge.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Portfolio VaR is maximised when the pairwise correlations between the returns of the underlying assets are perfectly negative.
cards.explanation: Perfect negative correlation gives the minimum portfolio VaR, not the maximum. The maximum occurs at perfect positive correlation.
cards.originalText: Perfectly negative
cards.correction: Portfolio VaR is maximised when the pairwise correlations between the returns of the underlying assets are perfectly positive.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain the role of correlation risk in market risk and credit risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Expected shortfall measures market risk for extreme events, typically for the worst 0.1%, 1% or 5% of possible future scenarios.
cards.explanation: Expected shortfall characterises tail risk: it is the average loss beyond the VaR cutoff, at typical confidence levels of 99.9%, 99% and 95%.
cards.originalText: It measures market risk for extreme events, typically for the worst 0.1%, 1%, or 5% of possible future scenarios.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain the role of correlation risk in market risk and credit risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Intersector default correlations are typically lower than intrasector default correlations, so lenders should create a sector-diversified loan portfolio.
cards.explanation: Defaults are more correlated within an industry than across industries, so spreading loans across sectors lowers default correlation and joint-loss risk.
cards.originalText: Intersector default correlations are typically lower than intrasector default correlations, so lenders should create a sector‑diversified loan portfolio.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain the role of correlation risk in market risk and credit risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Intersector default correlations are typically higher than intrasector default correlations.
cards.explanation: Default correlations are higher within a sector than across sectors, because systematic sector factors dominate.
cards.originalText: Intersector default correlations are typically higher than intrasector default correlations, so lenders should create a sector‑diversified loan portfolio.
cards.correction: Intersector default correlations are typically lower than intrasector default correlations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain the role of correlation risk in market risk and credit risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Intrasector default correlations are typically higher than intersector default correlations, so lenders should specialise in a single-sector loan portfolio.
cards.explanation: The relationship is right but the conclusion is wrong: a single-sector book concentrates highly correlated exposures. Lenders should diversify across sectors.
cards.originalText: Intrasector default correlations are typically higher than intersector default correlations, so lenders should specialize in a single‑sector loan portfolio.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain the role of correlation risk in market risk and credit risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Portfolio diversification based on correlations estimated over a period without a crisis will most likely fail in a major economic crisis and lead to losses, because correlations rise sharply in a crisis.
cards.explanation: Correlations are not stable and spike in systemic crises, for example US equity correlations rose from about 27% to over 50% in 2008-09. Diversification benefits disappear when they are needed.
cards.originalText: Portfolio diversification would most likely fail and lead to losses.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain the role of correlation risk in market risk and credit risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Well-diversified portfolios are not affected by a major economic crisis.
cards.explanation: Diversification does not protect in all states, because correlations rise in a crisis and assets fall together.
cards.originalText: The fund managers would not be affected as their portfolios are well diversified.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain the role of correlation risk in market risk and credit risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Creditors benefit by diversifying exposure across industries to lower the default correlations of debtors.
cards.explanation: Default correlations are higher within industries than across them, so cross-industry diversification lowers default correlation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain the role of correlation risk in market risk and credit risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: The default term structure increases with time to maturity for most investment-grade bonds.
cards.explanation: Investment-grade issuers have more time to suffer adverse changes, so the cumulative default probability rises with maturity.
cards.originalText: The default term structure increases with time to maturity for most investment‑grade bonds.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Describe how equity correlations and correlation volatilities behave throughout various economic states.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: Equity correlations estimated from a period of continuous economic expansion will understate the correlations that prevail in a recession, so the diversification benefit in stress is overstated.
cards.explanation: Average equity correlation is lowest in expansions (about 27.5%) and highest in recessions (about 37.0%). A sample with no recession therefore gives estimates below stressed levels.
cards.originalText: The estimated correlations will understate the correlations that prevail in a recession, so the diversification benefit in stress is overstated.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Describe how equity correlations and correlation volatilities behave throughout various economic states.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: Equity correlations estimated from a period of continuous economic expansion will overstate the correlations that prevail in a recession, so the diversification benefit in stress is understated.
cards.explanation: Expansion correlations are the lowest, not the highest, so an expansion-only sample understates recession correlations and overstates diversification in stress.
cards.originalText: The estimated correlations will overstate the correlations that prevail in a recession, so the diversification benefit in stress is understated.
cards.correction: Equity correlations estimated from a period of continuous economic expansion will understate the correlations that prevail in a recession, so the diversification benefit in stress is overstated.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Describe how equity correlations and correlation volatilities behave throughout various economic states.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: Equity correlations are independent of the state of the economy, so the choice of estimation window does not matter.
cards.explanation: Equity correlations are state dependent: about 27.5% in expansions against about 37.0% in recessions, so the window matters.
cards.originalText: Equity correlations are independent of the state of the economy, so the choice of window does not matter.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Describe how equity correlations and correlation volatilities behave throughout various economic states.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: The autocorrelation of equity correlations is a monotonically increasing function of the monthly lag, so higher lags imply higher autocorrelations.
cards.explanation: Autocorrelation of equity correlations decays as the lag lengthens, from about 22% at one month to about 10% at ten months.
cards.originalText: Autocorrelation is a monotonically increasing function of the monthly lag; higher lags imply higher autocorrelations.
cards.correction: The autocorrelation of equity correlations is a monotonically decreasing function of the monthly lag, so higher lags imply lower autocorrelations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Describe how equity correlations and correlation volatilities behave throughout various economic states.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: Mean reversion should be included in equity correlation models.
cards.explanation: Equity correlations show strong mean reversion, at a rate of about 78%, so a model of them should include it.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Describe how equity correlations and correlation volatilities behave throughout various economic states.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: For equity correlations, the Johnson SB distribution fits better than the normal or lognormal distribution.
cards.explanation: The bounded and flexible Johnson SB distribution was the best fit for equity correlations.
cards.originalText: For equity correlations, the Johnson SB distribution is better than the normal or lognormal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Describe how equity correlations and correlation volatilities behave throughout various economic states.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: Equity correlations are highest in recessions, while equity correlation volatility is highest in normal periods.
cards.explanation: Average correlation is 37.0% in recessions, 33.0% in normal periods and 27.5% in expansions, while correlation volatility is 83.0% in normal periods, 80.5% in recessions and 71.2% in expansions.
cards.originalText: correlations are highest for recessions, and correlation volatility is highest for normal periods.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.loText: Describe how equity correlations and correlation volatilities behave throughout various economic states.
cards.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
cards.statement: Equity correlations and equity correlation volatility are both highest in recessions.
cards.explanation: Correlation level peaks in recessions, but correlation volatility peaks in normal periods (about 83.0%) rather than recessions (about 80.5%).
cards.originalText: correlations and correlation volatility are highest for recessions.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: Flexible copula functions became popular around 2000 because they offered a simple way to correlate many assets, such as 100 or more in a CDO, with a single multidimensional function, but they fell out of favour when the 2007-2009 financial crisis began.
cards.explanation: Copulas were attractive for solving a complex correlation problem with simple methods, and their reputation suffered in the 2007-2009 crisis.
cards.originalText: They offered a simple way to correlate many assets (e.g., 100+ assets in a CDO) with a single multidimensional function, but fell out of favor when the 2007–2009 financial crisis began.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: Copula functions fell out of favour because they could only be applied when the marginal distributions were normal.
cards.explanation: A key advantage of a copula is that the marginals can have any shape, because they are mapped to a known distribution. Normal marginals are not required.
cards.originalText: They removed the need to specify marginal distributions, but fell out of favor because they could only be applied when the marginals were normal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: Copula functions allow default correlation to be estimated without any assumptions.
cards.explanation: Copulas still require assumptions, for example about the form of the copula and its correlation input.
cards.originalText: They allowed default correlation to be estimated without any assumptions, but fell out of favor after the 1998 collapse of Long‑Term Capital Management.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: A copula function specifies a single multivariate distribution as a function of various, even unusual, univariate marginal distributions by mapping them to distributions with an accessible form.
cards.explanation: A copula joins separate marginals of any shape into one joint distribution by mapping each to a well-behaved distribution such as the standard normal, where a correlation structure is easy to define.
cards.originalText: To specify a single multivariate distribution as a function of various (even unusual) univariate marginal distributions, by mapping them to distributions with an accessible form.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: The purpose of a copula function is to decompose a posterior conditional distribution into a combination of the prior probability, the likelihood and the marginal probability.
cards.explanation: That describes Bayes' theorem. A copula joins univariate marginal distributions into a multivariate distribution.
cards.originalText: To decompose a posterior conditional distribution into a combination of the prior probability, the likelihood, and the marginal probability.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: A copula function joins n univariate distributions into one multivariate, n-dimensional distribution.
cards.explanation: A copula maps n marginal distributions onto a known distribution and joins them, keeping the original marginals and adding a dependence structure.
cards.originalText: A copula function joins (n) univariate distributions to one multivariate (n‑dimensional) distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: A copula correlates a stock price and its volatility, which allows it to model the equity-implied volatility skew.
cards.explanation: Correlating a price with its volatility describes a stochastic volatility model. A copula joins univariate marginal distributions into a multivariate distribution.
cards.originalText: A copula correlates a stock price (S) and its volatility (σ) which allows it to model equity‑implied volatility skew.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: A copula function is a limiting special case of the Pearson model and analyses only the linear relationship between variables.
cards.explanation: A copula is not a special case of the Pearson model and is not limited to linear relationships. It is used precisely because Pearson correlation is limited.
cards.originalText: A copula function is a limiting (special) case of the Pearson model, such that it only analyzes the linear relationship between variables.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: A copula maps each marginal distribution, percentile to percentile, to a known distribution such as the standard normal, defines a correlation between the mapped variables, and so obtains a joint distribution that preserves the original marginals.
cards.explanation: Correlation cannot be directly and sensibly defined between skewed or heavy-tailed marginals. Mapping them to the standard normal makes it possible, and because the mapping is invertible each original marginal is preserved.
cards.originalText: Map each empirical marginal percentile‑to‑percentile to the standard normal distribution, define a correlation between the mapped variables, and thereby obtain a joint distribution that preserves both original marginals.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: All major copula functions natively ensure that a linear Pearson correlation input accurately describes the actual dependence structure, even if the dependence is dynamic.
cards.explanation: A copula adds flexibility on the marginals, but its dependence parameter is only as good as the correlation input. Pearson correlation measures only linear dependence, and a copula does not guarantee a correct or dynamic dependence structure.
cards.originalText: She used the linear Pearson correlation coefficient as an input to the copulas, and all major copula functions will natively ensure this parameter accurately describes the actual dependence structure, even if the dependence is dynamic.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: A copula approach enables simulation of the entire distribution of loss outcomes, not only the tails.
cards.explanation: A copula yields a full joint distribution that can be simulated across all outcomes.
cards.originalText: The copula approach will enable her to simulate the entire distribution (i.e., in addition to the tails) of loss outcomes.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: Given the same set of univariate marginal distributions, one can test, by simulation, various one-factor or two-factor copula functions.
cards.explanation: The marginals are fixed inputs, so alternative copulas can be run on the same marginals.
cards.originalText: Given the same set of univariate marginal distributions, she will be able to test (i.e., simulate) with various one‑or two‑factor copula functions.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: Copula functions place no requirements on the univariate distributions they join, so skewed or heavy-tailed marginal distributions can be accommodated.
cards.explanation: Each marginal is mapped to a known distribution, so the marginals can have any shape.
cards.originalText: Several of the univariate loss distributions are skewed and/or heavy‑tailed, but copula functions are flexible to this non‑normal variety, as copulas place no requirements on the univariate distributions that are joined.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: Gaussian copulas are often used to quantify the default correlation structure underlying structured credit products.
cards.explanation: The Gaussian copula is the standard and most widely applied copula in finance, notably for the default correlation structure of CDOs and other structured credit products.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: A copula maps a single univariate distribution to multiple multivariate distributions.
cards.explanation: The direction is reversed: a copula maps several univariate distributions into one multivariate distribution.
cards.correction: A copula maps multiple univariate distributions to a single multivariate distribution.

changes.from: a single univariate distribution to multiple multivariate distributions
changes.to: multiple univariate distributions to a single multivariate distribution

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: Fréchet copulas incorporate a single factor and have historically been the most widely applied copulas in the finance industry.
cards.explanation: The Gaussian copula, not the Fréchet copula, has been the most widely applied in finance, and Fréchet copulas are not single-factor copulas.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: A copula maps arbitrary marginal distributions, percentile to percentile, onto a well-behaved joint distribution such as the multivariate standard normal, and the correlation matrix of that joint distribution supplies the correlation structure.
cards.explanation: A copula links marginals of unknown shape to a well-defined joint distribution by percentile mapping, using the correlation matrix as the dependence structure while preserving each marginal.
cards.originalText: The marginals are mapped, percentile to percentile, to a well‑behaved joint distribution $F_{n}$ (such as the multivariate standard normal), and $\rho_{F}$ supplies the correlation structure between them.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: The marginal distributions joined by a copula must themselves be standard normal distributions for the copula to be defined.
cards.explanation: The point of a copula is that the marginals can have any, even unknown, shape. Only the target distribution they are mapped to, such as the standard normal, is normal.
cards.originalText: The marginals $G_{i}(u_{i})$ must themselves be standard normal distributions for the copula to be defined.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Explain the purpose of copula functions and how they are applied in finance.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: Applying a copula changes each variable's marginal distribution so that it takes on the shape of the joint distribution it is mapped to.
cards.explanation: The marginals are preserved. The mapping to a known distribution is used only to define the correlation structure.
cards.originalText: Applying the copula changes each variable’s marginal distribution so that it takes on the shape of $F_{n}$.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Summarize the process of finding the default time of an asset correlated to all other assets in a portfolio using the Gaussian copula.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: To simulate the default time of an asset under the Gaussian default time copula, a Cholesky decomposition of the correlation matrix is used to draw a correlated sample from the multivariate standard normal distribution, which is equated to the asset's cumulative default probability and solved for the default time, repeated over many samples.
cards.explanation: The correlated sample $M_n(\bullet)$ is set equal to $Q_i(\tau)$ and solved for $\tau$. There is no closed form, so the process is repeated by simulation.
cards.originalText: Use a Cholesky decomposition of the correlation matrix to draw a correlated sample $M_{n}(\bullet)$ from the n‑variate standard normal distribution (a value in \[0,1\]), equate it to the cumulative default probability $Q_{i}(\tau)$, solve for $\tau$, and repeat over many samples.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Summarize the process of finding the default time of an asset correlated to all other assets in a portfolio using the Gaussian copula.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: Under the Gaussian default time copula, default times can be computed analytically in closed form from the average pairwise correlation, without simulation.
cards.explanation: There is no closed-form solution, and an average correlation does not preserve the full correlation matrix, so random sampling is required.
cards.originalText: Compute the expected default time analytically in closed form by solving $Q_{i}(\tau) = M_{n}(\bullet)$ once, using the average pairwise correlation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Summarize the process of finding the default time of an asset correlated to all other assets in a portfolio using the Gaussian copula.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: In the Gaussian default time copula, the default dependence between assets is supplied by the correlation matrix of the n-variate standard normal distribution.
cards.explanation: Each cumulative default probability is mapped to a standard normal and fixes only that asset's marginal. The joint dependence is introduced solely through the correlation matrix.
cards.originalText: The correlation matrix $\rho_{M}$ of the n‑variate standard normal distribution, containing the default correlations of asset i with all n assets.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Summarize the process of finding the default time of an asset correlated to all other assets in a portfolio using the Gaussian copula.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: In the Gaussian default time copula, the cumulative default probabilities supply the default dependence between assets, because higher default probabilities imply higher default correlation.
cards.explanation: The cumulative default probabilities are the marginal inputs that set each asset's individual default probability. The dependence comes from the correlation matrix.
cards.originalText: The vector of cumulative default probabilities $Q_{i}(t)$, because higher default probabilities imply higher default correlation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Summarize the process of finding the default time of an asset correlated to all other assets in a portfolio using the Gaussian copula.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: In a Gaussian default time copula simulation of many assets, the correlated sample from the multivariate normal distribution is found through a Cholesky decomposition of the correlation matrix.
cards.explanation: The Cholesky decomposition factors the correlation matrix so that independent normal draws can be transformed into correlated ones, which are then mapped to default times.
cards.originalText: The Cholesky decomposition

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.loText: Summarize the process of finding the default time of an asset correlated to all other assets in a portfolio using the Gaussian copula.
cards.reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
cards.statement: In a Gaussian copula simulation, a company defaults within a given period if its correlated normal draw is below the inverse cumulative normal value of its cumulative default probability for that period.
cards.explanation: The cumulative default probability is transformed to a normal threshold, for example $N^{-1}(1\%) \approx -2.33$, and compared with a correlated normal draw, so default correlation is reflected.
cards.originalText: Simulate a value from a multivariate normal distribution for each company. If the value is less than the inverse cumulative normal distribution value at 1% (‑2.33), default occurs within the first year.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Compare and contrast level and change regressions.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: In regression-based hedging, the level regression regresses the yield of one bond on the yield of the other, whereas the change regression regresses changes in yield on changes in yield.
cards.explanation: The level regression is $y_t = \alpha + \beta x_t + \epsilon_t$ using yield levels; the change regression is $\Delta y_t = \beta \Delta x_t + \Delta\epsilon_t$ using first differences.
cards.originalText: It regresses $y_{t}$ on $x_{t}$ (yield on yield), whereas the change regression regresses $\Delta y_{t}$ on $\Delta x_{t}$.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Compare and contrast level and change regressions.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: In regression-based hedging, the level regression produces biased coefficient estimates, whereas the change regression produces unbiased estimates.
cards.explanation: Both approaches give unbiased and consistent coefficient estimates. The issue is efficiency, because the error terms are likely serially correlated.
cards.originalText: It produces biased coefficient estimates, whereas the change regression produces unbiased estimates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Compare and contrast level and change regressions.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: In regression-based hedging, both the level and the change regression give unbiased and consistent coefficient estimates, but their error terms are likely serially correlated, so the estimates are not efficient.
cards.explanation: Serial correlation in the errors leaves OLS unbiased and consistent but inefficient, in both specifications.
cards.originalText: Both approaches give unbiased and consistent coefficient estimates, but their error terms are likely serially correlated, so the estimates are not efficient.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Compare and contrast level and change regressions.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: In regression-based hedging, both the level and the change regression give efficient estimates because their error terms are independent over time.
cards.explanation: Independent errors are the classical assumption, not the empirical finding. The errors are likely serially correlated, so the estimates are not efficient.
cards.originalText: Both approaches give efficient estimates because the errors are independent over time.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Compare and contrast level and change regressions.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: In regression-based hedging, the change regression gives biased estimates, while the level regression gives unbiased estimates.
cards.explanation: Neither specification is biased. Both give unbiased and consistent estimates that are inefficient when the errors are serially correlated.
cards.originalText: The change regression gives biased estimates, while the level regression gives unbiased estimates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Compare and contrast level and change regressions.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: The problem created by serial correlation in regression hedges cannot be overcome, so one of the two approaches must be selected and some methodological imperfection is inevitable.
cards.explanation: A third approach, a level regression with autoregressive errors $\epsilon_t = \rho\epsilon_{t-1} + v_t$, handles the serial correlation, so the imperfection is not unavoidable.
cards.originalText: The problem created by serial correlation cannot be overcome, and one of the two approaches must be selected, as some methodological imperfection is inevitable

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Compare and contrast level and change regressions.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: If the error terms are independently and identically distributed with mean zero and uncorrelated with the independent variable, the regression coefficient estimators are unbiased, consistent and efficient.
cards.explanation: These are the classical regression conditions.
cards.originalText: If the error terms are independently and identically distributed with mean zero and uncorrelated with the independent variable, then the regression coefficient estimators are unbiased, consistent, and efficient

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Compare and contrast level and change regressions.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: If the error terms are serially correlated, the regression coefficients will not be efficient, although they likely remain unbiased and consistent.
cards.explanation: Serial correlation costs efficiency only, not unbiasedness or consistency.
cards.originalText: If the error terms are serially correlated, the regression coefficients will not be efficient, although they likely remain unbiased and consistent

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Compare and contrast level and change regressions.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: In both the yield-on-yield and the change-on-change regression approaches, the error terms are completely uncorrelated.
cards.explanation: Error terms are likely to be correlated over time in both approaches, so the OLS estimates are unbiased and consistent but not efficient.
cards.originalText: In both cases, the error terms are completely uncorrelated.
cards.correction: In both the yield-on-yield and the change-on-change regression approaches, the error terms are correlated over time.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain why and how a regression hedge differs from a hedge based on a reverse regression.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A regression hedge regresses the yield change of the bond being hedged on the yield change of the hedging instrument and uses the slope as the risk weight, whereas a reverse regression swaps the variables and gives a different hedge amount unless the fit is perfect.
cards.explanation: The two regressions have different dependent variables and hence different slopes. They are reciprocals only when $R^2 = 1$.
cards.originalText: A regression hedge regresses the corporate bond’s yield change on the Treasury’s yield change and sets the risk weight at that slope; a reverse regression regresses the Treasury’s yield change on the corporate bond’s, giving a different hedge amount unless the fit is perfect.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain why and how a regression hedge differs from a hedge based on a reverse regression.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A regression hedge regresses the yield change of the hedging instrument on the yield change of the bond being hedged, while a reverse regression does the opposite.
cards.explanation: The regression hedge regresses the yield change of the hedged bond on that of the hedging instrument. The reverse regression swaps the roles.
cards.originalText: A regression hedge regresses the yield change of the Treasury on the yield change of the corporate bond, while a reverse regression does the opposite.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain why and how a regression hedge differs from a hedge based on a reverse regression.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A regression hedge and a reverse-regression hedge give the same hedge amount, because the slope of the reverse regression is always the reciprocal of the original slope.
cards.explanation: The slopes are reciprocals only when $R^2 = 1$. With an imperfect fit their product is $R^2$, not 1, so the hedge amounts differ.
cards.originalText: Both approaches give the same hedge amount, because the reverse‑regression slope is always the reciprocal of the original slope.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain why and how a regression hedge differs from a hedge based on a reverse regression.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: Reversing the dependent and independent variables changes the OLS slope from $\rho\sigma_Y/\sigma_X$ to $\rho\sigma_X/\sigma_Y$, and these slopes are not reciprocals unless $\rho = \pm 1$.
cards.explanation: The product of the two slopes is $\rho^2$, so they are reciprocals only when the correlation is perfect. This is why regression and reverse-regression hedges differ.
cards.originalText: Reversing the dependent and independent variables changes the OLS slope from $\rho\sigma_{Y}/\sigma_{X}$ to $\rho\sigma_{X}/\sigma_{Y}$, and these are not reciprocals unless $|\rho| = 1$.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.loText: Explain why and how a regression hedge differs from a hedge based on a reverse regression.
cards.reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
cards.statement: A regression and its reverse regression produce the same slope, because the correlation between the two series does not depend on direction.
cards.explanation: Correlation is symmetric, but the slope also depends on the ratio of volatilities, which inverts when the variables are swapped.
cards.originalText: Both regressions produce the same slope because the correlation between the two series does not depend on direction.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Calculate the expected discounted value of a zero-coupon security using a binomial tree.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In a binomial interest rate tree, the branch with the higher rate at the next date is called the up-state and the branch with the lower rate the down-state.
cards.explanation: This is the standard terminology of the binomial tree.
cards.originalText: Up‑state

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Calculate the expected discounted value of a zero-coupon security using a binomial tree.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In a binomial interest rate tree, the value at a node is the average of the present values of the two possible values from the next period.
cards.explanation: The two next-period values, including any coupon, are discounted at the node's one-period rate and weighted by their probabilities, 50% each in the standard tree.
cards.originalText: average of the present values of the two possible values from the next period.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Calculate the expected discounted value of a zero-coupon security using a binomial tree.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In a binomial interest rate tree, the value at a node is the sum of the present values of the two possible values from the next period.
cards.explanation: Summing would double-count the cash flow. The probabilities of one half must be applied, which gives the average of the two present values.
cards.originalText: sum of the present values of the two possible values from the next period.
cards.correction: In a binomial interest rate tree, the value at a node is the average of the present values of the two possible values from the next period.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Construct and apply an arbitrage argument to price a call option on a zero-coupon security using replicating portfolios.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In arbitrage pricing of an interest rate derivative, the replicating portfolio must duplicate the derivative's cash flows in every possible interest rate scenario.
cards.explanation: The derivative's payoff depends on the future rate, so matching it in every rate state forces the replica and the derivative to have the same price by no-arbitrage.
cards.originalText: interest rate scenario

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Construct and apply an arbitrage argument to price a call option on a zero-coupon security using replicating portfolios.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In arbitrage pricing of an option by replication in a binomial tree, the real-world probabilities of up and down moves play no role in the option's price.
cards.explanation: The replica's composition and cost are fixed by the state payoffs and market prices alone, so the true probabilities never enter the arbitrage price.
cards.originalText: None; the arbitrage price does not depend on them

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Construct and apply an arbitrage argument to price a call option on a zero-coupon security using replicating portfolios.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In replicating an option in a binomial tree, the real-world probabilities of an up and a down move determine the number of units of the underlying bond in the replicating portfolio.
cards.explanation: The number of units is a ratio of payoff differences to price differences across the two states, and involves no probabilities.
cards.originalText: They determine the number of units of the underlying bond in the replicating portfolio

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Construct and apply an arbitrage argument to price a call option on a zero-coupon security using replicating portfolios.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In the risk-neutral world, the expected return on all assets is zero.
cards.explanation: In the risk-neutral world all assets earn the risk-free short rate in expectation, not zero.
cards.originalText: The replicating portfolio demonstrates that the expected return on all assets in the risk‑neutral world is zero
cards.correction: In the risk-neutral world, the expected return on all assets equals the risk-free rate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Construct and apply an arbitrage argument to price a call option on a zero-coupon security using replicating portfolios.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The expected discounted value of a bond computed with the risk-neutral probabilities returns the bond's market price.
cards.explanation: The risk-neutral probabilities are chosen so that the expected discounted value of the underlying securities reproduces their market prices.
cards.originalText: The expected discounted value (EDV) of the bond using the risk‑neutral probabilities returns the bond’s market price of \$959.76

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Construct and apply an arbitrage argument to price a call option on a zero-coupon security using replicating portfolios.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Securities whose prices are derived by constructing a replicating portfolio of the underlying securities are called contingent claims and are priced by arbitrage arguments.
cards.explanation: Underlying securities such as zero-coupon bonds have market prices taken as given. Securities whose payoffs depend on them, such as options on bonds, are contingent claims priced by no-arbitrage replication.
cards.originalText: contingent claims, priced by arbitrage arguments

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Construct and apply an arbitrage argument to price a call option on a zero-coupon security using replicating portfolios.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Contingent claims are priced by their real-world expected discounted value.
cards.explanation: Contingent claims are priced by arbitrage replication or, equivalently, by risk-neutral expected discounted value. Real-world probabilities ignore the replication argument.
cards.originalText: contingent claims, priced by their real‑world expected discounted value

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define risk-neutral pricing and apply it to option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Risk-neutral pricing is an efficient way to price many contingent claims under the same assumed interest rate process because the original process has to be modified only once.
cards.explanation: The risk-neutral probabilities are calibrated once to the market prices of the underlying securities. Afterwards any claim on the same process is priced as its expected discounted value.
cards.originalText: the original interest rate process has to be modified only once, and this modification only requires pricing the contingent claim(s) by arbitrage.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define risk-neutral pricing and apply it to option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Risk-neutral pricing is an efficient way to price many contingent claims because the original interest rate process does not need to be modified.
cards.explanation: The true probabilities must be changed to risk-neutral ones once, by calibrating to market prices. Without that change, expected discounted values would not equal arbitrage prices.
cards.originalText: the original interest rate process does not need to be modified, and there is no need to price the contingent claim(s) by arbitrage.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define risk-neutral pricing and apply it to option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The risk penalty implicit in the price of a call option on a zero-coupon bond priced by arbitrage is inherited from the premise that the market price of the zero is less than its expected discounted value.
cards.explanation: Risk-averse investors price the zero below its expected discounted value under true probabilities. Arbitrage transmits that penalty to the option.
cards.originalText: less than its expected discounted value.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define risk-neutral pricing and apply it to option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The risk penalty implicit in the price of a call option on a zero-coupon bond priced by arbitrage is inherited from the premise that the market price of the zero is greater than its expected discounted value.
cards.explanation: The sign is reversed: risk aversion pushes the market price below the expected discounted value.
cards.originalText: greater than its expected discounted value.
cards.correction: The risk penalty implicit in the price of a call option on a zero-coupon bond priced by arbitrage is inherited from the premise that the market price of the zero is less than its expected discounted value.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define risk-neutral pricing and apply it to option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The arbitrage-free price of an option equals its expected discounted value under the risk-neutral probabilities.
cards.explanation: Arbitrage forces the option price to equal its risk-neutral expected discounted value, in both the real and the imaginary economy.
cards.originalText: The arbitrage‑free price of the option equals its expected discounted value under the risk‑neutral probabilities.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define risk-neutral pricing and apply it to option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The price of a security that is priced by arbitrage depends on investors' risk preferences.
cards.explanation: Arbitrage prices are independent of risk preferences, which is why risk-neutral pricing works.
cards.originalText: The price of a security that is priced by arbitrage depends on investors’ risk preferences.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define risk-neutral pricing and apply it to option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The price of an option does not necessarily need to be the same in the real and the imaginary risk-neutral economies.
cards.explanation: The two economies are constructed to give identical prices for the underlying securities, and hence for any derivative priced by arbitrage.
cards.originalText: The price of an option does not necessarily need to be the same in the real and imaginary economies.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define risk-neutral pricing and apply it to option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Risk-neutral pricing uses risk-neutral probabilities as inputs into an expected discounted value.
cards.explanation: The expected-discounted-value form is kept, but the true probabilities are replaced with risk-neutral ones, so the risk penalty is carried by the probabilities while discounting uses the risk-free rate.
cards.originalText: Risk‑neutral probabilities as inputs into expected discounted value

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define risk-neutral pricing and apply it to option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In risk-neutral pricing, risk-neutral probabilities replace the risk-free rate in order to incorporate risk aversion.
cards.explanation: Probabilities do not replace the rate. Discounting stays at the risk-free rate and the risk penalty is absorbed in the probabilities.
cards.originalText: Risk‑neutral probabilities replace the risk‑free rate to incorporate risk aversion

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define risk-neutral pricing and apply it to option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: For risk-neutral pricing of contingent claims to be valid, the real-world expected return on the underlying security must equal the risk-free rate.
cards.explanation: Replication makes the real-world expected return irrelevant. The underlying earns the risk-free rate only under the risk-neutral probabilities.
cards.originalText: The real‑world expected return on the underlying security must equal the risk‑free rate for the method to be valid.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define risk-neutral pricing and apply it to option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In risk-neutral pricing of contingent claims, the risk-free rate is the appropriate discount rate.
cards.explanation: After moving to risk-neutral probabilities, the risk penalty is in the probabilities and the risk-free rate is the correct discount rate.
cards.originalText: The risk‑free rate is the appropriate discount rate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define risk-neutral pricing and apply it to option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: A derivative's price is the same in the imaginary risk-neutral world and in the real world.
cards.explanation: The imaginary economy is built to match the market prices of the underlying securities, so the arbitrage price of the derivative coincides in both worlds.
cards.originalText: The derivative’s price is the same in the imaginary (risk‑neutral) world and in the real world.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Define risk-neutral pricing and apply it to option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The argument that contingent claims can be valued with risk-neutral pricing rests on the no-arbitrage price being invariant to investor risk preferences.
cards.explanation: Replication hedges away the risky factor, so the no-arbitrage price does not depend on how risk-averse any investor is. Pricing in a risk-neutral world therefore gives the same answer.
cards.originalText: The no‑arbitrage price is invariant to investor risk preferences

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Explain how the principles of arbitrage pricing of derivatives on fixed-income securities can be extended over multiple periods.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Valuing a bond with a binomial interest rate tree is done by backward induction, working from the terminal nodes back to the root.
cards.explanation: The bond value at the final maturity nodes is its payoff. At each earlier node the average of the two next-period values, including coupons, is discounted at that node's one-period rate, until the root is reached.
cards.originalText: Backward induction

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Describe the rationale behind the use of recombining trees in option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: A binomial interest rate tree in which the rate rises or falls by constant additive amounts at every node is recombining, because an up move followed by a down move reaches the same rate as a down move followed by an up move.
cards.explanation: When the moves do not depend on the current rate level, the order of up and down moves does not matter, so the nodes merge.
cards.originalText: Yes, because the up‑down and down‑up paths both lead to the same rate (+20 bp from the starting rate)

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Describe the rationale behind the use of recombining trees in option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: A binomial interest rate tree with constant additive moves at every node is non-recombining if its up and down moves are of unequal size.
cards.explanation: Recombination depends on the moves being state-independent, not on their being symmetric. With constant additive moves the up-down and down-up paths reach the same rate even if the moves differ in size.
cards.originalText: No, because the up and down moves are of unequal size
cards.correction: A binomial interest rate tree with constant additive moves at every node is recombining even if its up and down moves are of unequal size.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Describe the rationale behind the use of recombining trees in option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: A binomial interest rate tree is non-recombining whenever the up-state probability differs from the down-state probability.
cards.explanation: Probabilities only set the weights used in pricing. Whether nodes merge depends on the sizes of the moves, not on the branch probabilities.
cards.originalText: No, because the up‑state probability of 60% differs from the down‑state probability of 40%
cards.correction: A binomial interest rate tree is recombining even when the up-state probability differs from the down-state probability.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Describe the rationale behind the use of recombining trees in option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: A non-recombining interest rate tree is the appropriate choice when the volatility or drift of rates is state-dependent.
cards.explanation: State-dependent volatility or drift makes an up move followed by a down move differ from a down move followed by an up move, which forces a non-recombining tree despite its computational burden.
cards.originalText: The volatility or drift of rates is state‑dependent

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Describe the rationale behind the use of recombining trees in option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Analytical tractability is a reason to use a non-recombining interest rate tree.
cards.explanation: Analytical tractability is the advantage of a recombining tree. Non-recombining trees are hard to compute and are used only when state-dependent rate behaviour requires them.
cards.originalText: It is analytically tractable
cards.correction: Analytical tractability is a reason to use a recombining interest rate tree.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Describe the rationale behind the use of recombining trees in option pricing.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: A non-recombining interest rate tree has fewer nodes than a recombining tree.
cards.explanation: A non-recombining tree has 2^n nodes at date n, compared with n+1 for a recombining tree, so it has more nodes.
cards.originalText: It has fewer nodes
cards.correction: A non-recombining interest rate tree has more nodes than a recombining tree.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of reducing the size of the time steps on the pricing of derivatives on fixedincome securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Reducing the size of the time steps in a binomial interest rate tree reduces the computational burden.
cards.explanation: Shorter time steps multiply the number of nodes, so computation time and complexity rise. This is the cost paid for greater accuracy.
cards.originalText: To reduce computational burden
cards.correction: Reducing the size of the time steps in a binomial interest rate tree increases the computational burden.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of reducing the size of the time steps on the pricing of derivatives on fixedincome securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Smaller time steps in a binomial interest rate tree help ensure that a security's cash flows fall near a date in the tree.
cards.explanation: Cash flows rarely fall on six-month dates, so finer steps place each cash flow closer to a tree date.
cards.originalText: To ensure the security’s cash flows are near a date in the tree

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of reducing the size of the time steps on the pricing of derivatives on fixedincome securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Smaller time steps in a binomial interest rate tree increase the granularity of the potential future rates.
cards.explanation: More steps give a finer set of possible future rates than a coarse six-month tree with only two states per step.
cards.originalText: To increase the granularity of potential future rates

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of reducing the size of the time steps on the pricing of derivatives on fixedincome securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Smaller time steps in a binomial interest rate tree increase the accuracy of the model's prices.
cards.explanation: Finer steps approximate the continuous evolution of rates more closely, so prices are more accurate.
cards.originalText: To increase accuracy

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of reducing the size of the time steps on the pricing of derivatives on fixedincome securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Using small time steps in a binomial model makes the model more accurate.
cards.explanation: Reducing the step size improves accuracy and realism, at the cost of more nodes, more calculations and greater computational expense.
cards.originalText: More accurate model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of reducing the size of the time steps on the pricing of derivatives on fixedincome securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Using small time steps in a binomial model makes the model less realistic.
cards.explanation: Finer steps approximate the continuous evolution of rates more closely, so the model becomes more realistic, not less.
cards.originalText: Less realistic model.
cards.correction: Using small time steps in a binomial model makes the model more realistic.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of reducing the size of the time steps on the pricing of derivatives on fixedincome securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Using small time steps in a binomial model makes the computations less complicated.
cards.explanation: Finer steps mean more nodes and more backward-induction calculations, so the computations become more complicated.
cards.originalText: Less complicated computations.
cards.correction: Using small time steps in a binomial model makes the computations more complicated.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of reducing the size of the time steps on the pricing of derivatives on fixedincome securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Using small time steps in a binomial model results in less computational expense.
cards.explanation: More nodes mean greater computational expense, not less. This is the trade-off for the added accuracy.
cards.originalText: Less computational expense.
cards.correction: Using small time steps in a binomial model results in greater computational expense.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the appropriateness of the Black-Scholes-Merton model when valuing derivatives on fixed-income securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Longer bond maturities are one of the reasons why the Black-Scholes-Merton model is difficult to apply to bond valuation.
cards.explanation: The model fails for bonds because of the pull to par (a price ceiling), volatility that declines toward zero at maturity and a random short-term rate. The length of the maturity is not one of these problems.
cards.originalText: Bonds have longer maturities

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the appropriateness of the Black-Scholes-Merton model when valuing derivatives on fixed-income securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The pull to par of a bond's price makes the Black-Scholes-Merton model difficult to apply to bonds, because it places a ceiling on the price while the model assumes no upper limit.
cards.explanation: A bond's price is capped and converges to face value at maturity, which contradicts the model's assumption of an unbounded underlying price.
cards.originalText: Bond price pulls to par

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the appropriateness of the Black-Scholes-Merton model when valuing derivatives on fixed-income securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The tendency of bond price volatility toward zero as maturity approaches makes the Black-Scholes-Merton model difficult to apply to bonds.
cards.explanation: The model assumes constant volatility, but the volatility of a bond's price shrinks toward zero as it approaches maturity.
cards.originalText: Bond price volatility tends to zero as maturity approaches

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the appropriateness of the Black-Scholes-Merton model when valuing derivatives on fixed-income securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The short-term interest rate not being constant makes the Black-Scholes-Merton model difficult to apply to bonds.
cards.explanation: The model assumes a constant risk-free rate, but the short-term rate moves randomly and drives bond prices.
cards.originalText: Short‑term interest rate is not constant

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the appropriateness of the Black-Scholes-Merton model when valuing derivatives on fixed-income securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The Black-Scholes-Merton option pricing model is one acceptable method for valuing fixed-income derivatives.
cards.explanation: The model assumes an unbounded underlying price, a constant risk-free rate and constant volatility, all of which are violated by bonds, so it is not an acceptable method.
cards.originalText: The Black‑Scholes‑Merton option pricing model is one acceptable method for valuing fixed‑income derivatives.
cards.correction: The Black-Scholes-Merton option pricing model is not an acceptable method for valuing fixed-income derivatives.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the appropriateness of the Black-Scholes-Merton model when valuing derivatives on fixed-income securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: A callable bond has a convex price-yield curve at high yields.
cards.explanation: At high yields the call option is far out of the money, so the callable bond behaves like an option-free bond and is convex. Negative convexity appears at low yields.
cards.originalText: A callable bond is assumed to have a convex price‑yield curve at high yields.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the appropriateness of the Black-Scholes-Merton model when valuing derivatives on fixed-income securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: A putable bond has a convex price-yield curve at low yields.
cards.explanation: At low yields the put option is far out of the money, so the putable bond behaves like an option-free bond and has positive convexity.
cards.originalText: A putable bond is assumed to have a convex price‑yield curve at low yields.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the appropriateness of the Black-Scholes-Merton model when valuing derivatives on fixed-income securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The price-yield curve of a bond with no embedded options is convex.
cards.explanation: Option-free bonds have positive convexity at all yields.
cards.originalText: The price‑yield curve for bonds that have no embedded options is convex.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
cards.loText: Evaluate the appropriateness of the Black-Scholes-Merton model when valuing derivatives on fixed-income securities.
cards.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
